entries.title: Core Science: What is RF Safe's position on wireless radiation, and why are the phone safety limits wrong?
entries.question: What is RF Safe's position on wireless radiation, and why are the phone safety limits wrong?
entries.text:
RF Safe's position is that the U.S. phone radiation limits guard against only one thing, heating, and heating is the wrong test for a living body. Biology runs on timing and electrical signaling that heating limits never measure.

The limits. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) set its radio-frequency (RF) limits in 1996. They cap the specific absorption rate (SAR), how fast the body absorbs a phone's radio energy, at 1.6 watts per kilogram (W/kg) over 1 gram of tissue and 0.08 W/kg over the whole body. They rest only on short-term heating in animal experiments: a 4 W/kg threshold, at which trained rats and monkeys stopped doing their tasks, divided by 50 for the public. Phones are then certified on a plastic mannequin head, with body tests allowed up to 2.5 centimeters away from the body.

Why timing matters. Cells run on voltage changes and calcium pulses, and the timing of those signals decides what the cell does. In 1998, Stanford researchers found that "specificity is encoded by the oscillation frequency" of calcium pulses (Dolmetsch, Xu and Lewis, Nature, 1998). Change the timing and you change which genes turn on, with no heating involved. RF Safe's low-fidelity biology hypothesis names the state this produces: the cell keeps working, but with worse timing, more noise, and incomplete recovery. RF Safe's position is that a heating test sees nothing wrong while the cell's reserve for the next stress is being used up. RF Safe calls this upstream disruption. Signaling goes wrong first, and disease can appear later in whichever system is weakest in that person. That is the meta-disease state RF Safe proposes, and it can be tested. RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin framework is its proposed, testable explanation of how this happens.

The evidence. On August 13, 2021, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit found the FCC's 2019 decision to keep its 1996 limits "arbitrary and capricious in its failure to respond to record evidence that exposure to RF radiation at levels below the Commission's current limits may cause negative health effects unrelated to cancer." The court sent that decision back, including on phone testing, children, long-term exposure, and environmental harm (Environmental Health Trust v. FCC). The FCC's comment window to answer the order closed October 22, 2026. The U.S. National Toxicology Program (NTP) found clear evidence of malignant heart tumors in male rats, with heating held under 1 degree Celsius. The Ramazzini Institute found the same tumor at an estimated whole-body dose of 0.1 W/kg, next to the 0.08 W/kg public limit. A 2025 World Health Organization-commissioned review (Mevissen and colleagues) rated the evidence for those heart tumors and for brain gliomas in male rats as high certainty; an August 2026 correction left both ratings at high. The review's dose for a 1 percent added heart-tumor risk has a lower bound of 0.056 W/kg, below the public limit. Melnick and Moskowitz, 2026, in Environmental Health, used the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's standard risk method and found the whole-body limit is 15 to 900 times too high for cancer risk and 8 to 24 times too high for male fertility. In power density, they found the FCC's public limit at 1.8 gigahertz "is approximately 4,200 times higher" than the 1-in-100,000 cancer-risk dose. And in 2023 the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the TheraBionic P1, which treats advanced liver cancer with amplitude-modulated radio signals. The FDA estimated the dose at "100 to 1000 times lower than the amount of electromagnetic fields delivered by cellular phones" and found that it "does not result in any thermal heating." The researchers traced the effect on cancer cells to a calcium channel (Cav3.2). A radio signal too weak to heat tissue is an approved cancer treatment. That is exactly the kind of effect a heating-only limit says cannot happen.

The questions science must ask. Did the timing of the cell's signals change? Did the cell spend extra energy to compensate? Did it recover before the next exposure? Did the result depend on the tissue, the stage of development, or the reserve left? Heating limits ask none of these.

What RF Safe wants changed. Health agencies should set limits based on biology. Public Law 90-602 already requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) to "establish and carry out an electronic product radiation control program designed to protect the public health and safety from electronic product radiation," including from phones. The HHS comment docket closed October 21, 2026. Phones should be tested touching the body. Europe has already adopted a 0-millimeter body-test standard; the older 5-millimeter standard remains valid until March 7, 2028. The United States still allows body tests up to 25 millimeters away. The FCC's own 2019 laboratory tests of popular phones at 2 millimeters found the 1.6 W/kg limit exceeded, including 5.20 W/kg for a Samsung Galaxy J3 and 2.34 W/kg for an Apple iPhone XS. Section 704 of the 1996 Telecommunications Act bars states and localities from regulating wireless facilities "on the basis of the environmental effects of radio frequency emissions" as long as they meet those heating rules. That clause should be repealed so communities can act on health evidence. Indoor data should move to wired connections and Li-Fi, which carries data on light.

entries.title: Core Science: Isn't phone radiation non-ionizing, and therefore harmless?
entries.question: Isn't phone radiation non-ionizing, and therefore harmless?
entries.text:
No. Non-ionizing means phone radiation cannot break chemical bonds directly the way X-rays and gamma rays do. It does not mean it has no effect on the body. Non-ionizing does not mean non-biological.

The "non-ionizing, so harmless" argument assumes the only two ways to harm a body are breaking bonds or heating tissue. Cells also run on electrical and calcium signals, and a weak field can disturb those signals without breaking anything or heating anything.

The evidence shows it:
- The TheraBionic P1 device, approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2023, uses non-ionizing radio waves to treat advanced liver cancer. The FDA says the dose is "100 to 1000 times lower" than what cell phones deliver, with no heating. It acts through a calcium channel, and the FDA tells doctors not to use it in patients taking calcium channel blockers.
- The U.S. National Toxicology Program (NTP) found clear evidence of malignant heart tumors in male rats exposed to phone-type radiation. Its companion tests found significant DNA damage in the brain (the hippocampus of male rats and the frontal cortex of male mice) and in the blood of female mice.
- The International Agency for Research on Cancer, part of the World Health Organization, classified radio-frequency radiation as possibly carcinogenic to humans, Group 2B, in 2011, "based on an increased risk for glioma, a malignant type of brain cancer, associated with wireless phone use."
- In Dr. Henry Lai's 2026 research summaries, 89 percent of the radio-frequency studies on oxidative stress report significant effects. Oxidative stress is chemical damage from reactive molecules, and it is one way DNA gets damaged without ionizing radiation.

Non-ionizing radiation does not need to break DNA directly to damage it. The NTP found DNA damage in exposed animals anyway. RF Safe's framework explains how: the damage starts upstream, with disturbed calcium timing and oxidative stress.

More: https://rfsafe.app/learn/nonthermal

entries.title: Core Science: What does "non-thermal" mean, and why does it matter for phone radiation?
entries.question: What does "non-thermal" mean, and why does it matter for phone radiation?
entries.text:
Non-thermal effects are changes in the body caused by radio-frequency (RF) radiation at levels too low to heat tissue. They matter because the U.S. limits protect only against heating, so any harm that happens without heating is not covered by them.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) limits, set in 1996, are based only on short-term heating. They cap the specific absorption rate (SAR), how fast the body absorbs a phone's radio energy, at 1.6 watts per kilogram (W/kg) over 1 gram of tissue and 0.08 W/kg over the whole body.

Non-thermal effects are real. In 2023 the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the TheraBionic P1, a device that treats advanced liver cancer with an amplitude-modulated 27.12 megahertz radio signal. The FDA's own summary says the dose is "100 to 1000 times lower" than what cell phones deliver and "does not result in any thermal heating." The device acts through a calcium channel in the cancer cells (the Cav3.2 T-type channel). The FDA tells doctors not to use it in patients taking calcium channel blockers. The Ramazzini Institute found a statistically significant increase in malignant heart tumors (schwannomas) in male rats at a whole-body SAR of 0.1 W/kg, barely above the 0.08 W/kg public whole-body limit and far too low to heat tissue. It is the same rare tumor type the U.S. National Toxicology Program found at higher doses. Dr. Henry Lai's running count of the research (updated June 8, 2026) lists 438 radio-frequency studies of oxidative stress, a kind of chemical damage inside cells. 390 of them, 89 percent, found significant effects. At a SAR of 0.40 W/kg or less, ten times below the heating threshold the limits are built on, 110 of 114 studies, 96 percent, found effects.

In 2021 a federal appeals court ruled that the FCC failed to respond to record evidence that radiation below its limits "may cause negative health effects unrelated to cancer." The court also found the FCC had not explained its conclusions on long-term exposure and on "RF pulsation or modulation." A heating limit cannot measure harm that does not come from heat.

More: https://rfsafe.app/learn/nonthermal

entries.title: Core Science: What does RF Safe mean by "upstream disruption"?
entries.question: What does RF Safe mean by "upstream disruption"?
entries.text:
Upstream disruption is RF Safe's term for this: the first thing that goes wrong is the body's signaling, its timing and control, long before any damage can be seen. Disease shows up later, downstream, in whatever system is weakest in that person.

RF Safe's framework lays out the chain step by step. A pulsed, structured wireless signal disturbs the gates that control calcium entry into cells. Calcium and mitochondria, the cell's power plants, fall out of step. That creates oxidative stress, a kind of chemical strain. The cell compensates by changing which genes and defenses are switched on. Regulation becomes less exact. Which disease appears depends on where a person's weakest control system sits.

This is why RF Safe says the same upstream problem can look different in different people: a structural birth defect in one embryo, a developmental difference in another child, or metabolic or immune drift in an adult. The common factor is the upstream loss of signal quality, not one single disease.

It is also why short tests miss the problem. A test that looks only for heating, or only for visible damage after a short exposure, is looking downstream. RF Safe asks for studies that measure the upstream signals directly: calcium timing, recovery, and how the body handles the next stress.

More: https://rfsafe.app/fidelity/

Related: What is low-fidelity biology?; How does wireless exposure throw off calcium signaling?; What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?; What is the meta-disease state, or "one exposure, many diseases"?

entries.title: Core Science: What is biological reserve, and what is the "five-minute problem"?
entries.question: What is biological reserve, and what is the "five-minute problem"?
entries.text:
Biological reserve is the body's spare capacity to handle the next stress and correct small errors. The five-minute problem is RF Safe's name for what short tests miss: a stressed cell protects itself for the next five minutes by spending that reserve, so it looks healthy at rest while its capacity is shrinking.

When a cell is disturbed, it raises emergency defenses: stress proteins such as HSP70, and antioxidant enzymes that clean up chemical damage. In RF Safe's map of the research, this follows the same five steps again and again:
1. Strain: exposure strains calcium handling, the cell's energy and chemical balance, and protective barriers such as the blood-brain barrier.
2. Short-term compensation: defenses rise, so the animal looks normal at rest.
3. Exhaustion: with repeated or long exposure, those defenses fall below normal and barriers open. In chick embryos, a short exposure raised protection against low oxygen, but repeated daily exposures, including a 915 megahertz signal, lowered it, and the stress protein HSP70 fell 27 percent after four days of low-frequency exposure.
4. Failure at the next stress: once reserve is drained, a second challenge hits much harder. Studies report lower seizure thresholds after 30 days of phone-signal exposure (a single exposure did not change them), worse damage to organs from drugs, and more chromosome damage from gamma radiation. In human blood cells, a single 15-minute phone-signal exposure at about 136 times below the international limit, given before gamma rays, raised chromosome damage "significantly more than the sum" of the two exposures.
5. Incomplete recovery: rats exposed to a 900 megahertz signal 2 hours a day for 45 days were given 15 days off. Antioxidant defenses in bone marrow, spleen and thymus did not recover, and rats first exposed at 2 weeks of age were hurt most. Studies from the same group found chromosome damage in bone marrow that had not returned to normal after the same 15-day break.

That is why "the cells looked fine" is not proof of safety. The real questions are how much the cell spent to look fine, and whether it recovered before the next exposure.

Related: Does wireless exposure make other health stresses worse?; Does the body recover after exposure stops?; Who is most vulnerable to wireless radiation?; What questions should science be asking about wireless radiation?

entries.title: Core Science: What is low-fidelity biology?
entries.question: What is low-fidelity biology?
entries.text:
Low-fidelity biology is RF Safe's name for a state in which the body's control systems keep working, but with worse timing, more noise, and incomplete recovery. The cell does not die. It spends more effort to deliver less performance.

In a healthy, high-fidelity state, a calcium signal inside a cell starts, spreads and switches off on time, voltage patterns across tissue hold their shape, and repair brings the cell back to its starting point. In the low-fidelity state, the same systems run with more delay, more false signals and more strain. RF Safe's framework holds that pulsed, modulated wireless signals push cells toward this state by adding timing noise to their electrical and calcium signaling.

The results are mistimed: genes switched on at the wrong time, mistimed pruning of connections in a developing brain, mistimed hormone and insulin release, and more chemical waste from oxidative stress. Because the cell stays alive, a short heating test sees nothing wrong.

Timing loss is measured directly in the research. In RF Safe's map of 1,465 harm-side studies, 124 measure signal timing and rhythm, including brain-wave recordings, heart-rate variability and body-clock genes, and 61 of those are human studies.

Low-fidelity biology is RF Safe's framework for reading the whole body of evidence. It makes testable predictions, and it explains why effects show up in so many different organs.

More: https://rfsafe.app/fidelity/

entries.title: Core Science: What is proven, and what is RF Safe's framework?
entries.question: What is proven, and what is RF Safe's framework?
entries.text:
The harm findings are established facts on the record. RF Safe's framework, S4-Mito-Spin and low-fidelity biology, is the explanation that ties those facts together and makes testable predictions. RF Safe states both directly and keeps them clearly labeled.

Established findings:
- In 2021 the federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. found the Federal Communications Commission's (FCC) 2019 decision to keep its 1996 limits "arbitrary and capricious in its failure to respond to record evidence that exposure to RF radiation at levels below the Commission's current limits may cause negative health effects unrelated to cancer." The court sent the decision back to the FCC. The ruling also covered the FCC's conclusions on long-term exposure, on "RF pulsation or modulation," on testing procedures and on children.
- The U.S. National Toxicology Program (NTP) found clear evidence of malignant heart tumors in male rats.
- A 2025 review commissioned by the World Health Organization rated the evidence for those heart tumors and for brain gliomas in male rats as high certainty.
- Melnick and Moskowitz, 2026, in Environmental Health, calculated that current public limits are 15 to 900 times higher than the exposure tied to a 1-in-100,000 cancer risk in the animal data, depending on hours of exposure per day. Ronald Melnick helped design the NTP study.
- The TheraBionic P1 device, approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2023, treats advanced liver cancer with a radio signal that the FDA says is "100 to 1000 times lower" than what cell phones deliver, with no heating. It acts through a calcium channel, and the FDA tells doctors not to use it in patients taking calcium channel blockers.
- In 2019 the FCC's own laboratory tested phones 2 millimeters from the body, about where a phone sits in a pocket. The FCC wrote that "at a 2 mm separation distance, the FCC RF exposure limits were exceeded." A Samsung Galaxy J3 measured 5.2 watts per kilogram, 3.25 times the 1.6 watts per kilogram limit. That phone was certified at 10 millimeters. 5 of the 8 models tested went over 1.6 watts per kilogram at 2 millimeters. The FCC left these results out of its public report, and they came out only through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request in 2023. Phones are certified at 5 to 15 millimeters from the body, a distance where people do not carry them.

RF Safe's framework explains why these effects happen without heating, why the brain, heart and testes are hit first, and why some studies find nothing. It names the tests that would confirm it.

This is a strength. RF Safe does not need to prove that radiation alone causes one specific disease in every person. The record already shows that non-thermal radiation is a biological stressor, and the limits ignore it.

entries.title: Core Science: What is the meta-disease state, or "one exposure, many diseases"?
entries.question: What is the meta-disease state, or "one exposure, many diseases"?
entries.text:
The meta-disease state is RF Safe's term for a shared, upstream loss of signal quality and reserve that can show up as many different diagnoses. One exposure can lead to many diseases because it degrades the control systems that protect against many diseases, and each person breaks at their weakest point.

Medicine splits illness into separate specialties: cancer, brain, hormones, immune system, fertility. That lets a small effect in any one specialty be dismissed as isolated. RF Safe looked across them. In its map of 1,465 harm-side studies in the rfsafe.app research catalog, 232 studies report harm in two or more organ systems at the same time from a single exposure. For example, in the U.S. National Toxicology Program's study, male rats exposed to a phone signal had malignant heart tumors, brain gliomas and adrenal tumors linked to the exposure, along with DNA damage in the brain. Only 37 of those studies state an absorption rate. Of those 37, 27 found effects at an exposure at or below the 1.6 watts per kilogram local limit, and 8 at or below the 0.08 watts per kilogram whole-body limit. Another 124 studies, 61 of them in people, measure direct loss of timing and rhythm, such as brain-wave coordination, daily heart-rate and blood-pressure rhythms, sleep patterns and daily hormone cycles.

So a link to many conditions is not a weakness in the argument. It is what a timing problem upstream predicts. Brain, heart, testes, pancreas and immune cells all depend on precise calcium timing and heavy energy use. RF Safe's density-gating hypothesis predicts these tissues will respond first, and those are the tissues where the research finds effects.

More: https://rfsafe.app/research

Related: What health effects has RF Safe mapped across the research?; What does RF Safe mean by "upstream disruption"?; What is low-fidelity biology?; What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?

entries.title: Core Science: What questions should science be asking about wireless radiation?
entries.question: What questions should science be asking about wireless radiation?
entries.text:
Science should ask whether wireless signals change the timing of the body's signals, and what it costs the body to cope, not only whether tissue gets hot. The 1996 limits ask one question: did the tissue heat up? RF Safe says that question misses how living things work.

The questions RF Safe demands are:
1. Did the timing or location of the cell's signals change?
2. Did the cell spend extra energy, or switch on protective systems, to keep working?
3. Did it fully recover before the next exposure?
4. Did the result depend on the type of tissue, the stage of development, the person's genes, or the reserve left?

These can be tested now with controlled exposures, live imaging of cells, a second challenge after exposure, and measurements of recovery. RF Safe's framework adds specific tests: measure the shape and timing of calcium signals, test whether the Cyb5b protein is needed for the effect, test whether shielding or calcium-channel drugs block it, and in people, compare results by genotype instead of averaging everyone together.

The authors of a 2025 review commissioned by the World Health Organization wrote that it may be critical to know whether a simple dose-response holds for cancer, and whether the specific absorption rate (SAR), the number the limits are built on, is even the right measure of harm. Those are RF Safe's questions too, and the heating limits do not answer them. In 2021 a federal appeals court found the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had failed to explain its conclusions on long-term exposure and on "RF pulsation or modulation," the signal-timing question at the center of RF Safe's work.

Related: What is biological reserve, and what is the "five-minute problem"?; Why does timing matter more than heat to a cell?; Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?; What is RF Safe's position on wireless radiation, and why are the phone safety limits wrong?

entries.title: Core Science: Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?
entries.question: Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?
entries.text:
Not every study finds an effect, and RF Safe's framework predicts exactly that. Whether an effect appears depends on the signal, the tissue, the person's genes and when you measure, so a study that changes any of those can find nothing even when the effect is real.

Here is what drives a "no effect" result:
- The signal: carrier frequency, pulsing, modulation and polarization all change the outcome. A smooth, unpulsed signal is not the same as a real phone signal.
- The tissue: RF Safe's framework predicts that cells with few voltage-sensing channels and low energy use, such as resting skin cells, respond least. The research fits: one lab found a drop in a growth enzyme in brain support cells at 1.5 watts per kilogram, below the phone limit, while standard laboratory cell lines showed essentially no response.
- The timing: after a short exposure, cells raise their defenses and look normal. Measure too early or only at rest, and you miss the cost.
- The genes: in 2025, a 5G signal changed sleep brain waves only in people with one variant of a calcium-channel gene. Averaging everyone together hides that.

Two studies show how this works. Rao and colleagues found that an 800 megahertz signal at 0.5 watts per kilogram, well below the phone limit, tripled calcium spikes in nerve cells grown from mouse stem cells, from about 5 to about 16 per cell per hour. The effect depended on the frequency, not on the absorbed power, across a tenfold range, and it ran through specific calcium channels. O'Connor and colleagues tested different cells (blood-vessel lining cells, a tumor cell line and rat brain cells) at 900 megahertz and found no change. Different cells, different signal, different result.

Funding also matters. A 2007 systematic review of 59 experiments by Huss and colleagues found that studies paid for only by the telecommunications industry were the least likely to report a significant result. Their odds of doing so were about one-ninth those of publicly funded studies (odds ratio 0.11). The authors concluded that sponsorship should be taken into account when reading these studies.

A "no effect" study does not cancel the studies that found harm. It shows where the boundaries are.

Related: How many studies found no effect, and does that cancel out the studies that found harm?; Does the pulsing or modulation of a wireless signal matter, or only its power?; What is biological reserve, and what is the "five-minute problem"?; What is proven, and what is RF Safe's framework?

entries.title: Core Science: Why does timing matter more than heat to a cell?
entries.question: Why does timing matter more than heat to a cell?
entries.text:
Cells do not read energy alone. They read patterns. A cell decides what to do from the timing of its electrical and calcium signals, so a signal too weak to heat anything can still change what a cell does if it changes that timing.

A calcium signal inside a cell is not just an amount of calcium. How often it fires, how long it lasts and where it happens decide whether the cell releases a chemical messenger, contracts, switches on a gene or changes its metabolism. Experiments have shown that cells decode these calcium patterns. The same total calcium switches on different genes depending on how often it pulses (Dolmetsch 1998), a key brain enzyme responds to the frequency of calcium pulses (De Koninck 1998), and mitochondria, the cell's power plants, turn calcium rhythms into changes in energy production (Hajnóczky 1995).

The research shows that timing, not energy, decides the response. In 1993, Litovitz and colleagues exposed cells to a 915 megahertz signal that roughly doubled the activity of a growth-related enzyme, ornithine decarboxylase. The effect appeared only when the signal's modulation pattern held steady for 10 seconds or longer. When the pattern switched every second, the effect disappeared, even though the cells absorbed exactly the same energy. In 1997 the same lab showed that a digital phone signal raised the enzyme, and that adding a random magnetic "noise" field, weaker than the Earth's own magnetic field, blocked the effect completely. No heating model predicts that adding noise would erase an effect. A timing model does. Separate laboratories found the same pattern. Adding the same kind of noise field blocked a microwave-caused learning loss in rats. In people, a pulsed 900 megahertz phone signal changed sleep and waking brain waves, and the same signal without pulsing did not. In 2026, a study in the journal Cell by Kim and colleagues showed in living mice that a pulsed low-frequency magnetic field switched genes on through a mitochondrial protein, Cyb5b. The authors found the switch was "activated by rhythmic oscillatory calcium dynamics rather than generic calcium influx." The cell responded to the rhythm of the calcium signal, not just to the amount. In 2025, in a double-blind, sham-controlled study, Sousouri and colleagues found that a 5G signal at 3.6 gigahertz sped up sleep spindles, a brain-wave pattern of non-rapid-eye-movement (non-REM) sleep, only in people who carry one variant of the CACNA1C calcium-channel gene. A 700 megahertz signal did not.

The 1996 limits ask only whether tissue heats. They never ask whether a cell's signals stayed on time.

Related: How does wireless exposure throw off calcium signaling?; Does the pulsing or modulation of a wireless signal matter, or only its power?; What does "non-thermal" mean, and why does it matter for phone radiation?; What questions should science be asking about wireless radiation?

entries.title: How It Works: Do power lines and wireless signals affect the body the same way?
entries.question: Do power lines and wireless signals affect the body the same way?
entries.text:
Yes, in an important way. Power-line fields and wireless signals are very different in frequency and energy, yet they produce the same biological changes in living tissue. RF Safe's position is that the carrier does not decide the harm; the disturbed biological timing does.

Power lines create extremely low frequency (ELF) fields, at 50 or 60 cycles per second. Phones and Wi-Fi use radio-frequency (RF) signals at hundreds of millions to billions of cycles per second. Heat cannot be the common factor, because ELF fields from everyday sources are far too weak to heat anything.

What the research shows:
- A 50 hertz field and a 4G phone produced the same pattern of blood and kidney changes.
- In the same human cell line (HL-60), a 50 hertz field and a 900 megahertz field at 120 microwatts per square centimeter, below the U.S. public limit at that frequency, produced the same oxidative DNA damage. Antioxidants (vitamin E, melatonin) blocked both.
- Schwann cells, the cell type behind the heart tumors in the NTP and Ramazzini rat studies, lost the tumor-suppressor protein merlin and switched to a dividing, migrating state under a strong 50 hertz field (0.1 tesla).
- RF Safe's filing to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) describes power-line and wireless fields driving the same inflammatory, liver and kidney markers across a dose gap of more than 6,000 times.
- Across RF Safe's research map, 285 radio-frequency studies and 100 power-line-frequency studies land on the same brain and behavior outcomes.

This matters because both kinds of fields fill homes and schools, and the same biology answers both.

Related: Does the pulsing or modulation of a wireless signal matter, or only its power?; What is Cyb5b, and why does the 2026 Cell study matter?; What health effects has RF Safe mapped across the research?; What does RF Safe mean by "upstream disruption"?

entries.title: How It Works: Does the pulsing or modulation of a wireless signal matter, or only its power?
entries.question: Does the pulsing or modulation of a wireless signal matter, or only its power?
entries.text:
The pattern matters, not just the power. Real phone and Wi-Fi signals are pulsed and modulated, and experiments show that the pulsing can produce effects that the same signal without pulsing does not. The 1996 limits measure only average energy, so they cannot see this.

The evidence:
- Huber and colleagues, 2002, Journal of Sleep Research: a pulse-modulated 900 megahertz field changed brain-wave activity before and during sleep and changed blood flow in the brain. The same field without pulse modulation did not change brain waves. The authors concluded that pulse modulation is necessary to cause the changes.
- Litovitz and colleagues, 1993: a 915 megahertz signal roughly doubled a growth-related enzyme in cells only when its modulation pattern held steady for 10 seconds or longer. Switching the pattern every second erased the effect, though the absorbed energy was unchanged. In 1997 the same lab found that a digital phone signal raised the enzyme, and that random magnetic noise weaker than the Earth's own field blocked it completely.
- Earthworms exposed to a 900 megahertz field for 2 hours had DNA damage at every field level tested, including levels below the U.S. limit. Adding modulation to the same field at the same strength increased the DNA damage.
- Under pulsed 2.45 gigahertz microwaves, cell membranes containing the pigment melanin stiffened at 0.2 watts per kilogram, while the same cells without melanin did not respond.
- A 2011 review of modulation studies by Juutilainen and colleagues pointed to the human brain as the place where amplitude-modulated signals showed specific effects and called for follow-up studies.

RF Safe's framework explains why: cells read rhythm. A field that carries a rhythm can interfere with the rhythms cells use to run themselves.

Related: How does wireless exposure throw off calcium signaling?; Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?; Does wireless radiation affect sleep, brain waves or the body clock?; What does "non-thermal" mean, and why does it matter for phone radiation?

entries.title: How It Works: How does wireless exposure throw off calcium signaling?
entries.question: How does wireless exposure throw off calcium signaling?
entries.text:
Calcium works as a code inside cells, and wireless exposure changes the code. RF Safe's position is that the problem is not just too much or too little calcium, but calcium signals arriving at the wrong time, with the wrong rhythm.

A calcium signal has a frequency, a peak, a rise time, a length and a location. Two signals with the same average amount of calcium can switch on different genes and lead to different cell fates. Cells contain enzymes that read the frequency of calcium pulses, so changing the rhythm changes the instruction.

The research shows calcium responding to fields without heating:
- Human nerve-derived cells (neuroblastoma) exposed to a 147 megahertz signal modulated at 16 pulses per second released calcium at 0.005 and 0.05 watts per kilogram, but not at 0.0005, 0.001, 0.01 or 0.1. The lower level is 320 times below the 1.6 phone limit. The effect comes in windows, which is why harm does not simply climb with dose, and why a heating limit cannot see it. The effect comes in windows, which is why harm does not simply climb with dose, and why a heating limit cannot see it.
- Heart cells exposed to 2.4 gigahertz could not raise their calcium signal when a stress hormone demanded it, and clustered cells then died, with heat-matched controls ruling out heating.
- Calcium is the shared step across many findings: the gate in the membrane and the calcium store inside the cell both respond.

Once calcium timing slips, the cell's power plants, the mitochondria, turn the error into oxidative stress, and the cell's gene program shifts. That is the start of what RF Safe calls low-fidelity biology.

More: https://rfsafe.app/fidelity/

Related: What is the S4 voltage sensor, and how could a wireless signal disturb it?; Why does timing matter more than heat to a cell?; Is there FDA proof that low-level radio waves affect the body without heating?; What does RF Safe mean by "upstream disruption"?

entries.title: How It Works: Is there FDA proof that low-level radio waves affect the body without heating?
entries.question: Is there FDA proof that low-level radio waves affect the body without heating?
entries.text:
Yes. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the TheraBionic P1, a device that treats advanced liver cancer with a low-level radio-frequency signal. The FDA's own summary says the amount delivered to the body is estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times lower than from cell phones and does not cause any heating. A radio signal that changes how cells behave without heating them is a non-thermal effect, approved by a U.S. health agency. The effect is specific to the cell type: the calcium rise occurred "within HCC cells only," meaning the liver cancer cells.

The details:
- Approval: FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption H220001, September 26, 2023, for adults with advanced liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) after first- and second-line treatments fail.
- Signal: a 27.12 megahertz carrier, amplitude-modulated at tumor-specific frequencies, delivered through a spoon-shaped mouthpiece on the tongue, one hour three times a day.
- Dose: a whole-body specific absorption rate of about 1.35 thousandths of a watt per kilogram, reported by Jimenez and colleagues in 2019.
- Mechanism: the signal opens a specific voltage-gated calcium channel, the Cav3.2 T-type channel, in liver cancer cells only. The researchers called this calcium entry "the necessary and sufficient initiating event" of the treatment effect. A drug that blocks T-type channels stopped the effect, and switching off the Cav3.2 gene removed it. The FDA says the device should not be used in people taking calcium channel blockers.
- Results: in a 41-patient study, 14 patients, about 34 percent, had stable disease for more than six months.

The heating-only argument says radio waves at these levels do nothing to the body. A device the FDA approved works at these levels. The questions RF Safe asks follow directly: if a designed signal can change cell behavior through calcium channels, what do the unplanned, constant signals of everyday devices do?

More: https://rfsafe.app/learn/nonthermal

Related: What does "non-thermal" mean, and why does it matter for phone radiation?; How does wireless exposure throw off calcium signaling?; Isn't phone radiation non-ionizing, and therefore harmless?; What is proven, and what is RF Safe's framework?

entries.title: How It Works: What is Cyb5b, and why does the 2026 Cell study matter?
entries.question: What is Cyb5b, and why does the 2026 Cell study matter?
entries.text:
Cyb5b is a protein on the outer surface of the mitochondria, the cell's power plants. A 2026 study in the journal Cell found that cells need Cyb5b to respond to an electromagnetic field, and that the field works by setting off rhythmic calcium waves that switch on a gene. It shows the body has molecular machinery that reads the rhythm of a field.

Kim and colleagues searched the whole genome to find what a cell needs to respond to a pulsed, low-frequency magnetic field. They identified Cyb5b and called it "an essential mediator likely acting as an EMF sensor." When they knocked Cyb5b out, the response disappeared. When they put it back, the response returned. The gene switch was turned on by "rhythmic oscillatory calcium dynamics rather than generic calcium influx," and it worked in living mice.

Why it matters for RF Safe's framework:
- It is direct proof that a field can act on cells through the rhythm of their calcium signals, through a specific molecule. The calcium waves also depended on a voltage-gated L-type calcium channel (Cacna1f), the same family of channels at the center of RF Safe's S4 framework.
- It shows that the rhythm of calcium, not just the amount, is what the cell reads.
- RF Safe's reasoning follows: if a clean, engineered field can write a coherent calcium code through Cyb5b, then the chaotic, pulsed fields of everyday wireless devices are a plausible source of corrupted calcium codes.

The field in this study was a pulsed low-frequency magnetic field, not a phone signal. RF Safe calls for testing whether everyday wireless signals act through the same machinery.

More: https://rfsafe.app/learn/cyb5b

Related: What is radical-pair spin chemistry, and why do red blood cells stack up after phone exposure?; Do power lines and wireless signals affect the body the same way?; What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?

entries.title: How It Works: What is density gating? Why are the brain, heart and testes hit first?
entries.question: What is density gating? Why are the brain, heart and testes hit first?
entries.text:
Density gating is RF Safe's explanation for why some tissues are hit first: the more voltage-sensing channels, mitochondria and field-sensitive chemistry a tissue packs in, and the less spare capacity it has, the sooner it crosses its failure point. The tissues that fit that description are the same tissues where the research finds harm.

In RF Safe's framework, the tissues with the highest density are heart Schwann cells, brain glial cells and neurons, testicular cells that make hormones and sperm, insulin-making cells in the pancreas, and immune cells. RF Safe states the rule as channel density times energy-and-oxidation load, divided by the cell's buffering capacity.

The match with the evidence:
- The U.S. National Toxicology Program (NTP) and the Ramazzini Institute both found malignant heart schwannomas, tumors of heart Schwann cells, in male rats. NTP also related brain gliomas to the exposure.
- A 2025 review commissioned by the World Health Organization rated the evidence for those heart tumors and brain gliomas in male rats as high certainty.
- In RF Safe's map of the research, sperm and testis are the most consistent target: 219 studies, measuring the same things again and again, including testis tissue, sperm movement, sperm count and testosterone. Of the 30 that state an absorption rate, 23 found effects at or below the 1.6 watts per kilogram phone limit, and 10 at or below the 0.08 whole-body limit.
- Brain and behavior make up the largest pathway group: 431 studies, mostly finding memory and learning problems, anxiety-like behavior and nerve cell damage.

This is also why some studies find nothing: low-density cells, such as resting skin cells, are the least likely to respond.

Related: What is the S4 voltage sensor, and how could a wireless signal disturb it?; Does cell phone radiation affect male fertility and sperm?; What does wireless radiation do to the brain?; Does wireless radiation affect the heart and blood?

entries.title: How It Works: What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?
entries.question: What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?
entries.text:
Oxidative stress is chemical damage caused when cells make more reactive oxygen molecules, often called free radicals, than their defenses can clean up. It is the most consistent finding in the research on wireless and power-line fields, and it is how a timing problem becomes physical damage.

In RF Safe's map of 1,465 harm-side studies, oxidative stress is the largest and most connected group: 400 studies. Different labs, tissues and frequencies keep reporting the same markers: fat damage in cell membranes (120 studies), reactive oxygen molecules (104), and the antioxidant enzymes and molecules that fight them (81 and 53). Of the 64 of these studies that state an exposure level, 54 found effects at or below the 1.6 watts per kilogram phone limit, and 24 at or below the 0.08 watts per kilogram whole-body limit.

Other reviews agree. Yakymenko and colleagues found in 2016 that 93 of 100 studies reported oxidative effects. Dr. Henry Lai's running count (updated June 8, 2026) finds that 390 of 438 radio-frequency studies of oxidative stress, 89 percent, report significant effects, including 110 of 114, 96 percent, at a SAR of 0.40 W/kg or less. For power-line and static fields the figure is 319 of 353, 90 percent.

The studies also show where it starts and what stops it. Under radio-frequency fields, the first reactive oxygen comes from the mitochondria, the cell's power plants. About 23 studies in the map name an antioxidant treatment, such as zinc, melatonin or coenzyme Q10, in their titles. When an antioxidant blocks the damage, oxidation is the step carrying it. In rats exposed to a 2.45 gigahertz signal at 3.68 volts per meter, far below the U.S. exposure limit at that frequency, garlic prevented the rise in DNA oxidation in the brain and blood.

More: https://rfsafe.app/research

Related: What is radical-pair spin chemistry, and why do red blood cells stack up after phone exposure?; What does RF Safe mean by "upstream disruption"?; Can non-ionizing wireless radiation damage DNA?; What health effects has RF Safe mapped across the research?

entries.title: How It Works: What is radical-pair spin chemistry, and why do red blood cells stack up after phone exposure?
entries.question: What is radical-pair spin chemistry, and why do red blood cells stack up after phone exposure?
entries.text:
Radical-pair spin chemistry is a kind of chemical reaction whose outcome depends on the magnetic orientation, or spin, of electrons, and weak magnetic and radio fields can change it. RF Safe's framework uses it to explain effects in cells that have no voltage-sensing channels and no mitochondria, such as red blood cells.

Some proteins, including cryptochrome, which helps animals sense the Earth's magnetic field and helps run the body clock, form short-lived pairs of molecules with unpaired electrons. A weak field can shift how those pairs react. In RF Safe's map of the research, 22 studies sit here, mostly in insects, bird embryos, plants and bats, and radio and power-line fields disturbed their magnetic orientation. The strongest test was published in Nature in 2014. European robins could not use their magnetic compass in ordinary university buildings. When the huts were screened against the radio noise from everyday electronics (50 kilohertz to 5 megahertz), they could use it again. When the noise was switched back on, they lost it. The tests were fully double-blind. One chain in the map shows cryptochrome responding to a static field, a 7 megahertz field and a 75 to 85 megahertz field.

Red blood cells are the test case. They have no nucleus, no mitochondria and few voltage-sensing channels, but they are packed with iron-containing hemoglobin, a molecule that takes part in radical chemistry. Brown and Biebrich reported in 2025, in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine, that after an idle but active smartphone sat against a volunteer's knee for 5 minutes, ultrasound of the vein behind the knee showed sluggish flow and the appearance typical of red blood cells stacking together, called rouleaux. The stacking was still visible 5 minutes after she walked around. The authors proposed this as a new way to measure the effect in people.

RF Safe's point is simple: a body has more than one way to respond to a field, and none of them needs heat.

Related: What is Cyb5b, and why does the 2026 Cell study matter?; What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?; S4-Mito-Spin: RF Safe's mechanism framework; Does wireless radiation affect the heart and blood?

entries.title: How It Works: What is the S4 voltage sensor, and how could a wireless signal disturb it?
entries.question: What is the S4 voltage sensor, and how could a wireless signal disturb it?
entries.text:
The S4 segment is the voltage sensor inside the channels that let calcium, sodium and potassium into and out of cells. RF Safe's framework holds that pulsed, polarized wireless signals push charged particles next to the cell membrane back and forth, and that this nudges the S4 sensor at the wrong moments, so the channel's timing goes wrong.

Each S4 segment carries a row of positively charged building blocks, and it moves when the voltage across the cell membrane changes. That movement opens and closes the channel. When the channel opens decides when calcium enters, and calcium timing decides what the cell does next. The idea that the field forces nearby ions to oscillate comes from Panagopoulos and colleagues, who published the model in 2000 and 2002. They showed mathematically how that forced vibration could open and close voltage-sensing channels at the wrong times, and why pulsed fields can be more active than continuous ones.

The calcium-channel link is on the record:
- In RF Safe's map of the harm-side research, 54 studies sit on this channel step. 33 report changes in calcium inside cells, and 28 name a specific channel type.
- Rao and colleagues found that 800 megahertz exposure at 0.5 watts per kilogram tripled the rate of calcium spikes in nerve cells grown from mouse stem cells, from about 5 to about 16 an hour. The effect depended on the frequency, not on the absorbed power, across a tenfold range, and ran through N-type calcium channels.
- The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says the TheraBionic P1 radio-frequency cancer device should not be used in people taking calcium channel blockers. Its published mechanism runs through calcium channels.

RF Safe names the tests: change the channel genetically, measure the sensor's movement directly, and change how many channels a cell has.

More: https://rfsafe.app/learn/nonthermal

Related: How does wireless exposure throw off calcium signaling?; What is density gating? Why are the brain, heart and testes hit first?; S4-Mito-Spin: RF Safe's mechanism framework; What is low-fidelity biology?

entries.title: Health Effects: Can non-ionizing wireless radiation damage DNA?
entries.question: Can non-ionizing wireless radiation damage DNA?
entries.text:
Yes. Wireless radiation cannot break DNA directly the way X-rays do, but studies show DNA damage through oxidative stress and through interference with DNA repair.

The evidence:
- The U.S. National Toxicology Program reported a significant increase in DNA damage in the hippocampus, a memory center of the brain, of male rats exposed to phone signals, measured by the comet test, which detects broken DNA strands (Smith-Roe and colleagues, 2020).
- Workers exposed to radar: when their blood cells were challenged with a standard chemical that damages DNA, they broke almost three times as often as controls' cells.
- Below the limits, before birth: exposure during pregnancy at 0.066 watts per kilogram in the uterus was followed by DNA damage in offspring kidney and testis months later.
- Repair blocked: phone signals blocked the formation of DNA repair sites in human white blood cells for up to 72 hours.
- People differ: blood cells from nine healthy donors differed widely in how much DNA damage an 1,800 megahertz signal caused, and the difference repeated three months later. Who is vulnerable is a lasting trait.
- In RF Safe's map, the cancer studies connect to the rest of the research through oxidative stress and DNA-damage markers.

RF Safe's point: you do not need ionizing radiation to damage DNA. Oxidative stress does it, and so does a repair system that has been slowed down.

Related: Isn't phone radiation non-ionizing, and therefore harmless?; What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?; Does wireless exposure make other health stresses worse?; Who is most vulnerable to wireless radiation?

entries.title: Health Effects: Can phone radiation affect hearing or the thyroid?
entries.question: Can phone radiation affect hearing or the thyroid?
entries.text:
Yes. Studies found the ear people hold their phone to hears worse than their other ear, and studies found thyroid hormones staying low even after the gland itself looked normal again.

Hearing:
- In people, years of daily phone use at handset levels below the local limit left the phone ear with higher hearing thresholds, meaning poorer hearing, than the same person's other ear, worst at high frequencies (Das 2017; Velayutham 2014).
- A phone held to the ear for minutes slowed the hearing nerve and brainstem signal on that side, and it came back within minutes. The short effect recovers; years of use leave a mark.
- Rats exposed to Wi-Fi from conception to puberty had raised hearing thresholds.

Thyroid:
- Under three months of a 50 hertz field from birth, the rat thyroid flattened. Three weeks after the field was switched off, its structure was back to normal, but the thyroid hormones T3 and T4 were still low.
- 5G exposure at about 0.06 percent of the U.S. limit flattened the young rat thyroid in two weeks.

This is the pattern RF Safe's framework predicts: tissue that looks normal under the microscope while its function stays low. Use speakerphone or an air-tube headset to keep the phone away from your ear.

Related: Does the body recover after exposure stops?; What is low-fidelity biology?; What else can I do besides a case?; What does wireless radiation do to the brain?; Can phone use cause ringing in the ears (tinnitus)?

entries.title: Health Effects: Can phone use cause headaches?
entries.question: Can phone use cause headaches?
entries.text:
Yes. Studies of mobile phone use have found higher odds of headache, including in children. RF Safe cannot diagnose or treat your headache. If you have a health concern, see a medical professional. Then use the study pages below. Each page has a summary, and you can click through to the original paper.

Key studies:
- A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 studies found a pooled odds ratio of 1.30, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 1.21 to 1.39, for headache associated with mobile phone use. The odds were higher still when call time was more than 100 minutes a week, an odds ratio of 1.41, with a confidence interval from 1.22 to 1.61. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000913-mobile-phone-electromagnetic-radiation-and-the-risk-of-headache-a-systematic-review-an
- A 2017 meta-analysis of 7 studies found 38 percent higher odds of headache in mobile phone users than in non-users, an odds ratio of 1.38 (95 percent confidence interval 1.18 to 1.61), and higher odds with longer and more frequent daily calls. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/002324-mobile-phone-use-and-the-risk-of-headache-a-systematic-review-and-meta-analysis-of-cro
- A 2012 study of 52,680 children found that both prenatal and postnatal cell phone exposure was linked to higher odds of migraines, an odds ratio of 1.30, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 1.01 to 1.68, and of headache-related symptoms, an odds ratio of 1.32, with a confidence interval from 1.23 to 1.40, compared with no exposure. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/003139-prenatal-and-postnatal-cell-phone-exposures-and-headaches-in-children
- A 2015 nationwide survey of 2,042 children aged 11 to 15 in Taiwan found that mobile phone use in the past month was linked to higher odds of headaches or migraine, an adjusted odds ratio of 1.42, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 1.12 to 1.81. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/004674-mobile-phone-use-and-health-symptoms-in-children
- A 2006 study of people living near mobile phone base stations found that some self-reported symptoms were related to the measured power density in bedrooms, and that the strongest of those links was for headaches. The highest bedroom reading was 4.1 milliwatts per square meter, about one-thousandth of the international guideline level at 900 megahertz. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/005134-subjective-symptoms-sleeping-problems-and-cognitive-performance-in-subjects-living-nea
- A 1998 article in Environmental Health Perspectives argued that headaches reported with handheld cellular telephone use are real and may be due to the phone's emissions. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/002434-headaches-from-cellular-telephones-are-they-real-and-what-are-the-implications

The Cohort Study of Mobile Phone Use and Health (COSMOS) also looked at headaches, and its own first estimates showed higher odds of weekly headache in the heaviest callers: 1.21 (1.02 to 1.43) in Sweden and Finland after adjustment for age, sex and country, falling to 1.13 (0.95 to 1.34) only after further adjustment for painkiller use, sleep disturbance, depression and general health; and 1.10 (1.01 to 1.22) in the Netherlands and the United Kingdom before texting was added to the model. Its papers do not clear radio-frequency exposure, and they do not cancel the studies above. See the COSMOS answer for who paid for that work, what it found, and why call time is not dose.

RF Safe does not claim that phone radiation caused your headache. RF Safe's low-fidelity biology hypothesis holds that reduced biological fidelity raises the risk of error, and its S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis proposes how that happens. The heating-only limits do not protect against non-thermal effects. To cut exposure during calls, use speakerphone or an air-tube headset and keep the phone off your head.

More studies: https://rfsafe.app/research?q=headache

Related: Personal health questions and diagnosis; What is wrong with COSMOS (Feychting, 2024)?; Nervous system (brain and nerves, neurological): What does the research show?; Is speakerphone or a headset better for calls?

entries.title: Health Effects: Can phone use cause ringing in the ears (tinnitus)?
entries.question: Can phone use cause ringing in the ears (tinnitus)?
entries.text:
Yes. Studies have found poorer hearing in the ear people hold their phone to. Case reports describe ringing in the ears (tinnitus) beginning after a 5G base station went up nearby, and easing after people moved to lower exposure. Even the industry-co-funded COSMOS study's own table shows higher odds of tinnitus in heavier callers. RF Safe cannot diagnose or treat tinnitus or hearing loss. If you have a health concern, see a medical professional. Then use the study pages below. Each page has a summary, and you can click through to the original paper.

Key studies:
- A 2023 case report describes tinnitus, sleeplessness and other symptoms of the microwave syndrome starting shortly after a 5G base station was installed 5 meters above a couple's bedroom, with most symptoms easing within days after they moved. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000587-case-report-the-microwave-syndrome-after-installation-of-5g-emphasizes-the-need-for-pr
- A 2024 summary of seven Swedish case reports, covering 16 people, lists tinnitus among the symptoms that began after nearby 4G and 5G base stations went up, and that eased when people reduced their exposure. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000114-summary-of-seven-swedish-case-reports-on-the-microwave-syndrome-associated-with-5g-rad
- In 100 mobile phone users, high-frequency hearing tests showed a statistically significant loss in the ear they used for the phone, compared with their other ear. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/003185-high-frequency-hearing-loss-among-mobile-phone-users
- In medical students who had used a mobile phone for 5 years, the phone ear had significantly higher air-conduction and bone-conduction hearing thresholds than the other ear, including at 2, 4 and 8 kilohertz (kHz). Higher thresholds mean poorer hearing. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/001314-a-study-on-the-effect-of-prolonged-mobile-phone-use-on-pure-tone-audiometry-thresholds
- In mostly right-handed mobile phone users, 21 percent failed a distortion-product otoacoustic emission test, a check of inner-ear hair-cell function, and 6 kHz was the frequency most often affected. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/001922-mobile-phone-users-and-its-effect-of-hearing-in-terms-of-distortion-product-otoacousti
- In human ear-canal hair-follicle cells, DNA damage markers were higher in mobile phone users than in controls, and the damage rose with more daily phone use. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/002116-mobile-phone-emf-induced-dna-damage-in-human-ear-canal-hair-follicle-cells
- In rats exposed to 2.45 gigahertz (GHz) Wi-Fi-band microwaves before birth and for 45 days after, auditory brainstem response thresholds, a test of the hearing pathway, rose at 5 volts per meter and higher, and cell-death markers in the cochlea, the hearing organ, rose at 10 and 15 volts per meter. The U.S. public limit at that frequency works out to about 61 volts per meter. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000213-effect-of-2-45-ghz-microwave-radiation-on-the-inner-ear-a-histopathological-study-on-2

A 2019 COSMOS paper reported no link between operator-recorded call time and self-reported tinnitus or hearing loss in Swedish and Finnish users, yet its own table shows 19 percent higher odds of tinnitus in people between the 75th and 90th percentiles of call time (odds ratio 1.19, 95 percent confidence interval 1.03 to 1.38). It used questionnaires, not hearing tests, and call time is not absorbed dose. That paper's own conflict-of-interest statement says one of its authors, Maria Feychting, "is vice chairman of the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection." See the COSMOS answer for who paid for that work and why RF Safe flags it.

RF Safe does not claim that phone radiation caused your tinnitus or hearing change. RF Safe's low-fidelity biology hypothesis holds that reduced biological fidelity raises the risk of error, and its S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis proposes how that happens. To cut exposure, use speakerphone or an air-tube headset and keep the phone off your ear.

More studies: https://rfsafe.app/research?q=tinnitus
https://rfsafe.app/research?system=sensory-auditory

Related: Personal health questions and diagnosis; Can phone radiation affect hearing or the thyroid?; Ears (sensory system, auditory): What does the research show?; What is wrong with COSMOS (Feychting, 2024)?; Is speakerphone or a headset better for calls?

entries.title: Health Effects: Can phones or Wi-Fi disrupt sleep or the sleep hormone melatonin?
entries.question: Can phones or Wi-Fi disrupt sleep or the sleep hormone melatonin?
entries.text:
Yes. Studies in people show changes in sleep brain waves under phone-type signals, and the research shows the body clock hit at several levels, including the sleep hormone melatonin. RF Safe cannot diagnose or treat insomnia or other sleep problems. If you have a health concern, see a medical professional. Then use the study pages below. Each page has a summary, and you can click through to the original paper.

Key studies:
- A 2025 double-blind, sham-controlled study of 34 people found that 30 minutes of a 5G signal at 3.6 gigahertz (GHz) before sleep made sleep spindles, a brain-wave pattern of non-rapid-eye-movement sleep, run faster, but only in people who carry one variant of the CACNA1C calcium-channel gene. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/002603-5g-radio-frequency-electromagnetic-field-effects-on-the-human-sleep-electroencephalogr
- In 2002, 30 minutes of a pulse-modulated 900 megahertz (MHz) field changed blood flow in the brain and increased brain-wave power before sleep and during stage 2 sleep. The same field without pulsing did not enhance waking or sleep brain-wave power. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/005288-electromagnetic-fields-such-as-those-from-mobile-phones-alter-regional-cerebral-blood
- In a 2024 double-blind crossover pilot study of 12 healthy adults, a 2.45 GHz baby monitor running at night made self-reported sleep quality significantly worse than a sham (inactive) monitor, and it increased brain-wave power during non-rapid-eye-movement sleep. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000029-does-radiofrequency-radiation-impact-sleep-a-double-blind-randomised-placebo-controlle
- In mice, prolonged 2.4 GHz exposure modulated by 100-hertz square pulses, at a non-heating output, increased time awake and cut both kinds of sleep. The same average output without the pulsing had little effect. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000684-specific-electromagnetic-radiation-in-the-wireless-signal-range-increases-wakefulness

A 2020 COSMOS paper found no link between operator-recorded call time and most sleep measures in Swedish and Finnish users, though insomnia was more common in the highest tenth of call time, an odds ratio of 1.24 (1.03 to 1.51). Even after the authors reweighted the data by network type, insomnia stayed significantly higher at 24 to 84 weighted minutes a week, an odds ratio of 1.17 (1.01 to 1.36). Call time is not dose, follow-up was 4 years, and industry money went into that work. That paper's own conflict-of-interest statement says one of its authors, Maria Feychting, "is vice chairman of the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection." See the COSMOS answer for the numbers and the limits.

The approved answer on sleep, brain waves and the body clock also covers melatonin, including a study of utility workers who used a cell phone more than 25 minutes a day and had lower nighttime melatonin breakdown products. Browse the melatonin and sleep lists for those records.

RF Safe does not claim that phone radiation caused your sleep problem. RF Safe's low-fidelity biology hypothesis holds that reduced biological fidelity raises the risk of error, and its S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis proposes how that happens. Keep phones off the body at night, and use airplane mode or power the phone down in bedrooms.

More studies: https://rfsafe.app/research?q=sleep
https://rfsafe.app/research?q=melatonin

Related: Personal health questions and diagnosis; Does wireless radiation affect sleep, brain waves or the body clock?; How can I cut my exposure at night and in the bedroom?; What is wrong with COSMOS (Feychting, 2024)?; Hormone glands (endocrine system): What does the research show?

entries.title: Health Effects: Can wireless exposure affect children who were never exposed themselves?
entries.question: Can wireless exposure affect children who were never exposed themselves?
entries.text:
Yes, in animal studies. Offspring that were never exposed showed effects from their parents' exposure, and fertility under continued exposure held for a while and then fell across breeding cycles.

The evidence:
- Young fish bred from Wi-Fi-exposed adults were malformed more often the longer their parents had been exposed (Mehta 2025, zebrafish).
- Sons of 5G-exposed father mice were anxious and had poorer sperm (Zhang 2026).
- After father mice were exposed to an electromagnetic pulse, the sex ratio of their offspring was still shifted in matings 21 and 28 days after the exposure ended (Li 2017).
- In male mice exposed to 900 megahertz for 35 days, DNA damage in sperm-forming cells was still raised 35 days after exposure stopped (Pandey 2017).
- In RF Safe's terms, biological reserve is spent across breeding cycles and generations. Under continued exposure, mice had fewer young with each mating until they became irreversibly infertile, and in worms the oxidative marker moved generations before reproduction failed.

RF Safe's reading: the parent carries the exposure forward through damaged sperm and eggs and through changes in how genes are read. This is part of why RF Safe treats reproductive-age adults, not only children, as a group whose exposure matters.

For anyone planning a family, RF Safe recommends keeping the phone out of front pockets and off the belly, using speakerphone or an air-tube headset for calls, and keeping phones out of the bedroom at night or in airplane mode.

Related: Does cell phone radiation affect male fertility and sperm?; Does wireless radiation affect female fertility or pregnancy?; Does the body recover after exposure stops?

entries.title: Health Effects: Can wireless radiation affect metabolism, blood sugar or insulin?
entries.question: Can wireless radiation affect metabolism, blood sugar or insulin?
entries.text:
Yes. The research shows exposure shifting blood sugar and insulin, and RF Safe's framework explains why: insulin is released in timed pulses driven by calcium, so a timing disturbance hits the pancreas directly.

The evidence:
- In RF Safe's map, 186 studies cover metabolism. 35 report changes in blood sugar and insulin, along with liver and thyroid changes, and 84 also found oxidative stress. Of the 24 that state an exposure level, 17 found effects at or below the 1.6 watts per kilogram phone limit and 5 at or below the 0.08 watts per kilogram whole-body limit.
- The insulin-making islets answer the first call and fail the second. A single 15-minute exposure to a 60 hertz magnetic field, the frequency of power lines, raised the first insulin peak and erased the second. In a separate study, 45 days of 2.45 gigahertz Wi-Fi left islets unable to answer a sugar challenge, with their antioxidants spent.
- A body already under strain fails first: diabetic rats exposed below the U.S. whole-body limit showed the larger oxidative shift, in brain, blood, fat, pancreas, muscle and bone.
- Metabolism is the section most tied to other body systems: 112 of 186 metabolic studies, 60 percent, also report an effect in another system, most often the brain.

RF Safe's chain: disturbed calcium timing, then distorted insulin pulses, then poorer sugar uptake and more sugar released by the liver, then drift toward metabolic syndrome. The first failure is a timing error, not cell death.

Related: How does wireless exposure throw off calcium signaling?; Who is most vulnerable to wireless radiation?; What is the meta-disease state, or "one exposure, many diseases"?; What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?

entries.title: Health Effects: Does cell phone radiation affect male fertility and sperm?
entries.question: Does cell phone radiation affect male fertility and sperm?
entries.text:
Yes. Sperm and the testes are the most consistent target in the entire body of research RF Safe has mapped, and a 2026 risk assessment found the U.S. whole-body limit is 8 to 24 times too high to protect male reproductive health.

The evidence:
- In RF Safe's map, 219 studies cover reproduction. They keep measuring the same things: damage to testis tissue (75 studies), sperm movement (36), sperm count (29), and testosterone and related hormones (32). 93 of them also found oxidative stress in the testis. Of the 30 that state an exposure level, 23 found effects at or below the 1.6 watts per kilogram phone limit and 10 at or below the 0.08 watts per kilogram whole-body limit.
- The corrected systematic review of animal studies commissioned by the World Health Organization rated a reduced pregnancy rate, when exposed males were mated, as high certainty: the odds of a failed pregnancy were 1.68 times higher.
- Melnick and Moskowitz, 2026, in Environmental Health, found the whole-body limit is 8 to 24 times higher than levels that protect male reproductive health.
- The barrier that protects developing sperm opens after a duration threshold, using the same sealing proteins that fail in the blood-brain barrier.
- Damage can pass on: sons of 5G-exposed father mice were anxious and had poorer sperm, and in male mice, DNA damage in sperm-forming cells was still raised 35 days after a 900 megahertz exposure stopped.

Phones are tested with a gap from the body, but many men carry them in a front pocket against the body. RF Safe's advice: keep the phone out of your pocket, or if you must, use a case with the shielded flap toward your body and turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

Related: What is density gating? Why are the brain, heart and testes hit first?; Can wireless exposure affect children who were never exposed themselves?; What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?; TruthCase and anti-radiation cases: what works

entries.title: Health Effects: Does the body recover after exposure stops?
entries.question: Does the body recover after exposure stops?
entries.text:
Often only partly. Short effects can reverse within minutes or hours, but after long or early exposure, the research shows damage that outlasts the exposure. RF Safe's position is that recovery is the missing measurement in safety testing.

The evidence:
- After 45 days of exposure, 15 days off did not restore antioxidant defenses in bone marrow and immune tissue, and young rats recovered least.
- In animals, six weeks of daily phone calls lowered heart rate variability and raised blood pressure, with nothing back after two weeks off.
- Below the limits, harm can peak after exposure ends: at 25 percent of the U.S. limit, a stress hormone peaked a month after a 4-month 5G exposure ended, while behavior looked normal.
- Thyroid structure returned to normal three weeks after a field was switched off, while thyroid hormones stayed low.
- Some losses cannot be rebuilt: fewer egg follicles after prenatal exposure, and nerve stem-cell pools disturbed into adulthood.
- Under continued exposure near an antenna park, at 0.17 to 1.05 microwatts per square centimeter, far below the U.S. limit, mice had fewer young with each of five matings until they became irreversibly infertile (Magras and Xenos, 1997). In water fleas, offspring recovered once exposure stopped.

So cutting back matters, and the earlier the better. Short-term effects reverse when the exposure stops. Developmental losses do not. That is why RF Safe puts children and pregnancy first.

Related: What is biological reserve, and what is the "five-minute problem"?; Does wireless radiation affect female fertility or pregnancy?; Can wireless exposure affect children who were never exposed themselves?; Children and cell phones

entries.title: Health Effects: Does wireless exposure make other health stresses worse?
entries.question: Does wireless exposure make other health stresses worse?
entries.text:
Yes. One of the clearest patterns in the research is that an exposure that shows little by itself makes the next stress hit much harder. RF Safe calls this the second hit, and it is why testing the exposure alone, at rest, misses the harm.

The evidence:
- More than added: an exposure that showed nothing on its own more than doubled the damage from a chemical that causes birth defects. A 15-minute phone exposure, about 136 times below international limits, made chromosome damage from gamma rays greater than the two added together (Panagopoulos and colleagues, 2024).
- Cancer: in mice exposed from before birth to a cancer-causing chemical, lifelong 3G-type phone signals raised lung and liver tumors and lymphomas. The authors wrote that many of these effects 'were seen at low to moderate exposure levels (0.04 and 0.4 W/kg SAR), thus well below exposure limits for the users of mobile phones.' This replicated an earlier study by a different team.
- Living animals: exposure lowered seizure thresholds and worsened stomach, heart and immune challenges, and in the one test of timing, only after repeated exposure.
- Infection: long-exposed mice cleared an infection worse and died more from it.
- Why: in power-line-frequency studies, the field raises the output of reactive molecules from a source already running, such as a drug, an enzyme or a metal, and a treatment that removes superoxide brings the combined damage back down. In radio-frequency studies, an antioxidant given with 2.45 gigahertz exposure at 3.68 volts per meter protected the brain from oxidative DNA damage.

Everyone lives with second hits: medications, infections, pollution, poor sleep. RF Safe's position is that safety limits must be tested against real life, where exposures combine.

Related: What is biological reserve, and what is the "five-minute problem"?; Does wireless radiation affect the immune system?; Who is most vulnerable to wireless radiation?; Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?

entries.title: Health Effects: Does wireless radiation affect female fertility or pregnancy?
entries.question: Does wireless radiation affect female fertility or pregnancy?
entries.text:
Yes, the research shows effects on the ovaries and on babies exposed before birth, and some of those effects last long after the exposure ends. RF Safe's position is that pregnancy is the time to reduce exposure the most, because development happens once.

The evidence:
- Egg supply: three separate labs found fewer primordial ovarian follicles, the lifetime stock of eggs, after exposure before birth, with more loss after longer exposure. That loss is banked at birth and paid out later.
- Below the limits: exposure to 3.5 gigahertz during pregnancy, at a peak specific absorption rate in the uterus of 0.066 watts per kilogram, with no exposure after birth, was followed by DNA damage in the offspring's kidney at 6 months and testis at 12 months (Gelenli Dolanbay and colleagues, Histochemistry and Cell Biology, 2026).
- Timing decides the target: the same 900 megahertz exposure harmed different nerve structures depending on whether it happened in mid or late pregnancy.
- In the U.S. National Toxicology Program study, rat pups exposed in the womb and during nursing weighed less at the higher doses.
- In RF Safe's map, 322 studies involve pregnancy and early life, and 39 of them are rated high or moderate quality.

What RF Safe recommends during pregnancy: keep the phone off the belly and body, use speakerphone or an air-tube headset, keep the phone out of the bed at night, turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth when not needed, and prefer wired internet at home.

Related: Can wireless exposure affect children who were never exposed themselves?; Does the body recover after exposure stops?; Children and cell phones; Who is most vulnerable to wireless radiation?; If I'm pregnant, should I reduce EMF and wireless exposure?

entries.title: Health Effects: Does wireless radiation affect sleep, brain waves or the body clock?
entries.question: Does wireless radiation affect sleep, brain waves or the body clock?
entries.text:
Yes. Studies in people show changes in sleep brain waves under phone-type signals, and the research shows the body clock hit at several levels, including the sleep hormone melatonin and the genes that keep daily time.

The evidence:
- Sousouri and colleagues, 2025, NeuroImage: in a double-blind, sham-controlled study of 34 people, 30 minutes of a 5G signal at 3.6 gigahertz before sleep made sleep spindles, a brain-wave pattern of non-rapid-eye-movement (non-REM) sleep, run faster. The effect appeared only in people who carry one variant of the CACNA1C calcium-channel gene. The authors say this implicates the L-type calcium channel in the body's response to radio-frequency fields.
- Huber and colleagues, 2002: a pulse-modulated 900 megahertz field changed brain waves before and during sleep. The same field without pulsing did not.
- Burch and colleagues, 2002: utility workers who used a cell phone more than 25 minutes a day had lower nighttime melatonin breakdown products than workers who did not use one.
- RF Safe's mechanism map shows the clock hit at several levels: daily hormone rhythms, core clock genes and the cryptochrome gene. Melatonin is both a target and a shield: exposure lowers it, and losing it removes a protection that works.
- In RF Safe's map, 352 studies involve a developmental window or the body clock, the group with the most high- or moderate-grade studies.

Sleep is when the body repairs and resets. RF Safe's advice: keep phones off the body at night, and use airplane mode or power the phone down in bedrooms.

Related: Does the pulsing or modulation of a wireless signal matter, or only its power?; What does wireless radiation do to the brain?; Who is most vulnerable to wireless radiation?; What else can I do besides a case?; Can phones or Wi-Fi disrupt sleep or the sleep hormone melatonin?

entries.title: Health Effects: Does wireless radiation affect the heart and blood?
entries.question: Does wireless radiation affect the heart and blood?
entries.text:
Yes. The research shows wireless exposure affecting heart rhythm, the heart's ability to respond to demand, blood pressure and red blood cells, and the two largest animal cancer studies found tumors in the heart's nerve-sheath cells.

The evidence:
- Heart tumors: the U.S. National Toxicology Program (NTP) found clear evidence of malignant heart schwannomas in male rats, and the Ramazzini Institute found the same tumor at far lower exposure (0.001 to 0.1 watts per kilogram, against 1.5 to 6 in NTP).
