A 2025 review commissioned by the World Health Organization rated this evidence high certainty. For one of the two studies, it calculated that a 1 percent added risk begins at about 0.1 watts per kilogram, close to the 0.08 watts per kilogram U.S. whole-body limit.
- Heart rate variability, the healthy beat-to-beat flexibility of the heartbeat: six weeks of daily phone calls lowered it in animals, with blood pressure and blood fats up and nothing back after two weeks off.
- Demand: heart cells exposed to 2.4 gigahertz could not raise their calcium signal when a stress hormone called for it, and clustered cells then died, with heat ruled out.
- Coupling: connexin 43, a protein that lets heart cells pass signals to each other, moved away from the cell junctions in heart tissue and other tissues.
- People: in a study of 212,046 people, new high blood pressure rose with weekly phone call time and was highest where genetic risk was also high.
- Blood: 5 minutes of a smartphone against the skin was followed by red blood cells stacking together in a leg vein, seen on ultrasound (Brown and Biebrich, 2025).

The heart runs on precise electrical timing, which is exactly what RF Safe's framework says these fields disturb.

Related: What is density gating? Why are the brain, heart and testes hit first?; What is radical-pair spin chemistry, and why do red blood cells stack up after phone exposure?; Does the body recover after exposure stops?; What is low-fidelity biology?

entries.title: Health Effects: Does wireless radiation affect the immune system?
entries.question: Does wireless radiation affect the immune system?
entries.text:
Yes. The research shows wireless and power-line exposure turning up inflammation, wearing down immune defenses over time, and making infections harder to fight.

The evidence:
- In RF Safe's map, 196 studies cover the immune system. They mostly measure inflammation signals: TNF-alpha in 21 studies and general inflammation markers in 61. Inflammation and oxidative stress travel together in 72 of them. Of the 27 that state an exposure level, 20 found effects at or below the 1.6 watts per kilogram phone limit, and 6 at or below the 0.08 watts per kilogram whole-body limit.
- Defenses hold, then fail: in mice exposed to 3G and 4G phone signals (TD-SCDMA and LTE-Advanced), innate immune defenses held for 4 weeks and then failed by 8 weeks.
- The second hit: long-exposed mice cleared an infection worse and died more from it.
- DNA repair in immune cells: Belyaev and colleagues reported in 2009 that 3G phone signals blocked the formation of DNA repair sites in human white blood cells, an effect that lasted up to 72 hours after exposure.
- One power-line study and one radio-frequency study reported the same inflammation panel.

Immune cells decide which genes to switch on based on the timing and size of their calcium signals (Dolmetsch and colleagues, Nature, 1998). RF Safe's framework adds the next step: corrupt that timing and the cell can misread a normal signal as danger.

Related: Does wireless exposure make other health stresses worse?; What is oxidative stress, and how is it tied to wireless exposure?; Can non-ionizing wireless radiation damage DNA?; How does wireless exposure throw off calcium signaling?

entries.title: Health Effects: Does wireless radiation affect wildlife, insects and plants?
entries.question: Does wireless radiation affect wildlife, insects and plants?
entries.text:
Yes. Studies show radio-frequency and power-line fields disturbing animals with a magnetic sense, stressing bees and earthworms below the limits, and the 2021 court ruling against the FCC specifically included environmental effects among the issues the agency failed to address.

The evidence:
- Magnetic orientation: in RF Safe's map, 22 studies cover the field-sensitive chemistry animals use to navigate, mostly in insects, bird embryos, plants and bats, and radio and power-line fields disturbed their magnetic orientation.
- Bees: below the public power-line limit, a high-voltage line plus pesticides broke honeybee colonies, while a power-line field switched on the bee heat-shock defense within minutes. Plants near the field got fewer honeybee visits and made fewer seeds, and the plant community changed. The authors called it 'conclusive evidence of detrimental impacts' on pollination (Science Advances, 2023). Bees raised their stress proteins more the longer they were exposed, in a pattern different from heat stress.
- Earthworms: below the U.S. field limit, earthworms raised their antioxidant enzymes and still took DNA, fat and protein damage, and modulation added damage at the same power.
- The public record: in the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) comment docket archived at rfsafe.app, 300 of the 2,415 filings RF Safe classified raise wildlife and the environment, and in the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) docket, 633 of the 7,080 comments do.

The U.S. limits were set from short-term heating experiments in laboratory animals, and they were never tested on bees, birds or trees. The Department of the Interior told the FCC in 2014 that the limits 'continue to be based on thermal heating, a criterion now nearly 30 years out of date and inapplicable today.' RF Safe's position is that environmental exposure needs its own review.

More: https://rfsafe.app/fcc-forum/topics/wildlife-environment/

Related: What is radical-pair spin chemistry, and why do red blood cells stack up after phone exposure?; Do power lines and wireless signals affect the body the same way?; What health effects has RF Safe mapped across the research?

entries.title: Health Effects: How many studies found no effect, and does that cancel out the studies that found harm?
entries.question: How many studies found no effect, and does that cancel out the studies that found harm?
entries.text:
No. Studies that found no effect do not cancel the studies that found harm. In a system where the result depends on the signal, the tissue, the genes and the timing of measurement, some studies will miss the effect, and a missed effect is not proof of safety.

The numbers: RF Safe's research database labels studies by effect. Of 6,498 papers in the database, 1,463 are labeled harm and 629 no effect, more than two harm papers for every no-effect paper. 1,919 are labeled mixed. RF Safe's map uses 1,465 harm-side studies. RF Safe keeps all of them in the catalog, with the original papers linked.

Why "no effect" results happen, and why they do not settle the question:
- A heating limit only needs one effect that is real to be shown inadequate. The U.S. National Toxicology Program found clear evidence of heart tumors in male rats, and a 2025 review commissioned by the World Health Organization rated that evidence high certainty. Other studies that missed it do not erase it.
- Many "no effect" studies used signals, cells or exposure lengths that RF Safe's framework predicts will show nothing: unpulsed signals, resting cells with few calcium channels, short exposures that cells temporarily compensate for, or averages that hide sensitive genotypes.
- Effects come in windows. Human neuroblastoma cells, a nerve-tumor cell line, released calcium under a 147 megahertz signal pulsed 16 times a second at 0.005 and 0.05 watts per kilogram, but not at the levels between or around them, so a study at the wrong level finds nothing.
- Funding matters: Huss and colleagues, in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2007, reviewed 59 experimental studies and found that those funded only by the telecommunications industry were the least likely to report a statistically significant effect.

The question is not how many studies found nothing. It is whether the limits protect against the effects that were found.

Related: Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?; What is proven, and what is RF Safe's framework?; What health effects has RF Safe mapped across the research?; RF Safe research database

entries.title: Health Effects: What does wireless radiation do to the brain?
entries.question: What does wireless radiation do to the brain?
entries.text:
The research links wireless exposure to the same few brain effects again and again: memory and learning problems, anxiety-like behavior, and damage to nerve cells, along with oxidative stress in the same brain tissue and leaks in the blood-brain barrier.

In RF Safe's map, 431 studies cover the brain and behavior. Memory and learning deficits appear in 94, anxiety- or depression-like behavior in 51, and nerve cell damage in 47, mostly in the hippocampus, the memory center, and the cortex. 128 of these studies also measured oxidative stress in the same tissue. Of the 72 that state an exposure level, 44 found effects at or below the 1.6 watts per kilogram phone limit, and 13 at or below the 0.08 watts per kilogram whole-body limit.

Specific findings:
- In people, Volkow and colleagues at the U.S. National Institutes of Health reported in 2011, in the Journal of the American Medical Association, that 50 minutes of a phone held to the ear raised brain sugar metabolism in the region closest to the antenna, compared with the same phone switched off.
- The blood-brain barrier, which keeps harmful substances out of the brain, opens after a duration threshold: the same sealing proteins fail in the brain barrier and the testis barrier.
- Under weeks of exposure, nerve cells survive by recycling their own parts, and in two labs that recycling stripped the synapses, the connection points between nerve cells. The cells look intact while the connections and behavior fail.

This is what RF Safe means by low-fidelity biology in the brain: the cells stay alive while the signaling degrades.

Related: What is low-fidelity biology?; Does wireless radiation affect sleep, brain waves or the body clock?; What is density gating? Why are the brain, heart and testes hit first?; Children and cell phones

entries.title: Health Effects: What health effects has RF Safe mapped across the research?
entries.question: What health effects has RF Safe mapped across the research?
entries.text:
RF Safe has mapped 1,465 studies that report harm from radio-frequency and power-line fields, and in RF Safe's reading they point to one pattern: the same upstream disruption of signaling and oxidative balance, showing up in the brain, reproductive system, heart, metabolism, immune system and developing bodies. Oxidative stress is the thread that ties them together in the data, and it links to every other group.

The studies come from RF Safe's research database at rfsafe.app/research. RF Safe linked them by what they measured, in which tissue, at what exposure. The biggest groups:
- Brain and behavior: 431 studies.
- Oxidative stress, the chemical damage inside cells: 400 studies, the common thread connecting all the others.
- Development and body-clock timing: 352 studies.
- Pregnancy and early life: 322 studies.
- Fertility and reproduction: 219 studies.
- Cancer: 206 studies.
- Immune system and inflammation: 196 studies.
- Metabolism, blood sugar and thyroid: 186 studies.
- Harm in two or more organ systems at once from one exposure: 232 studies.
- Direct loss of timing and rhythm: 124 studies, 61 of them in people.

Many effects appear below the U.S. limits. In the oxidative-stress group alone, 54 of the 64 studies that state an exposure level found effects at or below the 1.6 watts per kilogram phone limit, and 24 at or below the 0.08 watts per kilogram whole-body limit.

RF Safe also runs a nightly mechanism map that links studies into step-by-step chains: strain, compensation, exhaustion, failure at the next stress, and incomplete recovery. That pattern is what RF Safe calls the loss of biological reserve.

More: https://rfsafe.app/research

Related: What is RF Safe's position on wireless radiation, and why are the phone safety limits wrong?; What is the meta-disease state, or "one exposure, many diseases"?; What is biological reserve, and what is the "five-minute problem"?; RF Safe research database

entries.title: Health Effects: Who is most vulnerable to wireless radiation?
entries.question: Who is most vulnerable to wireless radiation?
entries.text:
The people most vulnerable are those with the least biological reserve: developing babies and children, people whose bodies are already under strain from illness such as diabetes, older people, and people whose genes make their calcium channels or antioxidant defenses more sensitive. RF Safe's framework says the receiver is part of the dose.

The evidence:
- Genes: a 5G signal changed sleep brain waves in people with one variant of the CACNA1C calcium-channel gene. Variants of the antioxidant enzyme genes MnSOD and catalase set how far cell tower exposure lowered those defenses in people.
- A lasting trait: blood cells from nine healthy donors differed widely in DNA damage from the same signal, and the differences repeated three months later.
- Illness: diabetic rats exposed below the U.S. whole-body limit showed the larger oxidative shift. Rats with kidney disease developed severe artery calcification under a weak field that left healthy rats untouched.
- Sex and age: sex sent the damage to testis or brain; age and genotype magnified the hit.
- Age: a 50 hertz field broke the DNA of aged human cells but not young ones.
- Children: children absorb more radiation in the brain than the adult test model, and development has no restore point.

Average-adult limits cannot protect the people with the thinnest margin. RF Safe asks for limits and studies that account for the most vulnerable, not the average.

Related: What is biological reserve, and what is the "five-minute problem"?; Does wireless exposure make other health stresses worse?; Can non-ionizing wireless radiation damage DNA?; Children and cell phones

entries.title: Symptoms: Anxiety, mood and irritability
entries.question: Anxiety, mood and irritability
entries.text:
This covers feeling anxious, low, on edge or easily irritated.

The studies in RF Safe's research directory look mostly at anxiety-like behavior and stress hormones in laboratory animals. These studies report what they measured. They do not show what is causing any one person's symptoms.

Study pages to start with (each page has a summary and a link to the original paper):
- A 2022 animal study looked at 2.45 GHz exposure, anxiety-like behavior and the stress hormone corticosterone. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000567-effects-of-2-45-ghz-non-ionizing-radiation-on-anxiety-like-behavior-gene-expression-an
- A 2022 animal study looked at stress during pregnancy combined with electromagnetic field exposure in rats. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000741-maternal-stress-induced-anxiety-like-behavior-exacerbated-by-electromagnetic-fields-ra
- A 2025 animal study looked at a brain receptor linked to anxiety-like behavior after dual-frequency exposure. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/002693-the-cb1r-of-mpfc-is-involved-in-anxiety-like-behavior-induced-by-0-8-2-65-ghz-dual-fre

All studies on this part of the body in RF Safe's research directory:
- Brain and nerves: https://rfsafe.app/research?system=nervous

This is a summary of research, not medical advice, and RF Safe cannot diagnose or treat any condition. See a doctor or other medical professional about anxiety or low mood, and get help right away if you have thoughts of harming yourself (in the U.S., call or text 988).

entries.title: Symptoms: Brain fog, memory and concentration
entries.question: Brain fog, memory and concentration
entries.text:
Brain fog is trouble thinking clearly, remembering things or keeping focus.

The studies in RF Safe's research directory look mostly at learning and memory in laboratory animals exposed to microwave and radiofrequency signals. These studies report what they measured. They do not show what is causing any one person's symptoms.

Study pages to start with (each page has a summary and a link to the original paper):
- A 2019 literature review looked at low-level radiofrequency exposure and spatial learning and memory in lab animals. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/001816-can-low-level-rf-exposure-affect-cognitive-behaviour-in-lab-animals-literature-review
- A 2025 animal study looked at learning and memory after combined 2.8 GHz and 9.3 GHz microwave exposure. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000276-compound-exposure-of-2-8-ghz-and-9-3-ghz-microwave-causes-learning-and-memory-impairme
- A 2022 animal study looked at spatial learning and memory in rats after exposure to two frequencies at once. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000381-changes-in-rat-spatial-learning-and-memory-as-well-as-serum-exosome-proteins-after-sim

All studies on this part of the body in RF Safe's research directory:
- Brain and nerves: https://rfsafe.app/research?system=nervous

This is a summary of research, not medical advice, and RF Safe cannot diagnose or treat any condition. See a doctor or other medical professional about memory or concentration problems that are new or getting worse.

entries.title: Symptoms: Dizziness and vertigo
entries.question: Dizziness and vertigo
entries.text:
Dizziness is feeling light-headed or unsteady. Vertigo is the feeling that you or the room is spinning.

The studies in RF Safe's research directory look at cells of the balance and hearing nerve in the lab, and at reports of symptoms near new antennas. These studies report what they measured. They do not show what is causing any one person's symptoms.

Study pages to start with (each page has a summary and a link to the original paper):
- A 2021 lab study looked at hearing-related genes in cells from the balance nerve after exposure. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/001069-transcriptomic-profile-reveals-deregulation-of-hearing-loss-related-genes-in-vestibula
- A 2023 case report described symptoms in two men after 5G antennas were installed on the roof above their office. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000548-development-of-the-microwave-syndrome-in-two-men-shortly-after-installation-of-5g-on-t
- A 2026 lab study looked at human nerve support cells and hearing-related genes after electromagnetic exposure. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/006851-electromagnetic-exposure-changes-human-schwann-cell-motility-and-transcriptomic-profil

All studies on this part of the body in RF Safe's research directory:
- Brain and nerves: https://rfsafe.app/research?system=nervous
- Ears and hearing: https://rfsafe.app/research?system=sensory-auditory

This is a summary of research, not medical advice, and RF Safe cannot diagnose or treat any condition. See a doctor or other medical professional about dizziness or vertigo, and get urgent care if it comes with fainting, chest pain or weakness.

entries.title: Symptoms: Electromagnetic sensitivity (EHS)
entries.question: Electromagnetic sensitivity (EHS)
entries.text:
Electromagnetic hypersensitivity (EHS) is when people report symptoms such as headaches, tingling or poor sleep that they link to phones, Wi-Fi or other wireless devices.

The studies in RF Safe's research directory look at proposed biological explanations for EHS and at immune markers in people who report it. These studies report what they measured. They do not show what is causing any one person's symptoms.

Study pages to start with (each page has a summary and a link to the original paper):
- A 2025 review looked at how the human body senses magnetic fields and what that may mean for EHS. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000291-a-mechanistic-understanding-of-human-magnetoreception-validates-the-phenomenon-of-elec
- A 2020 review looked at proposed mechanisms for EHS, also called microwave syndrome. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/001540-electromagnetic-hypersensitivity-ehs-microwave-syndrome-review-of-mechanisms
- A 2024 report looked at immune responses in people who report EHS. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/000076-hypersensitivity-to-man-made-electromagnetic-fields-ehs-correlates-with-immune-respons

All studies on this part of the body in RF Safe's research directory:
- Brain and nerves: https://rfsafe.app/research?system=nervous
- Skin: https://rfsafe.app/research?system=integumentary

This is a summary of research, not medical advice, and RF Safe cannot diagnose or treat any condition. See a doctor or other medical professional about the symptoms you notice.

entries.title: Symptoms: Eye strain and vision problems
entries.question: Eye strain and vision problems
entries.text:
This covers tired or sore eyes, blurry vision and other changes in eyesight.

The studies in RF Safe's research directory look mainly at the lens of the eye after microwave exposure, in animals, in the lab and in workplaces. These studies report what they measured. They do not show what is causing any one person's symptoms.

Study pages to start with (each page has a summary and a link to the original paper):
- A 1960 animal study looked at clouding of the eye lens after microwave exposure. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/006701-opacities-in-the-lens-of-the-eye-experimentally-induced-by-exposure-to-microwave-radia
- A 2005 lab study looked at the eye lens kept in culture and exposed to microwaves. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/006427-localized-effects-of-microwave-radiation-on-the-intact-eye-lens-in-culture-conditions
- A 1989 review looked at microwave radiation and the eye from a workplace health view. https://rfsafe.app/research/papers/006259-effects-of-microwave-radiation-on-the-eye-the-occupational-health-perspective

All studies on this part of the body in RF Safe's research directory:
- Eyes: https://rfsafe.app/research?system=sensory-ocular

This is a summary of research, not medical advice, and RF Safe cannot diagnose or treat any condition. See a doctor or other medical professional about any change in your vision.

entries.title: Symptoms: Fatigue and low energy
entries.question: Fatigue and low energy
entries.text:
Fatigue is tiredness or low energy that does not go away with normal rest.

The studies in RF Safe's research directory look at tiredness reported by phone users, and at how much people's expectations affect how tired they feel. These studies report what they measured. They do not show what is causing any one person's symptoms.

entries.title: Symptoms: Headaches and migraines

entries.text:

entries.title: Cancer Studies: Do cell phones cause brain tumors in people?
entries.question: Do cell phones cause brain tumors in people?
entries.text:
Studies of heavy phone users show increased risk of glioma, a malignant brain tumor, and acoustic neuroma, a tumor on the hearing nerve, on the side of the head where people hold the phone. Those are the same two tumor types the large animal studies found. RF Safe's position is that the human and animal evidence point the same way and the burden belongs on the limits, not on the public.

The human studies:
- Interphone, 2010, the largest case-control study, run in 13 countries: the overall results came out below 1, as if phones protected against brain cancer, which the authors said was possibly due to participation bias. People in the top tenth of cumulative call time, 1,640 hours or more, had a 40 percent higher glioma risk. The authors wrote of "suggestions of an increased risk of glioma at the highest exposure levels."
- A follow-up from five Interphone countries, which estimated the radiation absorbed at the tumor site, found glioma risk 2.8 times higher in the most exposed part of the brain among people with 10 or more years of phone use (Cardis and colleagues, 2011).
- CERENAT, France, 2014: people with 896 hours or more of calls had nearly 2.9 times the glioma risk.
- The Hardell group in Sweden, pooled analyses 2013 and 2015: glioma risk rose to 3 times higher after more than 25 years of mobile phone use, was highest on the side of the head where the phone was held, and was higher for people who started before age 20. Acoustic neuroma risk was also raised.
- In 2011 the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified radio-frequency radiation as possibly carcinogenic to humans, Group 2B, based on glioma and acoustic neuroma.

Context matters: the International Agency for Research on Cancer itself said the 1,640-hour cut-point, "spread out over 10 years, corresponds to about a half-hour per day." That is ordinary use today. Children now start using phones far younger, and brain tumors can take decades to appear.

What RF Safe does not say: that phone radiation alone has been proven to cause a specific person's cancer. What RF Safe does say: the evidence of risk is strong enough that limits must be set to prevent it, and you should keep the phone away from your head.

Related: What about the Danish cohort and COSMOS studies that found no link to brain tumors?; What does it mean that radio-frequency radiation is "possibly carcinogenic" (Group 2B)?; What did the U.S. government's NTP cell phone study find?; What else can I do besides a case?

entries.title: Cancer Studies: Weren't the NTP tumors caused by heat, or by control rats dying early?
entries.question: Weren't the NTP tumors caused by heat, or by control rats dying early?
entries.text:
No. Neither objection explains the tumors, and the Ramazzini Institute study answers both.

The heat objection: critics, including Germany's Federal Office for Radiation Protection, argued the U.S. National Toxicology Program (NTP) did not record body temperature during the two-year study, so heating could not be ruled out at the highest doses. But:
- The NTP doses were designed to limit body heating to under 1 degree Celsius, and heart tumors appeared at the lowest dose, 1.5 watts per kilogram, not only the highest.
- The 2026 Japan-Korea studies that critics hold up against NTP did not measure body temperature during their two-year exposures either.
- The Ramazzini Institute found the same malignant heart schwannoma at about 0.1 watts per kilogram, 15 to 60 times below the NTP doses. The same German office called that level "comparable" to the human limit values and said a heating cause was unlikely.
- A 2025 review commissioned by the World Health Organization, which assessed the quality of each study, still rated the heart tumor and glioma evidence as high certainty.

The survival objection: the unexposed male rats in the NTP study died earlier than the exposed rats, 28 percent survival against 50 to 68 percent. Critics said the controls did not live long enough to develop tumors. But:
- The NTP's statistical tests adjust for survival, and the heart tumor trend was still significant.
- In the Ramazzini study there was no survival difference between exposed and unexposed rats, and the same tumor still appeared only in exposed males.

Two labs, two designs, one tumor type, and the exposure in the second lab was near the public limit. Heat and early deaths do not explain that.

Related: What did the Ramazzini Institute study find, and at what exposure?; What did the U.S. government's NTP cell phone study find?; What does "non-thermal" mean, and why does it matter for phone radiation?; What did the 2026 Japan-Korea rat study find, and does it cancel out the NTP study?

entries.title: Cancer Studies: What about the Danish cohort and COSMOS studies that found no link to brain tumors?
entries.question: What about the Danish cohort and COSMOS studies that found no link to brain tumors?
entries.text:
Those studies do not show phones are safe. Their designs could not detect the risk in heavy users, and their own authors named the limits.

The Danish cohort:
- It started with 723,421 phone subscriptions from 1982 to 1995 and removed 200,507 corporate subscriptions, the business users who were likely the heaviest users. Those people were counted as unexposed.
- People who got a phone after 1995 were also counted as unexposed. The authors wrote that "the majority of our reference population consists of recent cellular telephone users, which is a potential source of underestimation of risk," and that excluding company subscriptions "excluded some of the most active users."
- The authors wrote that they "did not have information on the actual amount of mobile phone use" and "could not examine the risk restricted to the subgroup of heaviest users." Germany's Federal Office for Radiation Protection said "an underestimation of risk cannot be excluded."

COSMOS, 2024:
- It followed 264,574 people for a median of just over 7 years, short for brain tumors, which can take decades to appear.
- Almost everyone used a phone, so there was no unexposed group. The comparison group was the bottom half of call time, which averaged up to 10.6 minutes a day.
- Scientists of the International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields pointed out that the study could not rule out a 28 percent higher glioma risk after 10 years or a 52 percent higher risk after 15 years, and that call time is a poor stand-in for dose because a phone's output can vary by up to ten thousand times depending on the network and signal strength.
- Answering their critics, the COSMOS authors themselves wrote that "statistical power is the main current limitation of our study."

A study that cannot see heavy users, has no unexposed group, or stops before tumors have time to appear cannot clear phones of risk.

Related: Do cell phones cause brain tumors in people?; Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?; How many studies found no effect, and does that cancel out the studies that found harm?; What is wrong with COSMOS (Feychting, 2024)?

entries.title: Cancer Studies: What did the 2026 Japan-Korea rat study find, and does it cancel out the NTP study?
entries.question: What did the 2026 Japan-Korea rat study find, and does it cancel out the NTP study?
entries.text:
No, it does not cancel the U.S. findings. The 2026 Japan-Korea studies tested one signal at one dose in 70 male rats per group, too few to see the tumor in question, and the only heart schwannomas in the Korean arm were in the exposed rats.

The Korean study was not without a signal. Its control rats had zero of these heart tumors, and its exposed rats had two, the same kind of heart tumor (malignant schwannoma) that the U.S. National Toxicology Program and Italy's Ramazzini Institute studies found. With only 70 rats per group, two tumors is not enough to be statistically significant, but it points the same way as those studies.

What the studies did: two companion two-year rat studies, one in Korea and one in Japan, exposed male rats only to a 900 megahertz CDMA signal at a single whole-body dose of 4 watts per kilogram. They did not test the GSM signal, and they did not test the lower 1.5 and 3 watts per kilogram doses where several U.S. National Toxicology Program tumor counts were highest.

What they found:
- Korean arm: heart schwannomas in 0 of 70 cage-control rats, 0 of 70 sham-exposed rats, and 2 of 70 exposed rats. Too few to be statistically significant at that group size.
- Japanese arm: one heart schwannoma in each group.

What the Korean authors themselves wrote: "a sample size of 70 males per group provides limited statistical power for detecting rare tumors. In particular, an approximately 20% increase in the incidence of cardiac schwannomas or malignant gliomas would not be readily detectable with this sample size."

Independence: the principal investigator of the Korean study and last author of both papers, Young Hwan Ahn, joined the Main Commission of the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection, the group that writes the heating-based international limits, in July 2024.

The Japanese authors also wrote that "the primary purpose of the present study was not to replicate the NTP findings quantitatively." And neither study measured body temperature during the two-year exposure, the same gap Germany's Federal Office for Radiation Protection held against the NTP study.

A study designed too small to see the effect cannot rule it out.

Related: What did the U.S. government's NTP cell phone study find?; Weren't the NTP tumors caused by heat, or by control rats dying early?; Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?

entries.title: Cancer Studies: What did the Ramazzini Institute study find, and at what exposure?
entries.question: What did the Ramazzini Institute study find, and at what exposure?
entries.text:
The Ramazzini Institute in Italy found the same malignant heart tumor the U.S. government study found, in male rats, at an exposure far too low to heat tissue, close to the public whole-body limit. It is the strongest confirmation of the U.S. finding.

What the study did: the largest long-term rat study ever done on wireless radiation, with 2,448 rats. They were exposed from before birth until natural death to a 1.8 gigahertz GSM signal like a cell tower's, from a distance, at 0, 5, 25 and 50 volts per meter, for 19 hours a day (Falcioni and colleagues, 2018, Environmental Research).

What it found:
- Heart: malignant schwannomas rose significantly in males at the highest level, 50 volts per meter: 3 of 207 rats, against 0 of 412 unexposed rats.
- Brain: more malignant glial tumors in exposed females at the highest level, though not statistically significant.
- The highest level equals a whole-body absorption of about 0.1 watts per kilogram, just above the 0.08 watts per kilogram public limit, and 15 to 60 times below the doses in the U.S. study.

Why heat cannot explain it: Germany's Federal Office for Radiation Protection called 0.1 watts per kilogram "a comparable level to the basic limit values" for people, and said a heating cause was unlikely. The same office conceded the study's strengths: two to four times more animals per group, a longer study, blinded tissue exams, and no survival difference between exposed and unexposed rats.

The authors wrote that their findings "are consistent with and reinforce the results of the NTP study." Two labs, two exposure designs, one tumor.

The tumors are relevant to people: in 2024, scientists from the U.S. National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, the NTP's parent institute, and the Ramazzini Institute sequenced the Ramazzini tumors. The rat gliomas "histologically resemble low grade human gliomas" and "share some genetic alterations" with a common type of human glioma (IDH1-wildtype), and the heart schwannomas carried mutations in human cancer genes.

Related: What did the U.S. government's NTP cell phone study find?; Why does RF Safe say the FCC limit is 4,200 times too high?; What does "non-thermal" mean, and why does it matter for phone radiation?

entries.title: Cancer Studies: What did the U.S. government's NTP cell phone study find?
entries.question: What did the U.S. government's NTP cell phone study find?
entries.text:
The U.S. National Toxicology Program (NTP), the federal government's top toxicology program, ran a 30 million dollar study and in 2018 reported clear evidence that cell phone radiation caused malignant heart tumors in male rats, and some evidence that it caused brain tumors called gliomas.

What the study did: rats were exposed to the two main phone signal types of the time, called GSM and CDMA, at 1.5, 3 and 6 watts per kilogram, starting before birth and continuing for two years, for 9 hours a day, in 10-minute on and 10-minute off cycles across 18 hours 20 minutes.

What it found:
- Heart: malignant schwannomas, tumors of the nerve-sheath cells, rose in exposed male rats. Under the GSM signal, 0 of 90 unexposed rats had one, against 2, 1 and 5 of 90 at the three doses. Under the CDMA signal, 0 against 2, 3 and 6. The trend was statistically significant. NTP called this clear evidence, its highest level.
- Brain: malignant gliomas appeared in exposed male rats and none in unexposed ones. NTP called this some evidence.
- Adrenal gland: NTP also found some evidence of adrenal gland tumors (pheochromocytomas) in male rats exposed to the GSM signal.
- DNA: exposure caused significant DNA damage in the brain, measured by the comet test.
- Pups exposed in the womb and during nursing weighed less at the higher doses.

Why the study was done: in 1999 the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) asked for this study because of widespread cell phone use and "limited knowledge about potential health effects from long-term exposure." The government's own study then found cancer at exposures designed to keep body heating under 1 degree Celsius.

These are the same two tumor types studies in heavy phone users point to. RF Safe's position is that the U.S. government's own study answered the question the FCC refuses to ask, and the limits have not changed since.

Related: What did the Ramazzini Institute study find, and at what exposure?; Weren't the NTP tumors caused by heat, or by control rats dying early?; What did the World Health Organization-commissioned animal cancer review find?; What is density gating? Why are the brain, heart and testes hit first?

entries.title: Cancer Studies: What did the World Health Organization-commissioned animal cancer review find?
entries.question: What did the World Health Organization-commissioned animal cancer review find?
entries.text:
A 2025 systematic review of animal cancer studies, commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO), rated the evidence that radio-frequency radiation increases heart schwannomas and brain gliomas in male rats as high certainty, its top rating. A correction published in August 2026 kept both ratings at high.

What high certainty means: the reviewers were confident the effect is real and that further research is unlikely to change that conclusion.

Key points from the review and its correction:
- The correction's own highlight reads: "High Certainty of Evidence: RF EMF increased heart schwannomas and glial-cell tumors."
- It rated the evidence for adrenal tumors called pheochromocytomas as moderate.
- It noted that these two tumor types are "the same as those identified with limited evidence in humans" by the International Agency for Research on Cancer.
- The review calculated a dose for a 1 percent added heart-tumor risk from the Ramazzini data. In the correction, its lower bound is 0.056 watts per kilogram, below the 0.08 watts per kilogram U.S. whole-body limit.
- The reviewers questioned whether the specific absorption rate, the basis of the U.S. limits, "is the appropriate dose metric" for these effects, and whether more exposure always means more harm.

RF Safe's position: when a review commissioned by the World Health Organization rates the cancer evidence in animals as high certainty, at doses near the public limit, the heating-only limits can no longer be defended.

Related: What did the U.S. government's NTP cell phone study find?; What does it mean that radio-frequency radiation is "possibly carcinogenic" (Group 2B)?; How far off are the U.S. limits, according to the 2026 Melnick and Moskowitz risk assessment?

entries.title: Cancer Studies: What does it mean that radio-frequency radiation is "possibly carcinogenic" (Group 2B)?
entries.question: What does it mean that radio-frequency radiation is "possibly carcinogenic" (Group 2B)?
entries.text:
In 2011 the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the World Health Organization's cancer agency, classified radio-frequency electromagnetic fields, including phone radiation, as possibly carcinogenic to humans, Group 2B. The rating was based on limited evidence in people for glioma and acoustic neuroma.

What has happened since makes the case stronger, not weaker:
- 2018: the U.S. National Toxicology Program found clear evidence of malignant heart schwannomas and some evidence of gliomas in male rats, and the Ramazzini Institute found the same heart tumor at exposures near the public limit.
- 2025: a systematic review commissioned by the World Health Organization rated the animal evidence for both tumor types as high certainty, and a 2026 correction kept that rating. The review noted these are the same tumor types IARC found limited evidence for in people.
- Under IARC's own rules, Group 2A, probably carcinogenic to humans, generally applies when there is limited evidence in humans and sufficient evidence in experimental animals. In 2011, IARC rated the animal evidence as only limited. The animal evidence is now far stronger.
- In 2024, IARC's own advisory group made radio-frequency radiation a high priority for re-evaluation between 2025 and 2029, citing new human and animal cancer evidence.

People sometimes say Group 2B puts phones next to pickled vegetables, as if that makes it harmless. That misses the point. The group says how strong the evidence is, not how big the risk is, and the animal evidence that was rated only limited in 2011 has since been rated high certainty.

RF Safe's position: the 2B rating was the starting point. The evidence since 2011 has filled in the gap the rating described, and the U.S. limits have not been updated to reflect any of it.

Related: What did the World Health Organization-commissioned animal cancer review find?; Do cell phones cause brain tumors in people?; What is proven, and what is RF Safe's framework?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: Don't flat brain cancer rates prove phones are safe?
entries.question: Don't flat brain cancer rates prove phones are safe?
entries.text:
No. Population cancer rates cannot clear an exposure that was never measured in the people who got sick, and the trend papers used to claim safety are dated and narrow.

- Trend studies such as Chapman (Australia, 2016), Deltour (Nordic countries, 2012), Karipidis (Australia, 2018) and Little (United States, 2012) compare national tumor counts with modeled risk scenarios. None links an individual's phone use to that person's diagnosis.
- Their conclusions only rule out the specific risk sizes and delays they modeled. Chapman assumed a ten-year delay; brain tumors can take far longer.
- The Nordic glioma data were not flat: rates rose 0.4 percent a year in men and 0.3 percent in women from 1979 to 2008, and that paper ends in 2008.
- Glioma is only one tumor. Trends for meningioma, acoustic neuroma, thyroid and salivary gland tumors are separate questions.
- Little (2012) found that the raised risks in the INTERPHONE heavy-user group were compatible with United States trends.

RF Safe's position: rising tumor rates in later registry data, not flat rates up to 2008, are what matter now.

Related: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?; Do cell phones cause brain tumors in people?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What about the animal studies that found no cancer from phone signals?
entries.question: What about the animal studies that found no cancer from phone signals?
entries.text:
They do not cancel the positive findings. Each tested a narrow setup, often one dose in one strain, and the strongest animal studies found tumors.

- The United States National Toxicology Program found clear evidence of malignant heart schwannomas in male rats, and the Ramazzini Institute found more heart schwannomas in male rats at far lower exposure. A World Health Organization-commissioned review rated the evidence for gliomas and heart schwannomas in male rats high certainty.
- The Korea-Japan rat study (2026) used a single exposure, 4 watts per kilogram whole-body, 50 times the public whole-body limit. In the Korean half, malignant heart schwannomas appeared only in exposed rats, 2 of 70, versus none of 140 controls. A co-author joined the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection's Main Commission in July 2024.
- The lymphoma-prone mouse studies (Utteridge 2002, Oberto 2007) changed the exposure setup from the original 1997 positive study they were meant to check.
- Other negative studies used tumor-prone strains, one signal or one exposure level, which cannot speak for all signals and all people.

RF Safe's position: the National Toxicology Program and Ramazzini findings stand.

Related: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What about the lab studies that found no DNA damage from phone signals?
entries.question: What about the lab studies that found no DNA damage from phone signals?
entries.text:
They do not show phone signals are safe for DNA. They were short tests of one endpoint, often with a different method from the studies that found damage.

- The Washington University studies by Malyapa and colleagues (1997 and 1998) were set up after Lai and Singh reported DNA breaks in rat brain cells. Motorola contracted the group to try to reproduce the Lai and Singh result, according to Microwave News. The contract specified a different version of the comet assay from the one Lai and Singh used, and Lai and Singh said the experiments were flawed.
- Two of those studies used cells in a dish, not living brains, so they were not true replications.
- Other null tests (Hook 2004, Lagroye 2004, Vijayalaxmi 2013, O'Connor 2010) measured one endpoint for hours, in a few cell types or a few donors.

A short null test in cells does not erase the 1,465 harm-side studies in RF Safe's research map.

Related: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?
entries.question: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?
entries.text:
These studies could not see the heavy, long-term users where risk shows up, so their "no link" headlines do not clear phones.

- COSMOS (2024) followed 264,574 adults for a median of just over 7 years. Its comparison group was the bottom half of callers, not non-users. Its lead author was an ICNIRP Commission member from 2008 to 2020. The authors wrote that "statistical power is the main current limitation of our study."
- The Million Women Study followed women born from 1935 to 1950. The authors agreed very heavy users were few. Its 2013 report found 2.46 times the risk of acoustic neuroma after 10 or more years of use (95 percent confidence interval 1.07 to 5.64), rising with years of use.
- CEFALO (2011) found 1.36 times the odds of brain tumors in children who used phones regularly, and risk rose with time since subscription in children with phone company records.
- MOBI-Kids (2022) used appendicitis patients as controls, with 72 percent of cases but only 54 percent of controls taking part, and its authors said they could not exclude a small increased risk.
- The early United States studies looked at recent use. Muscat (2000) studied people with under 3 years of use on average and was funded in part by a Wireless Technology Research contract; the Inskip (2001) authors said their data were insufficient for long-term heavy users.

RF Safe's position: absence of proof from a study blind to heavy, long-term use is not proof of safety.

Related: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?; What about the Danish cohort and COSMOS studies that found no link to brain tumors?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Danish cohort studies of phone subscribers?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Danish cohort studies of phone subscribers?
entries.text:
The Danish cohort studies cannot clear phones, because they never measured who used a phone or how much, and they counted the heaviest users as unexposed.

- Exposure was only whether a person held a private phone subscription between 1982 and 1995. No call time, no side of the head, no cordless phones.
- Of 723,421 subscriptions, 200,507 corporate subscriptions were removed from the exposed group. The 2011 authors wrote that these users "will have been misclassified as unexposed."
- Anyone who first subscribed after 1995 was also counted as unexposed, even as phones spread to almost everyone.
- The first report (2001) was supported by grants from the two Danish phone companies, TeleDanmark Mobil and Sonofon, which also supplied the records.
- The 2001, 2006 and 2011 papers are updates of one cohort, not separate confirmations.

Söderqvist, Carlberg and Hardell reviewed all four publications in 2012 and found the subscription-based design too weak to support reassurance.

RF Safe's position: a study that cannot tell users from non-users cannot clear phones.

Related: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?; What about the Danish cohort and COSMOS studies that found no link to brain tumors?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/danish-2011/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the FDA, FCC, National Cancer Institute and European committee reviews that call phones safe?
entries.question: What is wrong with the FDA, FCC, National Cancer Institute and European committee reviews that call phones safe?
entries.text:
These agency documents restate selected studies as reassurance. They are not new evidence of safety.

- The Food and Drug Administration's 2020 review covered only cancer, searched mainly 2008 to 2018, and added a separate search specifically for negative results.
- The Federal Communications Commission's 2019 order kept its limits. In 2021 a federal appeals court sent it back for failing to explain how the limits protect against harms other than cancer.
- The National Cancer Institute fact sheet covers cancer only and leans on the same disputed studies, such as INTERPHONE, the Danish cohort and COSMOS.
- The European SCENIHR (2015) and SCHEER (2023) opinions relied mostly on earlier reviews.

RF Safe's position: in 2021 a federal court found the Federal Communications Commission failed to explain how its limits protect against non-cancer harm, and these reviews do not fill that gap.

Related: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?
entries.question: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?
entries.text:
INTERPHONE did not show phones are safe. Its heaviest users had raised glioma risk, and its own bias checks point to risk being understated.

INTERPHONE was a 13-country case-control study coordinated by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, with 2,708 glioma and 2,409 meningioma cases.
- At 1,640 or more lifetime hours of calls, glioma odds were 1.40 (95 percent confidence interval 1.03 to 1.89). That "heavy" group averaged about 27 minutes a day over 10 years.
- When the study used light users instead of non-users as the comparison, as its Appendix 2 did, that figure rose to 1.82 (1.15 to 2.89).
- Most lower-use groups showed odds below 1, as if phones protected the brain. That pattern is a sign of bias, not protection.
- Of about 19.2 million euros in funding, 5.5 million came from industry sources, including 3.5 million from the Mobile Manufacturers' Forum and the GSM Association.
- A 2017 bias-adjusted re-analysis of the Canadian INTERPHONE data found glioma odds of 2.2 (1.3 to 4.1) above 558 lifetime hours. The French CERENAT study found 2.89 (1.41 to 5.93) at 896 or more hours.

National arms of INTERPHONE, including the Danish, Swedish, United Kingdom, German and Japanese studies, share its recall and participation problems.

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of "heavy."

Related: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?; Do cell phones cause brain tumors in people?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/interphone-2010/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned reviews that found no harm in people?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned reviews that found no harm in people?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned reviews do not show phones are safe. Their "no effect" findings rest on weak exposure measures, short follow-up and evidence the reviewers themselves graded low or very low certainty.

- The human cancer review (2024) relied on crude measures such as "ever used a phone" and time since first use, and its authors acknowledged there was not enough evidence to pool tumor delays of 15 years or more.
- Its lead author has been Vice Chair of the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP), the body that writes the heating-based limits, since July 2024.
- The cognition, symptoms and fertility reviews in people found "little or no effect" with low or very low certainty, often from short follow-up, a handful of cohorts, or call time used as a stand-in for dose.
- The animal pregnancy review needed a published correction (2025).
- The same program's animal cancer review rated the evidence for gliomas and heart schwannomas in male rats high certainty, and its corrected animal male fertility review rated reduced pregnancy rates high certainty.

Published critiques include Frank and colleagues (2025), Hardell and Nilsson (2025), and an International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields review of eleven of these reviews (Melnick and colleagues, 2025).

RF Safe's position: "low certainty of no effect" is not safety, and reviewers tied to ICNIRP should not grade their own limits.

Related: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/karipidis-2024/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?
entries.question: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?
entries.text:
Today's limits rest on short-term heating and behavior experiments in animals, not on tests of long-term, non-thermal effects.

- In the 1970s and 1980s, rats and monkeys were exposed to microwaves while doing trained tasks. Researchers looked for the point where the animals stopped performing, which came with body heating.
- The National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (1986), the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard (1991) and the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) guidelines (1998 and 2020) used that roughly 4 watts per kilogram disruption level and divided it by safety factors to set limits.
- Those experiments lasted minutes to a few months and measured behavior and temperature, not cancer, fertility, DNA, or development.
- ICNIRP also rejected the National Toxicology Program and Ramazzini tumor findings in its own notes, then relied on that rejection in its 2020 guidelines.
- A 2022 analysis found the research behind ICNIRP 2020 comes from a small, tightly connected network of co-authors.
- In 2021 a federal appeals court sent back the Federal Communications Commission decision to keep these limits, because it failed to explain how they protect against harms other than cancer.

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/history/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?
entries.question: Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?
entries.text:
The studies most often quoted to say wireless radiation is safe do not show that. RF Safe has reviewed 70 of them, the studies, reviews and guidelines regulators and industry lean on, and each one has specific, documented shortcomings.

The same flaws come up again and again:
- Exposure never measured. The Danish cohort counted a phone subscription as exposure and put 200,507 corporate subscribers, the heaviest users, in the unexposed group.
- Heavy users missing or buried. INTERPHONE called 1,640 lifetime hours, about 27 minutes a day over 10 years, "heavy," and still found raised glioma risk in that group.
- Follow-up too short. Brain tumors can take decades to appear; COSMOS had a median of just over 7 years of follow-up.
- Short tests standing in for a lifetime. Many lab and animal studies tested one dose, one endpoint, for hours or weeks.
- "No significant effect" sold as "safe." Wide confidence intervals and low-certainty evidence cannot rule out harm.
- Industry money and rule-writers grading their own rules. INTERPHONE took 5.5 million euros from industry sources, the first Danish report was paid for in part by the two Danish phone companies, and authors of several null studies and reviews hold or held International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) roles.
- Limits built on heat. The 4 watts per kilogram threshold behind today's limits came from short-term heating and behavior experiments in animals.

Against these, the United States National Toxicology Program found clear evidence of malignant heart tumors in male rats, and a World Health Organization-commissioned review rated the animal tumor evidence high certainty.

Ask about any study by name, such as INTERPHONE, the Danish cohort, COSMOS, the Million Women Study, MOBI-Kids or the World Health Organization reviews, to hear exactly why RF Safe flags it.

Related: What is RF Safe's position on wireless radiation, and why are the phone safety limits wrong?; Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?; Does industry funding affect what studies find?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with CEFALO, the children's brain tumor study (Aydin, 2011)?
entries.question: What is wrong with CEFALO, the children's brain tumor study (Aydin, 2011)?
entries.text:
CEFALO does not show that phones are safe for children. Children who used phones regularly had higher odds of brain tumors, and where real phone company records existed, risk rose with time since the first subscription.

What it was: a case-control study by Aydin and colleagues in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute (2011) in Denmark, Sweden, Norway and Switzerland. It included 352 children and teenagers aged 7 to 19 with brain tumors and 646 controls. The authors argued against a causal link.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- The main result was raised. Regular phone users had 1.36 times the odds of a brain tumor (95 percent confidence interval 0.92 to 2.02). Not reaching statistical significance in a small study is not the same as safe.
- The best data showed a trend. In children with phone company records, brain tumor risk rose with the time since the subscription began.
- The study was too small and too early. For children who started 5 or more years before, the odds ratio was 1.26 (0.70 to 2.28), with too few cases to settle long-term childhood use.
- The authors' own defense leaves risk open. In reply, they argued against a large effect across the whole population, but allowed for risks limited to heavy use, early life or rare tumor types.

Published critique: Söderqvist and colleagues, Environmental Health (2011).

RF Safe's position: raised odds in children and a time trend in the record-based data are a warning, not a safety finding.

Related: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/cefalo-2011/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with COSMOS (Feychting, 2024)?
entries.question: What is wrong with COSMOS (Feychting, 2024)?
entries.text:
COSMOS does not show that phones are safe. It followed people for a median of about 7 years, it had no group of non-users, and its own authors call weak statistical power its main limitation. Industry money helped pay for the work in several countries, passed through public bodies under "firewall" contracts. COSMOS also published papers on headache, tinnitus, hearing and sleep. Those papers do not clear radio-frequency exposure either.

What it was: the Cohort Study of Mobile Phone Use and Health (COSMOS), led by Maria Feychting and published in Environment International in 2024. It followed 264,574 adults in five European countries for a median of 7.12 years and reported that call time was not linked to glioma, meningioma or acoustic neuroma.

Who paid for it. The 2024 paper's own funding statement names public research bodies and, in some countries, industry money passed through a public agency:
- Sweden: the Swedish Research Council, AFA Insurance, the Swedish Research Council for Health, Working Life and Welfare, the Swedish Radiation Safety Authority, and VINNOVA, Sweden's government innovation agency. VINNOVA received funds from TeliaSonera, Ericsson and Telenor Sverige to cover part of the data collection. That industry funding ended in 2012. The authors say agreements with VINNOVA guaranteed the researchers' scientific independence.
- Finland: the National Technology Agency (TEKES), with contributions from Nokia and the network providers TeliaSonera and Elisa, and an unrestricted grant from the Mobile Manufacturers' Forum, with Pirkanmaa Hospital District acting as a firewall.
- United Kingdom: for the first five years, the Mobile Telecommunications and Health Research (MTHR) programme, jointly supported by the UK Department of Health and the mobile telecommunications industry. Later funding came from the UK Department of Health and Social Care and other public bodies, without industry named as a joint funder.
- Denmark was funded by the Danish Strategic Research Council. The Netherlands was funded by the Netherlands Organization for Health Research (ZonMw) under its Electromagnetic Fields and Health Research programme. France was funded by the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES) and the International Agency for Research on Cancer. French data were not used in the 2024 brain-tumor analysis because recruitment was late.

The authors describe those industry payments as independent because of the firewall contracts. Industry money in the funding is still a conflict of interest. RF Safe does not treat a firewall as proof that the work is free of that conflict.

Why RF Safe flags the brain-tumor paper:
- Seven years is too short. Brain tumors can take decades to appear. Prior phone use before enrollment does not replace watching people over time, and the study saw only 149 gliomas, 89 meningiomas and 29 acoustic neuromas.
- There was no unexposed group. Almost everyone used a phone, so the comparison group was the bottom half of callers, who averaged up to 10.6 minutes of calls a day, by the count of scientists of the International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields (ICBE-EMF).
- The heavy-user result cannot rule out a large increase. For 1,908 or more hours of calls, the glioma hazard ratio was 1.07, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.62 to 1.86. ICBE-EMF scientists pointed out that the study could not rule out a 28 percent higher glioma risk after 10 years or a 52 percent higher risk after 15 years.
- Call time is not dose. A phone's power output depends on the network and signal strength.
- The lead author helped write the limits. Maria Feychting was a member of the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP), the non-governmental body that writes the heating-based limits, from 2008 to 2020, and its Vice Chair from 2012 to 2020, according to ICNIRP's own records. She was one of the scientists who prepared ICNIRP's 2020 radio-frequency guidelines. Her 2024 COSMOS disclosure lists her as Vice Chair only from May 2016, which leaves out her 2012 to 2016 term.
- The authors conceded the key point. Answering their critics, they wrote that "statistical power is the main current limitation of our study."

Did COSMOS look at headaches, tinnitus, hearing or sleep? Yes.
- A 2019 paper followed 21,049 people in Sweden and 3,120 in Finland for 4 years, using operator-recorded call time. People in the highest tenth of call time, more than 276 minutes a week, had 21 percent higher odds of weekly headaches, an odds ratio of 1.21 (95 percent confidence interval 1.02 to 1.43), after adjustment for age, sex and country. The authors then also adjusted for painkiller use, sleep disturbance, depression and general health, which brought it down to 1.13 (0.95 to 1.34). The authors reported no link for tinnitus or hearing loss, but their own Table 2 shows 19 percent higher odds of tinnitus in people between the 75th and 90th percentiles of call time, an odds ratio of 1.19 (1.03 to 1.38).
- A 2020 paper used the same Swedish and Finnish groups. Most sleep measures were not linked to call time. Insomnia was more common in the highest tenth of call time, more than 258 minutes a week, an odds ratio of 1.24 (1.03 to 1.51). After the authors weighted call time for lower exposure from third-generation (3G) networks than from second-generation Global System for Mobile Telecommunications (GSM) networks, the top-tenth figure fell to 1.09 (0.89 to 1.33), and they attributed the first result to other aspects of phone use. Their own weighted table still shows 17 percent higher odds of insomnia at 24 to 84 weighted minutes a week, an odds ratio of 1.17 (1.01 to 1.36).
- A 2024 paper pooled 78,437 people in the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. After call time and texting were put in the same model, high call time was not clearly linked to weekly headache, an odds ratio of 1.04 (0.94 to 1.15). High texting was, an odds ratio of 1.40 (1.25 to 1.56).

Those symptom papers have the same core limits: call time is not absorbed dose, there was no group of non-users, follow-up was short, and industry money went into COSMOS funding in Sweden, Finland and the United Kingdom, as each paper's own funding statement says. They do not show that radio-frequency exposure is harmless for headaches, tinnitus or sleep.

If you talk two hours a day with the phone held to your ear, that is far heavier use than those "highest tenth" cut-offs, which were about 37 to 39 minutes a day. COSMOS does not change RF Safe's advice: use speakerphone or an air-tube headset, and keep the phone off your head.

Published critiques of the 2024 tumor paper: Moskowitz and colleagues for the ICBE-EMF (2024); Michael Kundi (2024), both in Environment International.

RF Safe's position: a short, underpowered study with no non-user group, a former ICNIRP Vice Chair as lead author, and industry money in the funding is not proof of safety. RF Safe does not claim phones directly cause a person's disease. RF Safe's low-fidelity biology hypothesis holds that reduced biological fidelity raises the risk of error, and its S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis proposes how that happens.

Related: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?; Can phone use cause headaches?; Can phone use cause ringing in the ears (tinnitus)?; Can phones or Wi-Fi disrupt sleep or the sleep hormone melatonin?; Is speakerphone or a headset better for calls?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with MOBI-Kids (Castaño-Vinyals, 2022)?
entries.question: What is wrong with MOBI-Kids (Castaño-Vinyals, 2022)?
entries.text:
MOBI-Kids does not show that phones are safe for children. Its results made phones look protective for young brains, which its own authors rejected, and its authors admit bias stops them from ruling out an increased risk.

What it was: a 14-country study by Castaño-Vinyals and colleagues in Environment International (2022) of 899 people aged 10 to 24 with brain tumors and 1,910 controls. It reported no evidence of a causal link.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- The results point the wrong way. The odds of brain tumors appeared to fall as phone use rose. The authors themselves said the large number of odds ratios below 1 is unlikely to be a real protective effect, and they blamed recall by parents and symptoms that changed phone use before diagnosis.
- The authors could not rule out harm. They wrote that these biases "prevent us from ruling out a small increased risk."
- The comparison group was hospital patients. Controls were young people operated on for appendicitis, not the general population.
- Participation was lopsided. 72 percent of patients took part, but only 54 percent of controls.
- Some tumors were left out. Critics object to excluding centrally located tumors, and the authors admit there were too few cases for several age, timing, location and tumor-type analyses.

Published critique: Hardell and Moskowitz, Reviews on Environmental Health (2022).

RF Safe's position: a study whose results say phones protect children's brains has a bias problem, not a safety finding.

Related: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/mobi-kids-2022/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with NCRP Report 86 (1986)?
entries.question: What is wrong with NCRP Report 86 (1986)?
entries.text:
National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP) Report 86 (1986) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It sets limits to prevent heating, and it does not count non-thermal evidence it chose not to accept.

What it claimed: NCRP recommends exposure criteria despite acknowledged evidentiary limitations and expects future evaluation.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Behavior does not isolate mechanism: A behavioral marker alone cannot identify the underlying mechanism. NCRP states this limitation in the report itself.
- A reduction factor is a policy step: Margins around a threshold do not independently test all outcomes. The exposure rationale and reduction factors are set out in chapter 17.

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/ncrp-1986/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the 2006 Danish cohort update (Schüz)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the 2006 Danish cohort update (Schüz)?
entries.text:
The 2006 Danish cohort update (Schüz) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It never measured who used a phone or how much, and it counted the heaviest users as unexposed.

What it claimed: The authors reported no association and argued that large overall associations were excluded.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Subscription is not dose: The cohort identifies an administrative category, not a measured radiation dose. The exposure group derives from early subscription records; the 2011 methods describe the historical cohort.
- Same cohort, updated: The Danish reports are related observations, not separate replications. The 2006 and 2011 publications describe updates of the subscriber study.
- This update kept the same exposure design: subscription status from 1982 to 1995, with the 200,507 corporate subscriptions removed from the exposed group.

Published critiques: Fredrik Söderqvist and colleagues (2012).

RF Safe's position: a study that cannot tell users from non-users cannot clear phones.

Related: What is wrong with the Danish cohort studies of phone subscribers?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/danish-2006/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the 2011 Danish cohort update (Frei, BMJ)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the 2011 Danish cohort update (Frei, BMJ)?
entries.text:
The 2011 Danish cohort update does not show that phones are safe. Its own authors admit it misclassified phone users as unexposed.

What it was: an update by Frei and colleagues in the BMJ (2011) of the Danish subscriber cohort. It followed 358,403 private subscribers from the 1982 to 1995 phone company records, with follow-up through 2007. It reported no increased risk of brain and nervous system tumors.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- The authors admitted the misclassification. Corporate subscriptions (200,507 of them) were excluded, and the paper says: "Because we excluded corporate subscriptions, mobile phone users who do not have a subscription in their own name will have been misclassified as unexposed."
- Most of the "unexposed" group were phone users. Subscription data stopped in 1995, so everyone who got a phone after 1995 was counted as unexposed. Phone use spread widely after 1995, but none of those new users counted as exposed.
- There was no dose information. Exposure was only years since first private subscription. There was no call time, no side of the head and no cordless phone use.
- It is the same cohort, not a new test. This paper updates the 2001 report, which was paid for in part by the two Danish phone companies, TeleDanmark Mobil and Sonofon.

Published critique: Söderqvist, Carlberg and Hardell, Reviews on Environmental Health (2012).

RF Safe's position: when the authors say users were counted as unexposed, the "no risk" result cannot be used to clear phones.

Related: What is wrong with the Danish cohort studies of phone subscribers?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/danish-2011/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Auvinen Finnish brain tumor study (2002)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Auvinen Finnish brain tumor study (2002)?
entries.text:
The Auvinen Finnish brain tumor study (2002) is often listed among the studies said to show phones are safe, but its own data contain a harm signal, set out below.

What it claimed: Overall associations were absent; exposure limitations restricted interpretation.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Limited exposure information: The authors themselves regarded exposure information as inadequate for a strong risk assessment. The conclusion identifies limited exposure information as a weakness of the register-based approach.
- Analog-phone glioma signal: The authors found a glioma association with older analog phones. The abstract notes a weak glioma association with analog phones.

RF Safe's position: absence of proof from a study blind to heavy, long-term use is not proof of safety.

Related: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/auvinen-2002/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Chapman Australian brain cancer trends study (2016)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Chapman Australian brain cancer trends study (2016)?
entries.text:
The Chapman Australian brain cancer trends study (2016) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Population cancer rates cannot clear an exposure that was never measured in the people who got sick.

What it claimed: Observed patterns did not match the modeled phone-risk scenarios; older-age increases began before mobile adoption.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Ten-year model lag: The tested lag is a modeling condition, not a universal biological constant. The published abstract specifies a ten-year lag in its scenarios.
- No individual linkage: Individual phone use and individual cancer outcomes were not linked. The authors explicitly identify this as an ecological-trends analysis.

Published critiques: P. Bandara (2016); L. Lloyd Morgan and colleagues (2016); D. P. Wojcik (2016).

RF Safe's position: rising tumor rates in later registry data, not flat rates up to 2008, are what matter now.

Related: Don't flat brain cancer rates prove phones are safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/chapman-2016/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Christensen Danish acoustic neuroma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2004)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Christensen Danish acoustic neuroma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2004)?
entries.text:
The Christensen Danish acoustic neuroma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2004) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It is one national arm of INTERPHONE, whose pooled data found raised risk in the heaviest users, and its own result is too imprecise to rule out harm.

What it claimed: The authors found no evidence of increased acoustic-neuroma risk.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Wide rare-tumor interval: The null estimate is not a narrow exclusion of increased risk. Overall relative risk was 0.90 (95 percent confidence interval 0.51 to 1.57).
- Reference-group exposure dispute: The comparison group of non-regular users was not free of wireless-phone exposure. Hardell and Hansson Mild questioned cordless exposure and the regular-use definition.

Published critiques: Lennart Hardell (2004); Michael Kundi (2004).

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of 'heavy.'

Related: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/christensen-acoustic-2004/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Christensen Danish brain tumor study (INTERPHONE arm) (2005)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Christensen Danish brain tumor study (INTERPHONE arm) (2005)?
entries.text:
The Christensen Danish brain tumor study (INTERPHONE arm) (2005) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It is one national arm of INTERPHONE, whose pooled data found raised glioma risk in the heaviest users, and its own results show the same signs of bias.

What it claimed: The investigators reported no association for the tumor outcomes examined.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- A pattern that points to bias: The results made phones look protective for high-grade glioma, which no biology predicts. The abstract gives high-grade glioma odds ratio 0.58 (0.37 to 0.90) and low-grade odds ratio 1.08 (0.58 to 2.00).

Published critiques: Brian D. Gale (2006).

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of 'heavy.'

Related: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?
