entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the D'Andrea chronic rat study (1986)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the D'Andrea chronic rat study (1986)?
entries.text:
The D'Andrea chronic rat study (1986) is often listed among the studies said to show phones are safe, but its own data contain a harm signal, set out below.

What it claimed: The abstract reports multiple null physiological findings together with significant shuttlebox and lever-pressing differences.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Mixed findings, not a null: Labeling the whole paper as no effect would erase reported behavioral findings. The abstract distinguishes unchanged physiological measures from significant behavioral differences.

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the D'Andrea, Gandhi and Lords rat study (1977)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the D'Andrea, Gandhi and Lords rat study (1977)?
entries.text:
The D'Andrea, Gandhi and Lords rat study (1977) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It measured heating and short-term behavior, not the long-term, non-thermal effects people actually face.

What it claimed: The paper identifies resonance near 600 megahertz (MHz) and a short-term work-stoppage boundary between the tested 7.5 and 10 milliwatts per square centimeter (mW/cm²) continuous-wave (CW) settings.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute response versus chronic disease: The International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields (2022) cites this paper when it challenges using short-term behavior thresholds to set long-term health limits.
- Pulse comparison has a narrow meaning: The small pulse subset does not establish general pulse safety. Three animals received the selected pulse conditions, which did not produce work stoppage.

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/dandrea-gandhi-lords-1977/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Danish cohort skin cancer report (Poulsen) (2013)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Danish cohort skin cancer report (Poulsen) (2013)?
entries.text:
The Danish cohort skin cancer report (Poulsen) (2013) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It never measured who used a phone or how much, and it counted the heaviest users as unexposed.

What it claimed: The authors found little evidence that mobile-phone use increased skin-cancer risk.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- A subscription is not a dose: Holding a phone contract says nothing about how much radio-frequency (RF) energy reached a person's skin. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) review names this subscription-based design as a limitation.
- Long-term melanoma not ruled out: For head/neck melanoma in men after at least thirteen years, incidence rate ratio (IRR) was 1.20 (95 percent confidence interval 0.65 to 2.22).

RF Safe's position: a study that cannot tell users from non-users cannot clear phones.

Related: What is wrong with the Danish cohort studies of phone subscribers?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/danish-skin-2013/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the de Lorge and Ezell rat study (1980)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the de Lorge and Ezell rat study (1980)?
entries.text:
The de Lorge and Ezell rat study (1980) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It measured heating and short-term behavior, not the long-term, non-thermal effects people actually face.

What it claimed: The authors linked frequency-dependent performance disruption to penetration and anatomical absorption differences.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Behavior is not lifetime health: The measured endpoint is too narrow to establish a general chronic-safety conclusion. The outcome was observing behavior during irradiation, not lifetime tumor incidence.
- Small male-only sample: The tested population cannot characterize rare or subgroup-dependent health effects. The experiment involved eight male rats.

Published critiques: International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields (ICBE-EMF) (2022).

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the de Lorge rhesus monkey study (1984)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the de Lorge rhesus monkey study (1984)?
entries.text:
The de Lorge rhesus monkey study (1984) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It measured heating and short-term behavior, not the long-term, non-thermal effects people actually face.

What it claimed: Temperature change predicted behavioral disruption better than incident power or estimated whole-body specific absorption rate (SAR) in this experiment.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute-to-chronic extrapolation: A one-hour task experiment is being asked a question it did not test when used as universal safety proof. The primary paper tested 60-minute sessions and task performance.
- Five animals, one model: The population is narrow for general public-health extrapolation. Five rhesus monkeys were studied under the task protocol.

Published critiques: International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields (ICBE-EMF) (2022).

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the de Lorge squirrel monkey study (1979)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the de Lorge squirrel monkey study (1979)?
entries.text:
The de Lorge squirrel monkey study (1979) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It measured heating and short-term behavior, not the long-term, non-thermal effects people actually face.

What it claimed: The publisher abstract associates consistent task disruption with a rectal-temperature rise exceeding 1 °C under the tested conditions.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- No task disruption is not no change: The threshold depends on what was measured. The abstract reports temperature elevation at 10 milliwatts per square centimeter (mW/cm²), below the reported behavioral-disruption settings.

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/delorge-1979/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Deltour Nordic glioma trends study (2012)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Deltour Nordic glioma trends study (2012)?
entries.text:
The Deltour Nordic glioma trends study (2012) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Population cancer rates cannot clear an exposure that was never measured in the people who got sick.

What it claimed: Several proposed phone-risk scenarios did not fit the observed glioma trend under the modeled assumptions; smaller risks and longer induction remained possible.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Conditional risk exclusion: Excluded effects depend on both magnitude and induction time. The simulations reject some combinations but the conclusion allows smaller risks or longer induction.
- Population-level exposure: The analysis does not link each diagnosed person to a measured exposure history. It compares population incidence with modeled mobile-phone risk scenarios.
- “No change” is not a flat rate: The observed increase and the modeled attribution question are different findings. The 2012 abstract reports annual incidence increases of 0.4% in men and 0.3% in women over 1979 to 2008.
- Evidence ends in 2008: An older observation window cannot settle what later registry years show. The paper ends in 2008; the Nordic follow-up extends through 2016.
- Glioma is not every head or neck tumor: A result for glioma cannot stand in for meningioma, thyroid or salivary-gland cancer.

RF Safe's position: rising tumor rates in later registry data, not flat rates up to 2008, are what matter now.

Related: Don't flat brain cancer rates prove phones are safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/deltour-2012/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the European SCENIHR 2015 opinion?
entries.question: What is wrong with the European SCENIHR 2015 opinion?
entries.text:
The European Scientific Committee on Emerging and Newly Identified Health Risks (SCENIHR) 2015 opinion is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It restates selected studies as reassurance; it is not new evidence of safety.

What it claimed: The committee’s radio-frequency (RF) synthesis was reassuring for the health outcomes discussed in its official summary.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Evidence cutoff matters: Later evidence needs appraisal alongside the historical opinion. The opinion was adopted on 27 January 2015.

Published critiques: Cindy Sage and colleagues (2015).

RF Safe's position: in 2021 a federal court found the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) failed to explain how its limits protect against non-cancer harm, and these reviews do not fill that gap.

Related: What is wrong with the FDA, FCC, National Cancer Institute and European committee reviews that call phones safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/scenihr-2015/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the European SCHEER 2023 opinion?
entries.question: What is wrong with the European SCHEER 2023 opinion?
entries.text:
The European Scientific Committee on Health, Environmental and Emerging Risks (SCHEER) 2023 opinion is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It restates selected studies as reassurance; it is not new evidence of safety.

What it claimed: The committee recommended technical updating while judging evidence of adverse effects below existing limits insufficiently strong.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Review-of-reviews dependency: Several apparently separate summaries can depend on overlapping primary studies. The committee relied mainly on meta-analyses and systematic reviews rather than individual papers.
- Evidence strength is not zero risk: The conclusion reports an evidence-strength judgement, not proof that no effects exist. The abstract says moderate or strong adverse-effect evidence was not identified below limits.
- Guideline assessed in same synthesis: The opinion explicitly incorporates the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) 2020 rationale. Its recommendation addresses technical changes.

RF Safe's position: in 2021 a federal court found the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) failed to explain how its limits protect against non-cancer harm, and these reviews do not fill that gap.

Related: What is wrong with the FDA, FCC, National Cancer Institute and European committee reviews that call phones safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/scheer-2023/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the FCC 2019 order keeping its limits?
entries.question: What is wrong with the FCC 2019 order keeping its limits?
entries.text:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) 2019 order keeping its limits is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It restates selected studies as reassurance; it is not new evidence of safety.

What it claimed: The Commission considered the available evidence and agency advice sufficient to keep the exposure limits.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Decision is not new evidence: An agency decision must not be counted as an additional independent study. FCC 19-126 is an order assessing a record, not an exposure experiment.
- Noncancer reasoning remanded: A court required a more reasoned response to material noncancer and environmental evidence. The 2021 majority granted the petitions in part and remanded.
- In 2021 the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit sent this order back. It found the FCC failed to give a reasoned explanation that its limits protect against harms other than cancer. The court upheld the FCC's explanation on cancer.

Published critiques: International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields (ICBE-EMF) (2022).

RF Safe's position: in 2021 a federal court found the FCC failed to explain how its limits protect against non-cancer harm, and these reviews do not fill that gap.

Related: What is wrong with the FDA, FCC, National Cancer Institute and European committee reviews that call phones safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/fcc-2019/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the FDA's 2020 cancer literature review?
entries.question: What is wrong with the FDA's 2020 cancer literature review?
entries.text:
The Food and Drug Administration's (FDA's) 2020 review does not show that phones are safe. It looked only at cancer, it went out of its way to search for negative results, and it ends before the major studies of 2024 and 2025.

What it was: an FDA review from February 2020 of animal and human cancer studies, searched mainly from 2008 to 2018 with some updates through August 2019. It concluded that the evidence did not show phones cause tumors.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Cancer only. It did not assess non-cancer outcomes such as fertility, sleep, heart function or development, or directly review cell-level mechanisms, so it cannot support an all-health safety claim.
- It added a search just for null results. Section IV.A of the report describes a separate search for studies with negative results, which added six papers.
- It is out of date. It ends before the 2024 and 2025 World Health Organization-commissioned reviews, including the animal cancer review that rated the evidence for gliomas and heart schwannomas in male rats high certainty.
- It cannot cover the court's gap. In 2021 the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit found that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) failed to explain how its limits protect against harms other than cancer. A cancer-only review cannot answer that.

RF Safe's position: a dated, cancer-only review that added a hunt for negative studies is not proof that phones are safe.

Related: What is wrong with the FDA, FCC, National Cancer Institute and European committee reviews that call phones safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/fda-review-2020/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the first Danish cohort report (Johansen, 2001)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the first Danish cohort report (Johansen, 2001)?
entries.text:
The first Danish cohort report does not show that phones are safe. The phone companies helped fund it, it never measured phone use, and it left corporate users outside the exposed group.

What it was: a study of Danish phone subscribers from 1982 to 1995 by Johansen, Boice, McLaughlin and Olsen, published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in 2001. It found no link between holding a subscription and cancer.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Phone company money and phone company records. The study was supported by grants from the two Danish phone companies, TeleDanmark Mobil and Sonofon. Those same companies supplied the subscriber lists.
- Corporate users were excluded from the exposed group. Of 723,421 subscriptions, the authors removed 200,507 corporate subscriptions, the business accounts most likely to belong to the heaviest users. Those people were not counted as exposed, so they stayed in the comparison group with everyone else.
- A subscription is not a dose. The study had no call time, no record of which side of the head the phone was held on, and no cordless phone use. Light and heavy users were treated the same.
- Every later Danish paper reused this design. The 2006 and 2011 updates follow the same cohort, so they repeat the same flaws. They are not independent confirmations.

Published critique: Söderqvist, Carlberg and Hardell, Reviews on Environmental Health (2012), reviewed all four Danish cohort papers and found the subscription design too weak to support reassurance.

RF Safe's position: a study paid for in part by the phone companies, and unable to tell users from non-users, cannot clear phones.

Related: What is wrong with the Danish cohort studies of phone subscribers?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/danish-2001/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Hepworth UK glioma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2006)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Hepworth UK glioma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2006)?
entries.text:
The Hepworth UK glioma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2006) is often listed among the studies said to show phones are safe, but its own data contain a harm signal, set out below.

What it claimed: No substantially raised glioma risk was found within approximately ten years of first use.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Same-side tumor signal: Glioma was more common on the side of the head where people held their phone. Same-side odds ratio was 1.24 (1.02 to 1.52), versus opposite-side odds ratio 0.75 (0.61 to 0.93).
- Low and unequal participation: Only 51 percent of eligible glioma patients and 45 percent of eligible controls took part, and published letters point to social differences between the groups.
- Few long-term users: Morgan notes that only a small fraction of participants had used phones for ten years or longer.

Published critiques: Lennart Hardell (2006); L. Lloyd Morgan (2006).

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of 'heavy.'

Related: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/hepworth-2006/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Hook Molt-4 cell DNA study (2004)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Hook Molt-4 cell DNA study (2004)?
entries.text:
The Hook Molt-4 cell DNA study (2004) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. A short test of one endpoint in cells cannot show that years of exposure are safe.

What it claimed: Neither measured DNA damage nor apoptosis differed significantly from sham.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute endpoint is not lifetime safety: It tested one narrow question, so it cannot back a broad safety claim. A lymphoblastoid cell line and two acute endpoints were examined.
- Comet protocol differs: The earlier positive experiment and this study did not use identical comet processing. Phillips et al. identified proteinase K in their earlier protocol but not Hook’s.

Published critiques: J. L. Phillips (2009).

RF Safe's position: a short null test in cells does not erase the 1,465 harm-side studies in RF Safe's research map.

Related: What about the lab studies that found no DNA damage from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/hook-molt4-2004/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the ICNIRP 1998 guidelines?
entries.question: What is wrong with the ICNIRP 1998 guidelines?
entries.text:
The International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) 1998 guidelines are cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. They do not show that. They set limits to prevent heating, and they do not count non-thermal evidence it chose not to accept.

What it claimed: The committee considered the evidence sufficient for limits based on established short-term effects, but not for deriving restrictions from proposed long-term effects.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Chronic effects gap: The basis for the restrictions and the broad chronic-safety claim answer different questions. The Basis for Limiting Exposure section separates established immediate effects from insufficient long-term evidence.
- What safety factors cover: A reduction factor is not a direct chronic exposure experiment. The derivation reduces a whole-body radio-frequency (RF) starting level for occupational and general-public restrictions.
- Standards body authorship: The author is the same organization that proposes the exposure limits. ICNIRP is identified as the collective author.

Published critiques: International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields (ICBE-EMF) (2022).

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/icnirp-1998/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the ICNIRP 2018 note on the animal cancer studies?
entries.question: What is wrong with the ICNIRP 2018 note on the animal cancer studies?
entries.text:
The International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) 2018 note on the animal cancer studies is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It is the committee that writes the limits grading the evidence against its own limits.

What it claimed: ICNIRP concluded that the cited studies did not justify revising its exposure guidelines.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Rejection is not a null experiment: This note interprets positive animal reports; it does not add an independent exposed/control dataset. The note is an assessment of National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini rather than a new experiment.

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/icnirp-animal-2018/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the ICNIRP 2020 guidelines?
entries.question: What is wrong with the ICNIRP 2020 guidelines?
entries.text:
The 2020 guidelines of the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) do not show that wireless radiation is safe. They are built to prevent heating, and they count only the harms the commission itself accepts as substantiated.

What they are: exposure limits from 100 kilohertz to 300 gigahertz, published in Health Physics in 2020 by ICNIRP, a private organization registered in Munich, Germany. They say adverse effects below the limits are not substantiated.

Why RF Safe flags them:
- The limits are built on heating. They start from a whole-body level of about 4 watts per kilogram (W/kg), where animals in short experiments stopped performing trained tasks, and divide by safety factors down to 0.08 W/kg for the public.
- "Not substantiated" is not "safe." The commission sets its own bar for accepting a harm and then finds that non-thermal effects do not clear it.
- The commission graded challenges to its own work. ICNIRP rejected the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini rat tumor findings in its own notes, then relied on those notes in the 2020 guidelines. Ronald Melnick published a rebuttal in Health Physics (2020).
- A closed circle of authors. A 2022 analysis by Nordhagen and Flydal in Reviews on Environmental Health found that the research behind the guidelines comes from a small, tightly connected network of co-authors.
- A court rejected the non-cancer reasoning behind the United States decision. In 2021 the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit sent back the Federal Communications Commission's 2019 decision to keep its own heating-based limits, because the agency failed to explain how they protect against harms other than cancer.

Published critiques: International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields, Environmental Health (2022); Nordhagen and Flydal (2022).

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat do not protect against non-thermal effects, and the people who wrote them should not be the ones grading the evidence.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/icnirp-2020/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the ICNIRP critique of the NTP and Ramazzini studies (2020)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the ICNIRP critique of the NTP and Ramazzini studies (2020)?
entries.text:
The International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) critique of the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini studies (2020) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It is the committee that writes the limits grading the evidence against its own limits.

What it claimed: ICNIRP judged the limitations sufficient to prevent a carcinogenicity conclusion from those studies.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Published methodological dispute: The rejection of animal findings is contested, not an uncontested null result. Melnick’s published correspondence addresses the note; ICNIRP replies on pathology, survival, statistics and exposure.
- Hazard versus public dose: Evidence for a carcinogenic hazard and the size of risk at public exposure levels are different questions. The response emphasizes that the animal whole-body exposures exceed public restrictions.
- Guideline author evaluates challenge: The same standards organization evaluates evidence potentially relevant to revising its limits. ICNIRP is the collective author of the note and guideline.
- Pathology review disputed: A claim of insufficient blinding must be evaluated against the entire pathology-review process. Melnick describes independent quality assessment and masked pathology-working-group review; ICNIRP maintains that earlier unblinded stages could still bias outcomes.
- Multiple-comparison dispute: Counting many tests is not, by itself, a complete assessment of the reported tumor evidence. Melnick invokes rare-tumor statistics and the NTP weight-of-evidence approach; ICNIRP asks for formal control of the relevant multiple-comparison error.

Published critiques: Ronald Melnick (2020).

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/icnirp-animal-2020/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the IEEE C95.1-1991 standard (1992)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the IEEE C95.1-1991 standard (1992)?
entries.text:
The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) C95.1-1991 standard (1992) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It sets limits to prevent heating, and it does not count non-thermal evidence it chose not to accept.

What it claimed: The issuer presents recommendations intended to prevent harmful human effects, with a supporting rationale in the standard.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Adoption is not independent replication: A standard and a rule adopting it are linked judgments, not separate experiments. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) identifies the IEEE provisions underlying its rule.

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/ieee-1991-ansi-1992/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Inskip US brain tumor study (2001)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Inskip US brain tumor study (2001)?
entries.text:
The Inskip United States brain tumor study (2001) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its design could not see heavy, long-term users, so a 'no link' headline does not clear phones.

What it claimed: Recent-use results did not support causation; long-term heavy use remained unresolved.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Long-term use unresolved: The original conclusion did not settle heavy lifelong use. Authors state that their data were insufficient for long-term heavy users and long induction periods.
- Tumor-specific uncertainty: The ranges for each tumor type are far wider than a no-link headline implies. Above 100 cumulative hours, estimates included glioma 0.9 (0.5 to 1.6) and acoustic neuroma 1.4 (0.6 to 3.5).

RF Safe's position: absence of proof from a study blind to heavy, long-term use is not proof of safety.

Related: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/inskip-2001/

entries.title: Safety Evidence (overview): What is wrong with the INTERPHONE 13-country brain tumor study (2010)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE 13-country brain tumor study (2010)?
entries.text:
INTERPHONE does not show that phones are safe. It was the largest case-control study of phones and brain tumors at the time, and it found raised glioma risk in its heaviest users. Its own bias checks identify downward bias in its overall results.

What it was: a study in 13 countries, coordinated by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), with 2,708 glioma and 2,409 meningioma patients and matched controls. Gliomas are tumors arising from the brain's supporting cells. Published by the INTERPHONE Study Group in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2010.

What it claimed: no overall increase in risk, and the effects of long-term heavy use needed more study.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- The heaviest users had more glioma. At 1,640 or more lifetime hours of calls, the glioma odds ratio was 1.40 (95 percent confidence interval 1.03 to 1.89). That means 40 percent higher odds, and the result was statistically significant.
- "Heavy" was not heavy. 1,640 hours is about 27 minutes a day over 10 years. By any modern standard, that is light use.
- The study's own alternative comparison made the signal stronger. In Appendix 2 the authors compared heavy users with the lightest regular users instead of with non-users. The glioma odds ratio for the heaviest users rose to 1.82 (1.15 to 2.89). For people who had used a phone for 10 or more years, it was 2.18 (1.43 to 3.31).
- The main results contain an impossible pattern. Most lower-use groups had glioma odds ratios below 1, mostly about 0.7 to 0.8. Read literally, that says phones protect the brain. No biology predicts that. It points to selection bias: patients agreed to take part more often than healthy controls, and phone users more often than non-users.
- Recall was unreliable. Use was reconstructed from interviews after diagnosis, and the IARC reported substantial recall error.
- Industry paid part of the bill. Of about 19.2 million euros, 5.5 million came from industry sources, including 3.5 million from the Mobile Manufacturers' Forum and the GSM Association, a mobile industry trade group. The money was routed through the International Union Against Cancer.

Later studies backed up the heavy-user signal. A 2017 re-analysis of INTERPHONE's Canadian data that corrected for recall and selection bias (Momoli and colleagues, American Journal of Epidemiology) found glioma odds of 2.2 (1.3 to 4.1) above 558 lifetime hours. The French CERENAT study (Coureau and colleagues, 2014) found glioma odds of 2.89 (1.41 to 5.93) at 896 or more lifetime hours.

Published critique: Rodolfo Saracci and Jonathan Samet, International Journal of Epidemiology (2010), wrote that INTERPHONE cannot settle lifetime risk and that its low odds ratios point to bias.

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real. It was buried under bias and a definition of "heavy" equivalent to about half an hour a day over a decade.

Related: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?; Do cell phones cause brain tumors in people?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/interphone-2010/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE acoustic neuroma study (2011)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE acoustic neuroma study (2011)?
entries.text:
The INTERPHONE acoustic neuroma study (2011) is often listed among the studies said to show phones are safe, but its own data contain a harm signal, set out below.

What it claimed: No increase for ever-regular use; high-call-time findings remained unresolved.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Lag-sensitive high-use result: The most exposed group was not uniformly reassuring. For at least 1,640 hours, odds ratio was 1.32 (0.88 to 1.97); with a five-year lag it was 2.79 (1.51 to 5.16).
- Slow tumor development: The study window was too short for a slow-growing tumor. The authors identified acoustic neuroma’s slow growth as a limitation.

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of 'heavy.'

Related: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/interphone-acoustic-2011/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE radio-frequency dose study (Cardis) (2011)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE radio-frequency dose study (Cardis) (2011)?
entries.text:
The INTERPHONE radio-frequency dose study (Cardis) (2011) is often listed among the studies said to show phones are safe, but its own data contain a harm signal, set out below.

What it claimed: The authors reported suggestive increases among long-term users with high estimated radio-frequency (RF) exposure.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Earlier-dose signal: The 1.91 estimate concerns a specific time-lagged dose analysis. Highest modeled dose quintile for exposure seven or more years before diagnosis: glioma odds ratio 1.91 (95 percent confidence interval 1.05 to 3.47). Overall highest-dose quintile odds ratio was 1.35 (0.96 to 1.90).

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of 'heavy.'

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Japanese half of the Korea-Japan rat study (Imaida) (2026)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Japanese half of the Korea-Japan rat study (Imaida) (2026)?
entries.text:
The Japanese half of the Korea-Japan rat study (Imaida) (2026) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. One negative animal model does not cancel the clear tumor findings of the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini studies.

What it claimed: No reproducible exposure-related carcinogenic or genotoxic effect under the tested protocol.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Survival and tumor comparison: Different survival can change time available to observe tumors. Radio-frequency (RF)-exposed rats had higher survival and lower body weight/food consumption; the authors discuss these differences.
- Shared protocol boundaries: Two sites add replication, but do not erase limits of the common design. The country studies were jointly planned around the same male-rat, single-dose exposure.
- The rats were exposed at 4 watts per kilogram (W/kg) whole-body, 50 times the 0.08 W/kg whole-body limit for the public. Co-author Young Hwan Ahn joined International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP)'s Main Commission in July 2024.

RF Safe's position: the NTP and Ramazzini findings stand, and the World Health Organization-commissioned animal review rated the tumor evidence high certainty.

Related: What about the animal studies that found no cancer from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/imaida-japan-2026/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Justesen and King rat study (1970)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Justesen and King rat study (1970)?
entries.text:
The Justesen and King rat study (1970) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It measured heating and short-term behavior, not the long-term, non-thermal effects people actually face.

What it claimed: The authors considered their acute observations compatible with heating, while explicitly declining a broad human-safety inference.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Selected endpoints, not lifetime safety: The authors limited the reach of their reassuring observations. Their discussion explicitly cautions against generalizing rat findings to people and notes unknown long-term genetic effects.
- Unresolved cavity exposure details: The apparatus left some exposure characteristics uncertain. The authors discuss limited modulation control, ambient-temperature sensitivity and unknown instantaneous field peaks.

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/justesen-king-1970/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Karipidis Australian brain tumor trends study (2018)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Karipidis Australian brain tumor trends study (2018)?
entries.text:
The Karipidis Australian brain tumor trends study (2018) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Population cancer rates cannot clear an exposure that was never measured in the people who got sick.

What it claimed: The patterns did not support a phone-related increase, with smaller or longer-latency effects unresolved.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Adults aged 20 to 59: The analyzed population does not directly represent older adults or children. Eligibility was ages 20 to 59.
- Longer latency unresolved: The strongest conclusion stops short of excluding every delay. The discussion allows small risks or latency longer than fifteen years.
- Use prevalence assumptions: Population uptake does not encode every change in dose or use pattern. The model applied shared prevalence estimates across ages and sexes and lacked individual exposure histories.

RF Safe's position: rising tumor rates in later registry data, not flat rates up to 2008, are what matter now.

Related: Don't flat brain cancer rates prove phones are safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/karipidis-trends-2018/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Korean half of the Korea-Japan rat study (Kim) (2026)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Korean half of the Korea-Japan rat study (Kim) (2026)?
entries.text:
The Korean half of the Korea-Japan rat study (Kim) (2026) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. One negative animal model does not cancel the clear tumor findings of the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini studies.

What it claimed: The authors interpret the exposure as noncarcinogenic and nongenotoxic under their protocol.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Rare-tumor sensitivity: The experiment cannot reliably exclude modest increases in rare tumors. The authors acknowledge limited power at 70/group. Cardiac schwannomas occurred in 2/70 exposed animals, with no statistically significant increase.
- One dose; thermal checks limited: Dose dependence and lifelong temperature stability were not directly established. One specific absorption rate (SAR) was used; temperature was monitored in the 28-day study, not throughout the chronic phase.
- The rats were exposed at 4 watts per kilogram (W/kg) whole-body, 50 times the 0.08 W/kg whole-body limit for the public. Malignant heart schwannomas, the tumor the NTP found, appeared only in exposed rats: 2 of 70, versus none of 140 control rats.
- Co-author Young Hwan Ahn joined International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP)'s Main Commission in July 2024.

RF Safe's position: the NTP and Ramazzini findings stand, and the World Health Organization-commissioned animal review rated the tumor evidence high certainty.

Related: What about the animal studies that found no cancer from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/kim-korea-2026/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the La Regina rat study (2003)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the La Regina rat study (2003)?
entries.text:
The La Regina rat study (2003) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. One negative animal model does not cancel the clear tumor findings of the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini studies.

What it claimed: No significant spontaneous-tumor increase was reported under the tested signals.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Dose and waveform reach: Two handset signals do not span all exposures relevant to a broad safety claim. The experiment tested specified frequency-division multiple access (FDMA)/code-division multiple access (CDMA) conditions.
- Rare-tumor precision: A nonsignificant result needs an effect-size bound before it can be called evidence of no risk. The reported group sizes and null findings do not themselves specify the smallest excluded risk.

RF Safe's position: the NTP and Ramazzini findings stand, and the World Health Organization-commissioned animal review rated the tumor evidence high certainty.

Related: What about the animal studies that found no cancer from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/laregina-rats-2003/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Lagroye rat brain DNA study (2004)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Lagroye rat brain DNA study (2004)?
entries.text:
The Lagroye rat brain DNA study (2004) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. A short test of one endpoint in cells cannot show that years of exposure are safe.

What it claimed: No detected microwave-related damage using either assay variant.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute endpoint is not lifetime safety: It tested one narrow question, so it cannot back a broad safety claim. Only the specified acute brain-cell DNA endpoint was tested.
- Published assay-method dispute: Phillips and colleagues questioned the proteinase-K comparison. They argued that detergent in the digestion mixture could inactivate proteinase K.

Published critiques: J. L. Phillips (2009).

RF Safe's position: a short null test in cells does not erase the 1,465 harm-side studies in RF Safe's research map.

Related: What about the lab studies that found no DNA damage from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/lagroye-rat-comet-2004/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Lahkola five-country glioma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2007)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Lahkola five-country glioma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2007)?
entries.text:
The Lahkola five-country glioma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2007) is often listed among the studies said to show phones are safe, but its own data contain a harm signal, set out below.

What it claimed: No overall increase was found; long-term use in the most exposed region required further study.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Long-term laterality signal: The overall and long-term same-side estimates answer different questions. Overall odds ratio was 0.78 (0.68 to 0.91); >10-year same-side odds ratio was 1.39 (1.01 to 1.92), versus opposite-side 0.98 (0.71 to 1.37).

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of 'heavy.'

Related: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Lin, Guy and Caldwell rat study (1977)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Lin, Guy and Caldwell rat study (1977)?
entries.text:
The Lin, Guy and Caldwell rat study (1977) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It measured heating and short-term behavior, not the long-term, non-thermal effects people actually face.

What it claimed: National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP) treats the experiment as evidence relevant to behavioral disruption.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Historical basis is not a safety assay: The verified citation establishes a role in standards development, not a broad negative health result. NCRP places this paper in its work-stoppage rationale.

RF Safe's position: limits built on heat and short-term behavior do not protect against non-thermal effects.

Related: What studies are the phone exposure limits built on, and what is wrong with them?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Little US glioma trends study (2012)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Little US glioma trends study (2012)?
entries.text:
The Little United States glioma trends study (2012) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Population cancer rates cannot clear an exposure that was never measured in the people who got sick.

What it claimed: Some Swedish-study projections were incompatible with observed trends; modest INTERPHONE excesses could remain compatible.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- INTERPHONE excess compatible: The study cannot be accurately described as ruling out the INTERPHONE high-use signal. Its conclusion explicitly permits compatibility with modest INTERPHONE excess risks.
- Model assumptions contested: Critics dispute the mapping from study-specific risks to the United States population. Hardell and Carlberg question baseline selection and age/sex exposure assumptions in a BMJ rapid response.

Published critiques: Lennart Hardell and Michael Carlberg (2012).

RF Safe's position: rising tumor rates in later registry data, not flat rates up to 2008, are what matter now.

Related: Don't flat brain cancer rates prove phones are safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/little-2012/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Lönn Swedish brain tumor study (INTERPHONE arm) (2005)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Lönn Swedish brain tumor study (INTERPHONE arm) (2005)?
entries.text:
The Lönn Swedish brain tumor study (INTERPHONE arm) (2005) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It is one national arm of INTERPHONE, whose pooled data found raised glioma risk in the heaviest users, and it shares INTERPHONE's participation and recall problems.

What it claimed: The authors found no support for increased glioma or meningioma risk.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Participation and recall: A population-based frame does not remove every selection or reporting mechanism. Participation was 74% for glioma, 85% for meningioma and 71% for controls; use was reported retrospectively.
- INTERPHONE overlap: The national component and pooled project share an evidence family. The author list identifies the Swedish INTERPHONE group; the World Health Organization (WHO) review explicitly handles overlapping publications.

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of 'heavy.'

Related: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/lonn-2005/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Malyapa 2,450 megahertz cell study (1997)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Malyapa 2,450 megahertz cell study (1997)?
entries.text:
The Malyapa 2,450 megahertz cell study (1997) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. A short test of one endpoint in cells cannot show that years of exposure are safe.

What it claimed: No significant comet-assay difference under the specified conditions.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute endpoint is not lifetime safety: It tested one narrow question, so it cannot back a broad safety claim. Cultured-cell DNA migration was measured over hours, not disease over a lifespan.
- Cell culture is a different test: This was an extension to cultured cells, not an exact replication of the Lai–Singh rat-brain experiments. The original abstract describes in vitro experiments motivated by prior in vivo findings.
- Review author overlap: The later Moulder review shares Malyapa and Pickard with this experimental paper. Author lists establish the overlap.
- Motorola contracted this Washington University group to try to reproduce the Lai and Singh DNA-break findings, according to Microwave News. The contract specified a different version of the comet assay from the one Lai and Singh used, and Lai and Singh said the experiments were flawed.

RF Safe's position: a short null test in cells does not erase the 1,465 harm-side studies in RF Safe's research map.

Related: What about the lab studies that found no DNA damage from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/malyapa-2450-1997/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Malyapa cell phone band cell study (1997)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Malyapa cell phone band cell study (1997)?
entries.text:
The Malyapa cell phone band cell study (1997) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. A short test of one endpoint in cells cannot show that years of exposure are safe.

What it claimed: No detected DNA damage relative to sham at the tested dose and conditions.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute endpoint is not lifetime safety: It tested one narrow question, so it cannot back a broad safety claim. Two cell lines and their comet-assay response, rather than clinical disease, were tested.
- One specific absorption rate (SAR) does not map all signals: The two tested signals at one SAR do not establish a universal dose–response relationship. The abstract reports a SAR of 0.6 watts per kilogram (W/kg) for both signal types.
- Review author overlap: The later Moulder review shares Malyapa and Pickard with this experimental paper. Author lists establish the overlap.
- Motorola contracted this Washington University group to try to reproduce the Lai and Singh DNA-break findings, according to Microwave News.

RF Safe's position: a short null test in cells does not erase the 1,465 harm-side studies in RF Safe's research map.

Related: What about the lab studies that found no DNA damage from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/malyapa-cellular-1997/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Malyapa rat brain study (1998)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Malyapa rat brain study (1998)?
entries.text:
The Malyapa rat brain study (1998) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. A short test of one endpoint in cells cannot show that years of exposure are safe.

What it claimed: No significant exposed–sham difference; the authors preferred guillotine euthanasia because background damage and variability were lower.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute endpoint is not lifetime safety: It tested one narrow question, so it cannot back a broad safety claim. An acute brain-cell assay, not cumulative disease, was studied.
- International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC): not an exact replication: IARC rejected the study as a valid replication while retaining its independent contrary evidence. The Working Group identified protocol dependence in killing and tissue handling.
- Review author overlap: The later Moulder review shares Malyapa and Pickard with this experimental paper. Author lists establish the overlap.
- Motorola contracted this Washington University group to try to reproduce the Lai and Singh DNA-break findings, according to Microwave News.

Published critiques: IARC Working Group on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans (2013).

RF Safe's position: a short null test in cells does not erase the 1,465 harm-side studies in RF Safe's research map.

Related: What about the lab studies that found no DNA damage from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Million Women Study (2013 report)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Million Women Study (2013 report)?
entries.text:
The Million Women Study (2013 report) is often listed among the studies said to show phones are safe, but its own data contain a harm signal, set out below.

What it claimed: No increased glioma, meningioma or non-central nervous system (CNS) cancer incidence was detected.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Positive subgroup finding: The original report was not null for every tumor comparison. For acoustic neuroma, at least 10 years versus never use gave relative risk 2.46 (95 percent confidence interval 1.07 to 5.64).
- Older women only: Participants were middle-aged and older women, not children, teenagers or lifelong users.

RF Safe's position: absence of proof from a study blind to heavy, long-term use is not proof of safety.

Related: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/million-women-2013/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Million Women Study 2022 update (Schüz)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Million Women Study 2022 update (Schüz)?
entries.text:
The Million Women Study update does not show that phones are safe. Its top 2011 category began at just 20 minutes a week, and its own authors agreed that very heavy users were few.

What it was: a United Kingdom study by Schüz, Pirie, Reeves, Floud and Beral in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute (2022). It followed 776,156 women born from 1935 to 1950 for 14 years and counted 3,268 brain tumors. It concluded that usual phone use does not increase brain tumor incidence.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- The bar for "heavy" was tiny. In the 2011 survey, the top talking category was 20 minutes or more per week. That entry threshold is under 3 minutes a day; it is not a maximum for that group.
- Very heavy users were missing. In their reply to critics, the authors agreed that few participants were very heavy users.
- The exposure questions were crude. Women were asked about phone use only twice, around 2001 and around 2011. As Moskowitz pointed out, there was no record of cordless phone use or hands-free use.
- The wrong people were studied. These women were 51 to 66 years old in 2001. They were not children, teenagers or lifelong users.
- The same cohort found a signal before. The 2013 Million Women report found 2.46 times the risk of acoustic neuroma, a tumor of the hearing nerve, after 10 or more years of use (95 percent confidence interval 1.07 to 5.64), and the risk rose with years of use.

Published critiques: Joel M. Moskowitz (2022) and Linda S. Birnbaum and colleagues (2022), both in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute.

RF Safe's position: a study of older women with few very heavy users cannot clear heavy, lifelong phone use.

Related: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/million-women-2022/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Muscat US brain cancer study (2000)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Muscat US brain cancer study (2000)?
entries.text:
The Muscat United States brain cancer study (2000) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its design could not see heavy, long-term users, so a 'no link' headline does not clear phones.

What it claimed: No overall association was observed; longer-induction research remained necessary.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Short exposure history: The observed use history is short for a broad lifetime cancer claim. Mean duration of use was 2.8 years in cases and 2.7 years in controls.
- Records not obtained: The intended billing-record check did not provide the desired objective validation. Attempts to obtain carrier billing records were unsuccessful; use was reconstructed from patient reports.
- Industry-funded contract: The project was supported by a contract from Wireless Technology Research, the research program funded by the wireless industry, alongside three Public Health Service grants, and a co-author worked there.

RF Safe's position: absence of proof from a study blind to heavy, long-term use is not proof of safety.

Related: What is wrong with COSMOS, the Million Women Study, CEFALO, MOBI-Kids and other "no link" brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/muscat-2000/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the National Cancer Institute cell phone fact sheet (2026)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the National Cancer Institute cell phone fact sheet (2026)?
entries.text:
The National Cancer Institute cell phone fact sheet (2026) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It restates selected studies as reassurance; it is not new evidence of safety.

What it claimed: National Cancer Institute (NCI) states that the evidence to date suggests cell-phone use does not cause brain or other human cancers.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- From papers to public reassurance: The broad summary must be read alongside its study-specific qualifications. The page presents an overall reassuring assessment while describing mixed results and exposure-measurement problems.
- Cancer is the page’s scope: A conclusion about cancer is not a conclusion about every health endpoint. The topic and principal studies concern cancer and brain tumors.

RF Safe's position: in 2021 a federal court found the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) failed to explain how its limits protect against non-cancer harm, and these reviews do not fill that gap.

Related: What is wrong with the FDA, FCC, National Cancer Institute and European committee reviews that call phones safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/nci-cell-phones/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the O'Connor cell calcium study (2010)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the O'Connor cell calcium study (2010)?
entries.text:
The O'Connor cell calcium study (2010) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. A short test of one endpoint in cells cannot show that years of exposure are safe.

What it claimed: No detected alteration of the measured basal or stimulated calcium signals under the experimental conditions.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute endpoint: A short cellular assay cannot determine chronic whole-organism safety. The test measures calcium during an acute exposure; Scientific Committee on Emerging and Newly Identified Health Risks (SCENIHR) describes its 30-minute protocol.
- Limited parameter space: One set of waveforms and cell preparations cannot test all proposed radio-frequency (RF) interaction conditions. The protocol uses 900 megahertz (MHz) exposures and specified cell preparations.
- Funding disclosed: Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC) and Mobile Telecommunications and Health Research programme (MTHR) support is disclosed. The paper reports BBSRC/MTHR support.

RF Safe's position: a short null test in cells does not erase the 1,465 harm-side studies in RF Safe's research map.

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Oberto lymphoma-prone mouse study (2007)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Oberto lymphoma-prone mouse study (2007)?
entries.text:
The Oberto lymphoma-prone mouse study (2007) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. One negative animal model does not cancel the clear tumor findings of the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini studies.

What it claimed: No detected radio-frequency (RF)-related neoplastic or non-neoplastic lesion increase under the tested conditions.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Replication boundary: Exposure arrangement and background lymphoma rates differ across the Pim1 experiments. The comparative chapter identifies differences in restraint, tissue exposure and control tumor incidence.
- Model-specific result: A lymphoma-focused transgenic model cannot establish absence of every chronic health effect. The experiment uses Pim1 transgenic mice and a specified pulsed Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) signal.

Published critiques: James C. Lin (2009).

RF Safe's position: the NTP and Ramazzini findings stand, and the World Health Organization-commissioned animal review rated the tumor evidence high certainty.

Related: What about the animal studies that found no cancer from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Pinto animal cancer review (2023)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Pinto animal cancer review (2023)?
entries.text:
The Pinto animal cancer review (2023) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. One negative animal model does not cancel the clear tumor findings of the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini studies.

What it claimed: Low or inadequate evidence for a cancer association across assessed tissues, despite some tissue-level statistical signals.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Low certainty is not safety: Low or inadequate evidence of an association cannot be converted into high confidence of no effect. The review’s overall evidence assessment is low or inadequate.
- Pooling unlike conditions: The interpretation of a pooled estimate depends on biological comparability. The inventory includes multiple species, exposure patterns and doses.

RF Safe's position: the NTP and Ramazzini findings stand, and the World Health Organization-commissioned animal review rated the tumor evidence high certainty.

Related: What about the animal studies that found no cancer from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Rubin electromagnetic hypersensitivity provocation review (2010)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Rubin electromagnetic hypersensitivity provocation review (2010)?
entries.text:
The Rubin electromagnetic hypersensitivity provocation review (2010) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. It restates selected studies as reassurance; it is not new evidence of safety.

What it claimed: The review did not find robust support for electromagnetic field (EMF) exposure as the acute trigger in the tested conditions and supported a role for nocebo effects.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute symptoms versus chronic effects: An acute provocation conclusion cannot settle lifetime safety. The review assesses blinded exposure-detection and symptom experiments.

RF Safe's position: in 2021 a federal court found the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) failed to explain how its limits protect against non-cancer harm, and these reviews do not fill that gap.

Related: What is wrong with the FDA, FCC, National Cancer Institute and European committee reviews that call phones safe?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Schüz German glioma and meningioma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2006)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Schüz German glioma and meningioma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2006)?
entries.text:
The Schüz German glioma and meningioma study (INTERPHONE arm) (2006) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its long-term users had more than twice the odds of glioma, and its own data show participation and recall problems.

What it claimed: No overall increased risk was found; longer-duration glioma required further investigation.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Long-term users had more glioma: Morgan highlighted the at least 10-year glioma odds ratio of 2.20 (95 percent confidence interval 0.94 to 5.11).
- Historical-use reconstruction: Historical provider and start-date reports were sometimes inconsistent. The paper describes provider/date discrepancies among long-duration users.
- Participation can alter the comparison: Controls who took part used phones more than those who refused, which hides risk. The discussion identifies lower phone use among nonresponding male controls.
- Declared industry funding route: Some project support passed through an industry-funded intermediary. Funding included International Union Against Cancer (UICC) support originating from the Mobile Manufacturers’ Forum and Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) Association.

Published critiques: L. Lloyd Morgan (2006).

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of 'heavy.'

Related: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/schuz-germany-2006/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Takebayashi Japanese brain tumor study (INTERPHONE arm) (2008)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Takebayashi Japanese brain tumor study (INTERPHONE arm) (2008)?
entries.text:
The Takebayashi Japanese brain tumor study (INTERPHONE arm) (2008) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its highest-dose group had nearly six times the odds of glioma, and the authors put that down to recall bias instead of exploring it.

What it claimed: The authors found no overall increase in glioma or meningioma and considered recall bias a possible high-exposure explanation.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Modeled dose inherits recalled history: More detailed dosimetry does not remove uncertainty in historical phone-use inputs. Hocking questions unvalidated long-term recall used to build the modeled exposure indices.
- Imprecise high-exposure subgroup: The highest cumulative modeled-exposure glioma comparison is unresolved. For cumulative maximum specific absorption rate (SAR)-hour above 10 watts per kilogram (W/kg)-hour, odds ratio was 5.84 (95 percent confidence interval 0.96 to 35.60).
- Participation and selection checks: Incomplete participation leaves a selection concern, partly examined by the investigators. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) notes 51.2% full control participation and an additional brief survey; Hocking questions selection.

Published critiques: B. Hocking (2008).

RF Safe's position: INTERPHONE's heavy-user signal was real, and it was buried under bias and a low definition of 'heavy.'

Related: What is wrong with the INTERPHONE brain tumor studies?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/takebayashi-2008/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Tillmann mouse cancer study (2007)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Tillmann mouse cancer study (2007)?
entries.text:
The Tillmann mouse cancer study (2007) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. One negative animal model does not cancel the clear tumor findings of the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini studies.

What it claimed: No evidence of carcinogenic potential under the tested exposure conditions.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Exposure schedule: A two-year study still has a defined daily exposure pattern. The reported schedule was two hours/day on five days/week.

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Toler mammary tumor mouse study (1997)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Toler mammary tumor mouse study (1997)?
entries.text:
The Toler mammary tumor mouse study (1997) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. One negative animal model does not cancel the clear tumor findings of the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini studies.

What it claimed: No significant differences in mammary-tumor onset, growth, incidence or longevity.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Strain and endpoint: A mammary-tumor-prone mouse model does not represent every susceptible human tissue. The experiment uses female C3H/HeJ mice selected for mammary-tumor susceptibility.
- One exposure condition: The experiment does not map a dose–response or compare modern communication waveforms. A single 435 megahertz (MHz) pulse-wave exposure was compared with sham.

RF Safe's position: the NTP and Ramazzini findings stand, and the World Health Organization-commissioned animal review rated the tumor evidence high certainty.

Related: What about the animal studies that found no cancer from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Utteridge lymphoma-prone mouse study (2002)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Utteridge lymphoma-prone mouse study (2002)?
entries.text:
The Utteridge lymphoma-prone mouse study (2002) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. One negative animal model does not cancel the clear tumor findings of the National Toxicology Program (NTP) and Ramazzini studies.

What it claimed: No significant lymphoma increase or dose–response relative to sham.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Changed confirmation protocol: The original and follow-up experiments differ in exposure arrangement and schedule. Scientific Committee on Emerging and Newly Identified Health Risks (SCENIHR) notes restraint and a once-daily exposure in the later experiment, alongside dosimetry and necropsy improvements.

Published critiques: Michael Kundi (2003); Alexander Lerchl (2003); James C. Lin (2009).

RF Safe's position: the NTP and Ramazzini findings stand, and the World Health Organization-commissioned animal review rated the tumor evidence high certainty.

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the Vijayalaxmi blood cell study (2013)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the Vijayalaxmi blood cell study (2013)?
entries.text:
The Vijayalaxmi blood cell study (2013) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. A short test of one endpoint in cells cannot show that years of exposure are safe.

What it claimed: Micronucleus incidence did not differ significantly between radio-frequency (RF) and sham or between the tested RF modulations.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute endpoint is not lifetime safety: It tested one narrow question, so it cannot back a broad safety claim. This was an in vitro micronucleus test, not an epidemiological or lifetime exposure study.
- Four donors: Donor-level biological diversity is limited. The abstract identifies four volunteers.
- Specific absorption rate (SAR) is not temperature: The thermal conditions of the culture cannot be inferred from SAR alone. The abstract reports 10.9 watts per kilogram (W/kg) but does not provide the temperature-control trace.

RF Safe's position: a short null test in cells does not erase the 1,465 harm-side studies in RF Safe's research map.

Related: What about the lab studies that found no DNA damage from phone signals?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned animal pregnancy review (Cordelli) (2023)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned animal pregnancy review (Cordelli) (2023)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned animal pregnancy review (Cordelli) (2023) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its own pooled results include harmful effects on birth measures, and it needed a published correction.

What it claimed: Results and certainty differ by endpoint; several adverse birth measures appear in the synthesis.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Temperature and timing: A pooled pregnancy result must preserve the actual exposure conditions. The review separately examines exposure levels and maternal-temperature changes.
- Delayed effects coverage: Normal birth measurements do not by themselves settle later functional outcomes. The review distinguishes birth endpoints from delayed offspring tests and narratively includes some unpooled results.
- Corrected after publication: The authors published a correction in Environment International in 2025.

Published critiques: Ronald L. Melnick and colleagues (2025); Else K. Nordhagen and Einar Flydal (2024).

RF Safe's position: 'low certainty of no effect' is not safety, and reviewers tied to International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) should not grade their own limits.

Related: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned reviews that found no harm in people?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/cordelli-2023-pregnancy/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned cognition experiments review (Pophof) (2024)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned cognition experiments review (Pophof) (2024)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned cognition experiments review (Pophof) (2024) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its 'no effect' conclusion rests on weak exposure measures, short follow-up and low-certainty evidence.

What it claimed: High-to-low-certainty evidence generally supports no short-term performance reduction; uncertainty remains in several subdomains.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Acute-to-chronic leap: Short-term cognitive performance does not directly measure chronic neural health. The review question explicitly concerns short-term exposure and cognitive performance.
- Uneven task evidence: A pooled null is more precise for some tasks than others. The review reports uncertainty in 16 of 35 subdomains and no executive-function studies.

Published critiques: Ronald L. Melnick and colleagues (2025).

RF Safe's position: 'low certainty of no effect' is not safety, and reviewers tied to International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) should not grade their own limits.

Related: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned reviews that found no harm in people?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/pophof-2024/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned cognition review (Benke) (2024)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned cognition review (Benke) (2024)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned cognition review (Benke) (2024) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its 'no effect' conclusion rests on weak exposure measures, short follow-up and low-certainty evidence.

What it claimed: Low or very low certainty of little-to-no association for assessed cognitive outcomes.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Limited follow-up: “Long-term” here is much shorter than a lifetime exposure claim. Most included cohorts have approximately one year of follow-up.
- Few independent cohorts: The evidence base is small and partly overlapping. The five studies represent four cohorts; the paper discusses overlapping Swiss participants.

Published critiques: Ronald L. Melnick and colleagues (2025).

RF Safe's position: 'low certainty of no effect' is not safety, and reviewers tied to International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) should not grade their own limits.
