entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned female reproduction review (Johnson) (2024)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned female reproduction review (Johnson) (2024)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned female reproduction review (Johnson) (2024) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its 'no effect' conclusion rests on weak exposure measures, short follow-up and low-certainty evidence.

What it claimed: The body of evidence is very uncertain about effects on female reproductive outcomes.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Exposure-window uncertainty: Phone-use and job categories do not measure the dose reaching a fetus during critical windows of development. The included sources range from mobile phones to radar, diathermy, surveillance and welding equipment.
- Uncertainty-to-safety leap: Very uncertain evidence cannot independently justify a strong no-harm claim. The review’s overall conclusion is very uncertain; Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA) discusses it within below-limit safety messaging.

Published critiques: Ronald L. Melnick and colleagues (2025).

RF Safe's position: 'low certainty of no effect' is not safety, and reviewers tied to International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) should not grade their own limits.

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned human cancer review (Karipidis, 2024)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned human cancer review (Karipidis, 2024)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned human cancer review by Karipidis and colleagues does not show that phones are safe. It was led by an officer of the body that writes the limits, it leaned on crude exposure measures, and it could not assess the long tumor delays that matter most.

What it was: a systematic review in Environment International (2024) of 63 human studies. It gave moderate-certainty reassurance that mobile phones do not raise the risk of several head tumors.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- The lead author helps write the limits. Ken Karipidis has been Vice Chair of the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) since July 2024. Co-author Martin Röösli's advisory roles are also disclosed in the paper.
- It pooled weak measures. It relied on "ever used a phone" and time since first use, which blur heavy and light users together.
- It could not see long delays. In reply to critics, the authors acknowledged there was not enough evidence to pool tumor delays of 15 years or more.
- Its key data are not open. Data or analysis code is released only on approved request.
- Hardell and Nilsson object that it treated the Danish cohort and Million Women studies favorably, despite their documented exposure problems.
- The same World Health Organization program found the opposite in animals. Its animal cancer review rated the evidence for gliomas and heart schwannomas in male rats high certainty.

Published critiques: Frank and colleagues, Environment International (2025); Hardell and Nilsson (2025); and the International Commission on the Biological Effects of Electromagnetic Fields' review of eleven World Health Organization-commissioned reviews (Melnick and colleagues, Environmental Health, 2025).

RF Safe's position: reviewers tied to ICNIRP should not grade the evidence against ICNIRP's own limits.

Related: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned reviews that found no harm in people?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

More: https://rfsafe.net/safety-evidence/dossiers/karipidis-2024/

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned human cancer review (Karipidis, Part 2) (2025)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned human cancer review (Karipidis, Part 2) (2025)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned human cancer review (Karipidis, Part 2) (2025) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its 'no effect' conclusion rests on weak exposure measures, short follow-up and low-certainty evidence.

What it claimed: Selected associations were not increased, with low or very low certainty.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Low-certainty reassurance: Uncertain evidence cannot be turned into a confident "no harm." The conclusions assign low or very low certainty to the reported null associations.
- Sparse outcome coverage: Pooling rare and heterogeneous settings cannot establish a general non-thermal safety boundary. The review organizes 26 papers across many distinct exposure–outcome pairs.

Published critiques: Ronald L. Melnick and colleagues (2025).

RF Safe's position: 'low certainty of no effect' is not safety, and reviewers tied to International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) should not grade their own limits.

Related: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned reviews that found no harm in people?; Which studies does RF Safe flag as false proof that phones are safe, and why?

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned male fertility review in people (Kenny) (2024)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned male fertility review in people (Kenny) (2024)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned male fertility review in people (Kenny) (2024) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its 'no effect' conclusion rests on weak exposure measures, short follow-up and low-certainty evidence.

What it claimed: The available evidence is too uncertain to establish the effect reliably.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Phone time is not gonadal dose: Time using a phone is not a direct measure of exposure to reproductive tissue. The review relies substantially on phone-use duration, with few phone-position studies.
- Very uncertain evidence: The review’s conclusion is uncertainty, not demonstrated reproductive safety. Very-low-certainty ratings accompany the main semen-outcome estimates.

Published critiques: Ronald L. Melnick and colleagues (2025).

RF Safe's position: 'low certainty of no effect' is not safety, and reviewers tied to International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) should not grade their own limits.

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned oxidative stress review (Meyer) (2024)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned oxidative stress review (Meyer) (2024)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned oxidative stress review (Meyer) (2024) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its 'no effect' conclusion rests on weak exposure measures, short follow-up and low-certainty evidence.

What it claimed: Very-low-certainty evidence with inconsistent and tissue-dependent findings.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Biomarker validity: Assay and exposure quality limit both positive and negative interpretations. The review identifies high risk of bias in exposure and outcome measurement.
- Waveform coverage: A broad eligible frequency range is not the same as a broad tested evidence base. The included experiments used 800 to 2450 megahertz (MHz) and mostly continuous-wave exposure.

Published critiques: Ronald L. Melnick and colleagues (2025).

RF Safe's position: 'low certainty of no effect' is not safety, and reviewers tied to International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) should not grade their own limits.

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned provocation-symptoms review (Bosch-Capblanch) (2024)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned provocation-symptoms review (Bosch-Capblanch) (2024)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned provocation-symptoms review (Bosch-Capblanch) (2024) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its 'no effect' conclusion rests on weak exposure measures, short follow-up and low-certainty evidence.

- Acute conditions: Brief provocation tests cannot directly resolve prolonged everyday exposure. The authors identify differences in duration, frequency, distance and position from real-life conditions.
- Population coverage: Older and chronically ill populations are not adequately represented. The review notes that many participants were young healthy volunteers.

Published critiques: Michael Bevington (2024); Ronald L. Melnick and colleagues (2025).

entries.title: Safety Evidence: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned symptoms review (Röösli) (2024)?
entries.question: What is wrong with the World Health Organization-commissioned symptoms review (Röösli) (2024)?
entries.text:
The World Health Organization-commissioned symptoms review (Röösli) (2024) is cited as evidence that wireless radiation is safe. It does not show that. Its 'no effect' conclusion rests on weak exposure measures, short follow-up and low-certainty evidence.

What it claimed: No consistent symptom association, with important uncertainty in the evidence.

Why RF Safe flags it:
- Exposure and symptom measurement: Measurement quality limits interpretation of weak associations. Frank and colleagues question the validity and appraisal of primary observational studies.
- Symptoms is not all effects: The absence of a symptom association cannot establish whole-body safety. The review’s outcomes are specific symptom categories.

Published critiques: John W. Frank and colleagues (2024); Ronald L. Melnick and colleagues (2025).

RF Safe's position: 'low certainty of no effect' is not safety, and reviewers tied to International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) should not grade their own limits.
