entries.title: Children and Pregnancy: Do studies link phone use to behavior or memory problems in kids?
entries.question: Do studies link phone use to behavior or memory problems in kids?
entries.text:
Yes. Studies of children and teenagers have found links between phone exposure and behavior problems and memory, and the animal research shows the brain's memory center is a consistent target.

The studies:
- Divan and colleagues, 2008, in the journal Epidemiology, studied 13,159 Danish children and found that those exposed to cell phones both before and after birth had 80 percent higher odds of behavior problems, such as emotional and hyperactivity problems, at age 7. The same team repeated the analysis in a separate group of 28,745 children in 2012 and found the link again.
- Foerster and colleagues, 2018, in Environmental Health Perspectives, followed about 700 Swiss adolescents for a year and found that a higher cumulative radio-frequency dose to the brain from phone calls was linked to weaker figural memory, the memory for shapes and images, especially in teens who held the phone to the right side of the head, where that kind of memory is mostly processed. Phone use that sends little radiation to the brain did not show the effect. That points to the radiation, not the screen time.
- In RF Safe's map of the research, 431 studies cover the brain and behavior, with memory and learning deficits the most common finding, in 94 studies, mostly in the hippocampus and cortex.

Why kids are different: children absorb more radiation in the brain than the adult test model, and their brains are still being built, in timing windows that do not reopen.

RF Safe's position, as John Coates approved it: we don't recommend that children use cell phones. If they do, we recommend an air-tube headset, and cell phone use by developing bodies should be limited as much as possible.

Related: What does wireless radiation do to the brain?; Why do children absorb more radiation than adults?; Children and cell phones

entries.title: Children and Pregnancy: If I'm pregnant, should I reduce EMF and wireless exposure?
entries.question: If I'm pregnant, should I reduce EMF and wireless exposure?
entries.text:
Yes, it's worth taking steps, because pregnancy is the time to cut exposure the most.

If you are pregnant, RF Safe advises reducing electromagnetic field (EMF) and wireless exposure as much as possible. General avoidance of electromagnetic exposure is highly recommended. A baby's development happens in timing windows that never reopen, so pregnancy is the time to cut exposure the most.

What to do:
- Do not rest a tablet or laptop that is connected to Wi-Fi or a cellular network against your belly, or on your lap over the womb. Put the device in airplane mode or use a wired connection, and keep it off your body. Keep the charger and its cord away from your belly too. A 2012 study of laptops held against a pregnant woman's belly found that the power supply induced electric currents in the fetus above the international safety limit for those currents. The BioInitiative chapter on fetal effects says putting the laptop "on a table or desk and not on the body of the user" will "result in significant reduction" of exposure "in both mother and fetus."
- Keep the phone off your belly and off your body. Use speakerphone or an air-tube headset for calls.
- At night, keep the phone off the nightstand, in airplane mode or powered down, and out of the bed. Keep the Wi-Fi router away from the bed, or turn it off at night.
- Prefer wired internet at home, and turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on devices when you are not using them.

The 2012 Yale School of Medicine study by Aldad, Gan, Gao and Taylor, "Fetal radiofrequency radiation exposure from 800-1900 MHz-rated cellular telephones affects neurodevelopment and behavior in mice," was published in Scientific Reports. The researchers positioned muted and silenced 800- to 1,900-megahertz-rated cell phones, each with a specific absorption rate (SAR) of 1.6 watts per kilogram, above each cage over the feeding bottle area, 4.5 to 22.3 centimeters from the mice, and kept the phones on an uninterrupted active call. The 1.6 watts per kilogram is the phones' rating, the same as the U.S. phone limit. The paper does not report a measured dose in the mice. Thirty-three pregnant mice were exposed this way 24 hours a day from day 1 through day 17 of pregnancy. Control cages held a deactivated phone under the same conditions. The offspring were hyperactive and had impaired memory. They also spent less time in the dark, which the authors read as decreased anxiety. A fear test, the step-down assay, showed no significant difference. In the brain, the offspring had reduced glutamate signaling onto layer V pyramidal neurons in the prefrontal cortex, and that reduction grew as daily exposure rose from 0 to 9, 15 and 24 hours a day. The authors wrote that these recordings "revealed that these behavioral changes were due to altered neuronal developmental programming," and called the work "the first experimental evidence of neuropathology due to in-utero cellular telephone radiation." The authors used tests they said identify impairments often associated with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). A 2013 correction changed only the mothers' stress-hormone figures; the authors said it did not change the conclusions, and the groups still did not differ significantly.

In people, Divan and colleagues, 2008, in the journal Epidemiology, studied 13,159 Danish children and found that children whose mothers used cell phones while pregnant, and who used cell phones themselves, had 80 percent higher odds of behavior problems, such as emotional and hyperactivity problems, at age 7. The authors found the link for exposure "prenatally-and, to a lesser degree, postnatally." The same team repeated the analysis in a separate group of 28,745 children in 2012 and found the link again: children exposed both before and after birth had 50 percent higher odds of behavior problems than children exposed in neither period. In 2016 the team followed the children to age 11. Among children with no problems at age 7, those exposed only before birth had 41 percent higher odds of emotional and behavioral problems at age 11.

A 2017 analysis of 83,884 mothers and children in Denmark, Korea, the Netherlands, Norway and Spain found that the children of mothers who were high cell phone users during pregnancy had 28 percent higher odds of clinical-range hyperactivity or inattention problems than children of low users. Mothers who did not use a cell phone during pregnancy were less likely to have a child with behavior, hyperactivity or emotional problems.

Pregnancy loss is also at stake. In a Kaiser Permanente study of 913 pregnant women, those exposed to higher power-line-frequency magnetic fields had 2.72 times the risk of miscarriage. A 2021 pooled analysis of 17 studies with 57,693 participants found 27 percent higher odds of pregnancy loss with electromagnetic field exposure.

The BioInitiative Report, edited by Cindy Sage and David Carpenter (2007 and 2012), called for precautionary limits and special care during pregnancy and childhood. The 2007 report concluded that existing public safety limits were inadequate to protect public health. The 2012 report reprints the 2009 Seletun Scientific Statement, written by a panel of scientists that included Cindy Sage and met in Seletun, Norway, and published in 2010 in Reviews on Environmental Health. The Panel "strongly recommends against the use of mobile (cell) and cordless phones and PDAs by pregnant women," meaning personal digital assistants, or handheld computers. It also recommends that use of these phones "be curtailed near children or pregnant women." The report's chapter on fetal and newborn effects, by Carlo Bellieni and Iole Pinto, calls for "common sense measures" to limit these exposures, including education of "the pregnant mother with respect to laptop computers, mobile phones and other sources" of these fields. It concludes: "It is not in the public interest to wait."

RF Safe's reasoning is prudent avoidance, and ALARA, which means "as low as reasonably achievable." Under RF Safe's framework, development has no restore point: a timing error during pregnancy cannot be rewound.

Related: Why does the timing of development matter so much?; Why do children absorb more radiation than adults?; Is it safe to use a phone while pregnant?; Does wireless radiation affect female fertility or pregnancy?; How can I cut my exposure at night and in the bedroom?

entries.title: Children and Pregnancy: Is it safe to use a phone while pregnant?
entries.question: Is it safe to use a phone while pregnant?
entries.text:
RF Safe's position is that pregnancy is the time to cut exposure the most, because the baby's development happens in timing windows that never reopen. A review commissioned by the World Health Organization found that exposure in the womb "likely affects offspring health at birth."

What the research shows:
- In the U.S. National Toxicology Program study, rat pups exposed in the womb were born smaller at the higher doses.
- In rats exposed to a 3.5 gigahertz 5G-band signal 2 hours a day during pregnancy, at a peak of 0.066 watts per kilogram in the uterus, about 4 percent of the localized limit and with no heating, the offspring still had raised DNA damage in the kidney at 6 months and in the testis at 12 months, with no exposure after birth. Damage was worst after exposure through the whole pregnancy.
- Three separate labs found fewer egg follicles, the supply a female is born with and cannot replace, in female offspring exposed before birth.
- In people: in the Danish National Birth Cohort, children whose mothers used cell phones during pregnancy, and who later used phones themselves, had 80 percent higher odds of behavior problems at age 7. A second, separate group of 28,745 children showed the same link.

What RF Safe recommends during pregnancy:
- Keep the phone off your belly and off your body. Do not rest a phone, tablet or laptop on your lap or belly.
- Use speakerphone or an air-tube headset for calls.
- Keep the phone out of the bed at night, in airplane mode or powered down.
- Turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth when you are not using them.
- Use wired internet at home where you can, and keep the router away from the bedroom.
- If you carry the phone, use a bag rather than a pocket.

Why this matters to RF Safe: John Coates founded RF Safe after his first daughter, Angel Leigh, was born in 1995 with anencephaly, a neural tube defect, and did not survive.

Related: Does wireless radiation affect female fertility or pregnancy?; Why does the timing of development matter so much?; RF Safe's mission and history; What else can I do besides a case?; If I'm pregnant, should I reduce EMF and wireless exposure?

entries.title: Children and Pregnancy: What does RF Safe recommend for Wi-Fi in schools?
entries.question: What does RF Safe recommend for Wi-Fi in schools?
entries.text:
RF Safe recommends wired connections and Li-Fi, internet carried by light, in classrooms, so children are not sitting in a radio-frequency field all day while their brains and bodies develop.

What to ask your school or district for:
- Wired Ethernet for classroom computers and teacher stations where possible.
- Li-Fi-first indoors, so high-speed data moves to light and the radio background in classrooms drops.
- Turning off Wi-Fi access points when they are not needed, such as after hours.
- Devices kept on desks, not laps, with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth off when not in use.
- Antenna mapping for every campus, with no direct line-of-sight from antennas to classrooms and playgrounds.
- Exposure audits for every campus, published and repeated annually and after new installations.
- A setback of at least 1,500 feet between schools and permanent transmitters or rooftop arrays.

Why: children absorb more radiation than the adult test model, development happens once, and the 1996 limits were set only to prevent short-term heating, based on experiments in adult rats and monkeys, with phones tested on a plastic head modeled on large adult military recruits. In 2021 a federal appeals court ordered the FCC to 'address the impacts of RF radiation on children.' Five years later, the FCC has issued no answer. It only asked for public comment in September 2026.

More: https://rfsafe.app/learn/704 and https://rfsafe.app/lifi

Related: What did commenters say about children and schools?; Li-Fi and RF Safe's Light-Age position; Can my town or school stop a cell tower over health concerns?; Why do children absorb more radiation than adults?

entries.title: Children and Pregnancy: Why do children absorb more radiation than adults?
entries.question: Why do children absorb more radiation than adults?
entries.text:
Yes. Children's heads are smaller, their skulls are thinner, and their brains are still developing, so radiation from a phone reaches deeper into the brain. Studies found children absorb more than twice the radiation in parts of the brain compared with the adult test model, and more than ten times as much in the bone marrow of the skull. For a 10-year-old, the peak absorption can be up to 153 percent higher than the test model shows.

The evidence:
- Christ and colleagues, 2010, at the IT'IS Foundation in Zurich, an engineering institute that builds the anatomical models used in exposure science, compared children's head models with the adult test model. The fields induced in children were significantly higher in the cortex, the hippocampus, which is the memory center, the hypothalamus, which controls the body's hormones, and the eye. Gandhi and colleagues, 2012, found the same pattern.
- Phones are tested on a plastic head called SAM, the Specific Anthropomorphic Mannequin, which represents 'the top 10% of U.S. military recruits in 1989' and is filled with one liquid that has 'the average electrical properties of the head.' That liquid 'cannot indicate differential absorption of specific brain tissue, nor absorption in children or smaller adults.' Since 1997, compliance testing has relied on 'a large, homogenous, adult male head phantom' (Fernández and colleagues, 2018).
- Scientists at the Environmental Working Group ran the U.S. National Toxicology Program heart-damage data through the benchmark-dose method used for toxic chemicals. With a standard extra safety factor for children, they derived a children's whole-body limit of 0.2 to 0.4 thousandths of a watt per kilogram, 200 to 400 times lower than the current public limit of 0.08 watts per kilogram.

Why it matters more for children: development happens once, in timing windows that do not reopen. A child also has more years of exposure ahead.

RF Safe's position, as John Coates approved it: we don't recommend that children use cell phones. If they do, we recommend an air-tube headset. Children aren't just small adults, so cell phone use by developing bodies should be limited as much as possible.

See the kid-versus-adult absorption view for any phone: https://rfsafe.app/sar

Related: Children and cell phones; What is the SAM test model, and why does it matter that it is based on a large adult man?; Why does the timing of development matter so much?; Do studies link phone use to behavior or memory problems in kids?

entries.title: Children and Pregnancy: Why does the timing of development matter so much?
entries.question: Why does the timing of development matter so much?
entries.text:
Because development is written once, in timing windows that never reopen. An adult can recover from a bad night. An embryo cannot rewind a missed window. RF Safe's position is that development has no restore point, so precaution during pregnancy and childhood is a duty, not a preference.

How development works: cells have to divide, stop dividing, move, and become the right kind of cell, each at the right time and in the right order. Those steps are driven by calcium signals, and the timing of those signals helps decide what each cell becomes: cells read the rhythm of calcium, not just the amount (Dolmetsch 1998).

An example: the neural tube, which becomes the brain and spinal cord, closes at about day 25 of pregnancy. Closure runs on calcium timing. In the landmark 1991 Medical Research Council trial, folic acid taken around conception prevented 72 percent of repeat neural tube defects. Medicine already accepts that a missing input in one short window changes a child for life. Under RF Safe's bioelectric fidelity framework, a corrupted timing signal in the same window can do the same.

The evidence that weak fields reach those windows:
- Farrell and colleagues, 1997, exposed more than 2,500 chick embryos to pulsed or 60 hertz magnetic fields of about 1 microtesla, far too weak to heat anything. Four of five study campaigns found abnormality rates 2 to 7 times higher than in unexposed embryos. The one campaign that did not respond used breeding stock whose genetics the breeder had changed, which the authors proposed as the reason.
- In human brain organoids, lab-grown clusters of brain cells, a 2.4 gigahertz Bluetooth source at about 2.5 milliwatts per square meter, about 4,000 times below the U.S. public limit of 10 watts per square meter, kept the stem cells that build the brain's cortex in an immature state, delayed their development, and changed the resulting neurons' structure, electrical activity and calcium signaling (Cakir and colleagues, 2025, Cell Reports).
- U.S. National Toxicology Program rat pups exposed in the womb were born smaller at the higher doses.

An adult tissue under stress repairs and resets. A developing tissue builds the error into its structure. There is no second day 25.

Related: Is it safe to use a phone while pregnant?; Does wireless radiation affect female fertility or pregnancy?; Why does timing matter more than heat to a cell?; Children and cell phones

entries.title: Everyday Habits: Does a weak signal (one bar) mean my phone puts out more radiation?
entries.question: Does a weak signal (one bar) mean my phone puts out more radiation?
entries.text:
Yes. Phones adjust their transmit power to reach the tower. When the signal is weak, the phone and network turn the power up, so a call on one bar can mean much more radiation than the same call on full bars. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) puts it plainly: 'When you have a weak signal, your phone works harder, emitting more radiation.'

The facts:
- The phone and the network manage transmission power automatically, based on conditions.
- Phones transmit at higher power when the signal is weak or when they are sending a lot of data.
- A phone's output can vary by up to ten thousand times depending on the network and signal strength, as independent scientists pointed out in their critique of the COSMOS phone study. That is one reason call time alone is a poor measure of dose in studies.
- SAR, the lab rating, is measured at full power. It does not tell you how often your phone runs at high power in your home, car or office. The FTC itself says the single worst-case SAR value 'is not necessarily representative of the absorption during actual use.'

What to do:
- Avoid long calls, video streaming and big downloads when you have one or two bars. Wait until the signal is better, or make the call from a landline or from a computer on a wired Ethernet connection.
- In weak-signal places such as elevators, basements and rural roads, use speakerphone and keep the phone away from your body.
- At home, if the cell signal is poor, a wired internet connection for data cuts how hard the phone has to work.
- Avoid cases that block the signal, such as full-wrap or metal designs, which can make the phone work harder.

Related: Is it worse to use my phone in a car?; Can a phone case make a phone put out more radiation?; What exactly is SAR, and what does watts per kilogram mean?

entries.title: Everyday Habits: How can I cut my exposure at night and in the bedroom?
entries.question: How can I cut my exposure at night and in the bedroom?
entries.text:
Keep the phone off your body and out of the bed at night, and put it in airplane mode or power it down. Night is when the body repairs and resets, and it is the easiest time to cut exposure for many hours at once.

What to do:
- Put the phone in airplane mode, or turn it off, in the bedroom. Even when you are not on a call, a phone keeps sending short signals to stay connected to the tower, and Wi-Fi and Bluetooth send their own signals while they are on.
- Never sleep with the phone under your pillow or in the bed. Put it across the room.
- Turn off the home Wi-Fi router at night, or put it on a timer, and keep it out of bedrooms.
- Use a wired connection for anything that has to stay online overnight.
- Keep sleeping areas as far as possible from smart meters and other transmitters on the other side of a wall.
- For children's rooms, the same rules apply, and more strictly.

Why it matters: studies in people have found changes in sleep brain waves under phone-type signals (Huber 2002), and utility workers who used a cell phone more than 25 minutes a day had lower nighttime melatonin breakdown products, a marker of the sleep hormone (Burch 2002). In 2025, a 5G signal changed sleep brain waves in people with one version of a calcium-channel gene (Sousouri 2025). RF Safe's mechanism map shows the body clock hit at several levels.

RF Safe's position: a bedroom should be a low-radio room by default.

Related: Does a phone give off radiation when not on a call?; Does wireless radiation affect sleep, brain waves or the body clock?; RF Safe's mission and history; Why does RF Safe say to use wired Ethernet first?

entries.title: Everyday Habits: Is it OK to keep my phone in my pocket or bra?
entries.question: Is it OK to keep my phone in my pocket or bra?
entries.text:
RF Safe does not recommend it. Phones are tested with a gap between the phone and the body, and a pocket or bra has no gap. Carry the phone in a bag instead.

Why:
- U.S. rules let phones be tested for body exposure at up to 5 millimeters from the body model, or up to 25 millimeters for belt clips and holsters.
- When the FCC tested popular phones in its own lab at 2 millimeters in 2019, five of eight went over the limit, up to 5.2 watts per kilogram for a Samsung Galaxy J3, more than three times the limit. The FCC said the phones met the limit at 5 millimeters and called the 2-millimeter results 'inconsistent with FCC practice.' A pocket is closer than either.
- Europe has adopted testing at 0 millimeters, direct contact. The old standard that allowed a gap is withdrawn on March 7, 2028.
- Reproductive organs and breast tissue sit right where pockets and bras put the phone. In RF Safe's map of 219 reproductive studies, sperm and the testes are the most consistent target. A 2014 meta-analysis that pooled studies in people and in the lab found that phone exposure lowered sperm motility, how well sperm swim, by about 8 percent.

What to do:
- Carry the phone in a bag or purse, with the shielded flap of a QuantaCase facing toward you. For men, a briefcase or any bag is better than a pocket.
- If you have no other option, close the shielded cover over the screen, facing your body, with the camera lenses facing outward, and turn off Bluetooth and Wi-Fi first.
- Take the phone out of your pocket as soon as you arrive.
- At night, keep it out of the bed.

RF Safe's position: create distance. No case makes a phone risk-free.

Related: How far from the body are phones tested?; Which way should the QuantaCase flap face, and how should I carry my phone?; Does cell phone radiation affect male fertility and sperm?; QuantaCase and the TruthCase philosophy

entries.title: Everyday Habits: Is it worse to use my phone in a car?
entries.question: Is it worse to use my phone in a car?
entries.text:
Yes, it can be. A car is a metal-lined, enclosed space that can reflect radio energy back into the cabin. The car body also weakens the signal on its way out, so the phone has to transmit harder. And a moving phone keeps reaching the edges of cell coverage and handing off between towers, where it transmits at higher power.

What RF Safe's usage guide recommends:
- Use a dashboard phone holder that props the phone with its back facing the windshield. That points the phone's main radio-emitting surface outward and is intended to reduce reflections back into the cabin.
- Do not keep the phone on the seat, in your lap or in a pocket while driving or riding.
- Avoid carrying an active phone in your pocket while in transit.
- Turn off Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and hotspot when you do not need them.

The same applies to buses, RVs and other enclosed metal vehicles. Pointing the phone's back toward the windshield, away from the people inside, is the simplest fix.

Keep children's devices off their laps in the car as well, and use offline downloads instead of streaming over the cell network on long trips.

Related: Does a weak signal (one bar) mean my phone puts out more radiation?; Which way should the QuantaCase flap face, and how should I carry my phone?; What else can I do besides a case?

entries.title: Everyday Habits: Is speakerphone or a headset better for calls?
entries.question: Is speakerphone or a headset better for calls?
entries.text:
Distance is the most important thing, so speakerphone with the phone away from your body is the simplest choice, and RF Safe recommends an air-tube headset when you need privacy. Holding the phone against your head should be a last resort.

The options, best first:
- Speakerphone, phone held away from you or set on a table or stand. With a QuantaCase, flip the cover behind the phone to form a lip and hold it by the lip so your hand is not wrapped around the phone.
- An air-tube headset, which RF Safe recommends, especially for children who use a phone. Even the FCC says a headset moves 'the greatest source of RF energy' away from the head and 'can greatly reduce total exposure to the head,' and it notes that 'wired earpieces may conduct some energy to the head.'
- Holding the phone to your ear, only if you must: close the shielded flap between your head and the phone, and turn off Bluetooth and Wi-Fi first.

About Bluetooth earbuds: Bluetooth sends its own signals whenever it is on, and Bluetooth earbuds put a transmitter right at your head. When Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are on at the same time as the cell signal, a phone's reported SAR, how fast your body absorbs its radio energy, goes up. If you want to cut exposure, turn Bluetooth off when you do not need it.

RF Safe's position: create distance first. No case makes a phone risk-free, and design and use both matter.

Related: Children and cell phones; Which way should the QuantaCase flap face, and how should I carry my phone?; Why does turning off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth lower my exposure?; What else can I do besides a case?

entries.title: QuantaCase: Can a phone case make a phone put out more radiation?
entries.question: Can a phone case make a phone put out more radiation?
entries.text:
Yes. A case that blocks or detunes the phone's antennas can make the phone raise its transmit power to stay connected to the tower. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) warns that such shields 'may interfere with the phone's signal, cause it to draw even more power to communicate with the base station, and possibly emit more radiation.' That is why RF Safe warns against cases with metal near the antennas, magnets, or full-wrap designs.

How it happens:
- The phone and the network constantly adjust how much power the phone transmits. When the signal path to the tower gets harder, the phone's power control turns its output up.
- Metal clasps, rings or strap loops near antenna regions can detune the antenna.
- Magnets or detachable magnet-and-plate wallets can make the phone ramp up its power.
- 360-degree full-wrap, pouch or thick wallet designs can block the signal to the tower, so the phone transmits harder.

How QuantaCase is designed around this: shielding sits only in the front flap, on your side, so the phone's antennas are not blocked. It is ultra-thin near antenna zones, and it has no metal loops, magnets or steel plates. Those choices are meant to avoid antenna detuning and the power increases that can come with it.

What QuantaCase does not claim: the case does not control the phone's power. The phone and network manage transmission power. QuantaCase's thin, antenna-conscious design is intended to avoid unnecessary interference, not to guarantee the lowest output under all conditions.

Disclosure: RF Safe sells these products.

Related: What are the five red flags to look for in a radiation phone case?; QuantaCase and the TruthCase philosophy; TruthCase and anti-radiation cases: what works

entries.title: QuantaCase: What are the five red flags to look for in a radiation phone case?
entries.question: What are the five red flags to look for in a radiation phone case?
entries.text:
RF Safe tells people to check any case for five design red flags. Each one can make the phone work harder or mislead you about protection. RF Safe calls this five-point checklist TruthScore, and TruthCase is designed to avoid all five.

The five red flags:
1. Metal near the antennas: metal clasps, rings or strap loops near antenna regions can detune the phone's antenna.
2. Magnets: magnets or detachable magnet-and-plate wallets can make the phone ramp up its power.
3. Full wrap: 360-degree full-wrap, pouch or thick multi-slot wallet designs can block the signal to the tower, so the phone's power control raises its transmit power.
4. Open ear side: large unshielded ear-side openings leave the area closest to your head unprotected.
5. "99%" claims: a "blocks 99%" claim usually describes a shielding fabric or material in a lab test, not a phone in use. A material's test percentage is not the same as a measured change in a person's exposure.

How QuantaCase avoids them: directional shielding only in the front flap, which sits between you and the phone; no metal carrying loops; no detachable magnet stacks; a thin build near antenna zones; conductive mesh at the ear-side opening (check your model's product page for its exact features); and no "99% protected" promise.

No case makes a phone risk-free, and RF Safe says so. Distance does the most. Pair the right case with speakerphone, a bag instead of a pocket, and radios off when you don't need them.

entries.title: QuantaCase: Which way should the QuantaCase flap face, and how should I carry my phone?
entries.question: Which way should the QuantaCase flap face, and how should I carry my phone?
entries.text:
The shielded front flap always goes between you and the phone. For a call, close the flap and keep it toward your head. For carrying, keep the flap toward your body. Distance comes first.

From the QuantaCase usage guide:
- Speakerphone, the best way to talk: flip the front cover behind the phone so it forms a small lip. Hold the phone by the lip with your thumb, without wrapping your fingers around its sides, and keep it away from your body.
- Holding to your ear, a last resort: if you must hold the phone against your head, close the shielded cover over the front so it sits between your head and the phone. Turn off Bluetooth and Wi-Fi first. Whenever possible, use speakerphone or a headset instead. Even the FCC says a headset or speakerphone moves 'the greatest source of RF energy … from proximity to the head and thus can greatly reduce total exposure to the head.'
- Pocket carry, not recommended: if there is no other option, close the shielded cover over the screen, facing your body, with the camera lenses facing outward. Turn off Bluetooth and Wi-Fi first, and take the phone out as soon as you arrive.
- In a bag, the preferred way to carry: put the phone in a bag or purse with the shielded cover facing toward you. For men, a briefcase or any bag is better than a pocket.
- In the car: use a dashboard mount with the back of the phone facing the windshield, not on the seat or a vent.

Turn off radios you don't need, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and hotspot, to cut how often the phone transmits. The result depends on the phone, its position and the conditions. No case makes a phone risk-free.

More: https://www.rfsafe.com/class/user-guide/

entries.title: Li-Fi and Wired: How fast and practical is Li-Fi today?
entries.question: How fast and practical is Li-Fi today?
entries.text:
Li-Fi is real and standardized. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) approved the 802.11bb standard in June 2023. It defines Wi-Fi-style networking over light in the 800 to 1,000 nanometer infrared band, with two-way speeds from 10 megabits to 9.6 gigabits per second, and light carries the upload as well as the download.

How it works in a room: an Ethernet cable feeds an optical access point, usually in the ceiling. Invisible infrared light carries data down to a compatible receiver on your device, and light also carries the return traffic. With the room's radios switched off, that connection does not depend on a microwave signal.

What to know:
- Light does not pass through walls, which keeps the signal in the room. It also means opaque objects, including people, can block the light path.
- That is why engineers pair Li-Fi with Wi-Fi in hybrid networks: when the light path is blocked, the device can hand over to Wi-Fi and switch back when the light returns.
- Coverage depends on where the device is and which way it faces.
- The standard is still being developed, with a follow-on project adding more light bands.

RF Safe's position: fiber to the building, wire to the room, light for the final meters, and radio only where mobility is essential. That keeps the connection and changes the carrier.

Disclosure: RF Safe founder John Coates is the inventor on U.S. patent US11700058B2, on Far-UV Li-Fi.

More: https://rfsafe.app/lifi

Related: Li-Fi and RF Safe's Light-Age position; What is the Clean Ether Act?; Why does RF Safe say to use wired Ethernet first?

entries.title: Li-Fi and Wired: What is the Clean Ether Act?
entries.question: What is the Clean Ether Act?
entries.text:
The Clean Ether Act is RF Safe's proposed legislative framework to move indoor data off microwaves and onto light. It is modeled on the Clean Air Act of 1970. It is an RF Safe proposal and model bill. It has not been introduced in Congress.

The idea: most wireless data, and most exposure, happens indoors, where Wi-Fi routers and devices transmit around the clock in the rooms where children learn and sleep. The 1996-era rules were never built for that kind of chronic exposure.

What it asks for:
- Li-Fi compatibility in every device: optical wireless under the IEEE 802.11bb standard built into phones, laptops, tablets and routers.
- Li-Fi pilots in schools and public buildings, with wired Ethernet as the backbone.
- Incentives and purchasing preference for Li-Fi-enabled lighting and devices.
- Stricter limits on microwave communications near homes and schools.
- A restored local say over where wireless infrastructure goes.
- Safety research and standards kept current.

Does it mean giving up wireless? No. Radio stays where mobility is essential, outdoors and on the move. Indoors, fiber feeds the building, wire feeds the room and light carries the last few meters.

RF Safe has published a model bill, the "Clean Aether Act of 2026," with the sponsor and bill number left blank. This is RF Safe's advocacy position, not a regulatory finding.

Disclosure: RF Safe founder John Coates is the inventor on U.S. patent US11700058B2, on Far-UV Li-Fi.

More: https://rfsafe.app/clean-ether-act

Related: Li-Fi and RF Safe's Light-Age position; How fast and practical is Li-Fi today?; What does RF Safe recommend for Wi-Fi in schools?; What would RF Safe change about Section 704?

entries.title: Li-Fi and Wired: Why does RF Safe say to use wired Ethernet first?
entries.question: Why does RF Safe say to use wired Ethernet first?
entries.text:
Because a wired connection carries your data without putting a radio signal into the room. It is the simplest, cheapest way to cut around-the-clock indoor exposure today, and it is usually faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi.

How to start:
- Plug computers, TVs, game consoles and desk setups into the router with Ethernet cables.
- Use an Ethernet adapter for laptops, tablets and phones at a desk.
- Then turn off the router's Wi-Fi, or put it on a timer so it is off at night.
- Turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on devices when you are not using them.
- Keep the router out of bedrooms and away from where people sit for long periods.

Where it fits in RF Safe's plan: fiber to the building, wire to the room, light for the final meters. Wired Ethernet is the backbone that Li-Fi access points plug into, so wiring your home now is the first step toward a light-based network later.

RF Safe's position: use radio only where mobility is essential, and carry most indoor data over wired Ethernet and light. RF Safe says moving schools to wired and light-based networking is one of the fastest ways to cut chronic exposure without giving up bandwidth.

entries.title: About RF Safe: Does industry funding affect what studies find?
entries.question: Does industry funding affect what studies find?
entries.text:
Yes. Huss and colleagues reviewed 59 experimental studies of phone-type radiation in people and reported in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2007 that studies funded only by the telecommunications industry were the least likely to report a statistically significant effect. Compared with studies paid for by public agencies or charities, their odds of reporting an effect were about one-ninth. Adjusting for study quality did not change the result. The authors concluded that results 'should take sponsorship into account.'

Why this matters when you hear "studies show no harm":
- Study design decides what a study can find: which signal, which tissue, how long, and when it is measured. A design can be set up so effects are unlikely to show.
- The people who write the heating-based international guidelines also author reviews that grade the evidence against them. In the World Health Organization-commissioned review of pregnancy and birth outcomes, the authors' own conflict statement lists one member of the main commission of ICNIRP, the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection, since 2012, and another who sat on ICNIRP's scientific expert group from 2013 to 2021. ICNIRP is a private non-profit association registered in Munich, Germany.
- Industry-independent work, such as the U.S. National Toxicology Program and the Ramazzini Institute, found the same rare heart tumor.

How to read a study yourself:
- Who paid for it, and do the authors declare ties to industry or to the groups that write the limits?
- Did it use real pulsed phone signals, or a steady signal without pulsing?
- Was it long enough, and did it look at sensitive groups, such as the young, or people with specific genes?
- Did it have an unexposed comparison group?

RF Safe's position: funding is not proof by itself, but it is a fact the public deserves to know, and independent science with conflict-of-interest firewalls should set the limits.

Related: What is ICNIRP, and who writes the international limits?; Why do some studies find no effect from phone radiation?; How many studies found no effect, and does that cancel out the studies that found harm?

Most of RF Safe's advice costs nothing: distance, speakerphone, keeping the phone off the body and out of the bedroom, turning off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth when not in use, and using wired internet. entries.title: About RF Safe: How are the study summaries in RF Safe's research database made?
entries.question: How are the study summaries in RF Safe's research database made?
entries.text:
The study summaries are AI-assisted summaries of third-party papers, and the original paper is linked on every record so you can read it yourself.

How the database works:
- RF Safe's research database at rfsafe.app/research holds 6,477 original source records on radio-frequency and electromagnetic field effects, 6,165 of them structured records.
- Each study is labeled by effect, evidence level and study type, and the whole list can be searched and filtered by effect, evidence, study type and year.
- The labels, including which studies count as showing harm, are AI-assisted grades. They help you find and sort studies. The paper itself is the authority.
- The database keeps studies that found no effect and studies with mixed results, not only studies that found harm.

How RF Safe uses it: RF Safe's harm-study map links 1,465 harm-side studies by what they measured, in which tissue, at what exposure, and its answers cite the specific studies and documents behind each claim.

If you find a summary that does not match its paper, tell RF Safe at info@rfsafe.app so it can be corrected.

Search the database: https://rfsafe.app/research

Related: RF Safe research database; What health effects has RF Safe mapped across the research?; How many studies found no effect, and does that cancel out the studies that found harm?

entries.title: About RF Safe: Isn't RF Safe just fearmongering?
entries.question: Isn't RF Safe just fearmongering?
entries.text:
No. RF Safe's position rests on documented findings from government studies, peer-reviewed research and a federal court, and its advice is practical, mostly free, and does not ask anyone to give up their phone.

What RF Safe points to:
- The U.S. government's own National Toxicology Program found clear evidence of malignant heart tumors in male rats exposed to cell phone radiation.
- The Ramazzini Institute found the same tumor at exposures near the public limit.
- A review commissioned by the World Health Organization rated that animal cancer evidence as high certainty.
- A federal appeals court ruled in 2021 that the FCC acted in an "arbitrary and capricious" way when it failed to respond to evidence that exposure below its limits "may cause negative health effects unrelated to cancer." The court sent the decision back to the FCC and ordered it to address children, long-term exposure and the environment. Five years later, the FCC has not answered.
- When the FCC's own lab tested store-bought phones at 2 millimeters from the body in 2019, five of eight went over the limit, up to 5.2 watts per kilogram for a Samsung Galaxy J3, more than three times the limit. The FCC wrote that 'the FCC RF exposure limits were exceeded.' Europe has adopted body-contact testing at 0 millimeters, with the old standard allowed until March 7, 2028.
- The Food and Drug Administration approved a cancer treatment that works with a low-level radio signal, without heating.

What RF Safe does not say: that every study shows harm, that phone radiation alone has been proven to cause a specific person's illness, or that a case makes a phone risk-free. RF Safe keeps no-effect studies in its database and links the original papers.

What RF Safe asks people to do: keep distance, use speakerphone, keep the phone off the body and out of the bedroom, turn off radios you are not using, and prefer wired connections.

RF Safe's position: telling people what the government's own studies found, and how to cut exposure for free, is not fear. It is information people have a right to have.

Related: What is RF Safe's position on wireless radiation, and why are the phone safety limits wrong?; What is proven, and what is RF Safe's framework?; Who funds RF Safe, and doesn't selling cases bias you?; What did the U.S. government's NTP cell phone study find?

entries.title: About RF Safe: Personal health questions and diagnosis
entries.question: Personal health questions and diagnosis
entries.text: This is not medical advice. If you have symptoms or a health concern, get proper medical care. What RF Safe offers is a research synthesis: a summary of what the published studies show. Its purpose is to push research funding and government safety rules to match the weight of the research, which points to biological effects that happen at levels too low to heat tissue (called non-thermal effects).

entries.title: About RF Safe: Who funds RF Safe, and doesn't selling cases bias you?
entries.question: Who funds RF Safe, and doesn't selling cases bias you?
entries.text:
RF Safe is a brand of Quanta X Technology LLC, a private company owned and run by CEO Katie Webb. Quanta X owns the RF SAFE trademark and sells products built from RF Safe designs, including QuantaCase phone cases. RF Safe discloses this, along with founder John Coates's role as inventor on a U.S. patent on Far-UV Li-Fi, and asks people to weigh its product and Li-Fi views with that in mind.

How RF Safe guards against bias:
- Every claim points to its source: government studies, peer-reviewed papers, court rulings and agency records, which anyone can check.
- The research database keeps studies that found no effect and mixed results, not only harm, and links every original paper.
- RF Safe treats SAR as a useful comparison tool, not a health score, and calls out "anti-radiation" designs that break the physics, including the "99%" claims many case sellers make.
- Its case designs and red-flag checklist are published openly, so anyone can judge any case.
- Most of its advice costs nothing and has nothing to do with buying a case: distance, speakerphone, off the body at night, radios off when not in use, wired internet.

The bigger question about bias: the U.S. limits are set by a spectrum agency whose job includes auctioning the airwaves. The FCC's own 2026 notice asking for comment on the court's remand opens by saying that leading the world in 5G and 6G 'will require the Commission to auction large amounts of licensed spectrum.' The international guidelines are written by ICNIRP, a private non-profit association registered in Germany, whose members also author reviews that grade the evidence. RF Safe asks for health agencies and independent scientists with conflict-of-interest firewalls to set the limits, so no one has to take anyone's word for it, including RF Safe's.

Related: Does RF Safe sell products?; Isn't RF Safe just fearmongering?; Does industry funding affect what studies find?; RF Safe's mission and history

entries.title: About RF Safe: Who is John Coates, and why did he start RF Safe?
entries.question: Who is John Coates, and why did he start RF Safe?
entries.text:
John R. Coates founded RF Safe in 1998. In 1995 his firstborn daughter, Angel Leigh, died shortly after birth with a neural tube defect. In the years that followed he read studies on electromagnetic fields and embryonic development, including Farrell and colleagues' 1997 study on chicken embryos, and he founded RF Safe so other families would have the information he wished he had.

RF Safe's mission: warn families, especially pregnant women and children, about radio-frequency risks regulators were ignoring, and design practical tools that actually reduce exposure. RF Safe has been online since 1998.

His own story, as he told it in his 2026 FCC and HHS comments: he grew up on a military air base near a radar site. He was diagnosed with kidney cancer at age 7, in 1977, and his left kidney was removed at age 8. In his words, his cancer and the loss of his daughter, Angel Leigh, are 'why I have spent my life reading this science.'

RF Safe is clear that this is its own history. It is not a claim that radio-frequency radiation caused any particular medical condition.

What he does now: John Coates is the founder of RF Safe. Quanta X Technology LLC, owned and run by CEO Katie Webb, owns the RF SAFE trademark and handles all sales of products built from RF Safe designs. He writes on the science and policy of wireless radiation, filed comments with the FCC and HHS in October 2026, and is the inventor on U.S. patent US11700058B2, a system for wireless communication using germicidal far-ultraviolet light (Far-UV Li-Fi), granted in 2023.

More: https://rfsafe.app/about

Related: RF Safe's mission and history; Does RF Safe sell products?; What did RF Safe file with the FCC?; Is it safe to use a phone while pregnant?

entries.title: Body Systems: Development and pregnancy (developmental and prenatal): What does the research show?
entries.question: Development and pregnancy (developmental and prenatal): What does the research show?
entries.text:
Studies of pregnancy and early development in RF Safe's directory found changes in brain development, behavior, pregnancy outcomes and organ growth after exposure in the womb, and many of them found the strongest effects at the earliest stages.

What this system does. An embryo builds its body by following electrical and calcium signals that tell each cell when to divide, move and specialize. Those instructions are given once, in a fixed order, during short windows. A mistake made in a window is built into the tissue and carried for life. That is why RF Safe says development has no restore point.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 709 studies to the development and pregnancy (after removing 3 retracted papers and retraction notices and 10 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 239 report harm, 255 report mixed results and 13 report a benefit. Together, 507 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 81 found no effect, and 121 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 17 as high and 71 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are changed brain development and nerve-cell growth, behavior and attention problems in children, miscarriage and birth-weight changes, organ changes in animals exposed before birth, and childhood cancer risk near strong power-line fields.

Key findings:
- Across five birth cohorts with 83,884 mother-child pairs, children of mothers with high phone use in pregnancy had 1.28 times the odds (1.12 to 1.48) of hyperactivity or inattention problems in the clinical range (Environment International, 2017).
- Human brain organoids, small lab-grown models of the developing cortex, exposed to 800 to 2,400 MHz kept their stem cells in an immature state longer and delayed nerve-cell development. Blocking BET proteins, gene-control proteins, reversed the defects (Cell Reports, 2025).
- Rat pups exposed to 900 MHz before and after birth at 0.08 and 0.4 W/kg had less brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), fewer dividing brain cells and a shifted balance of excitatory and inhibitory connections. 0.08 W/kg is the U.S. whole-body public limit (Neurotoxicology, 2025).
- In pregnant women in Yazd, Iran, longer phone call time went with more miscarriage, abnormal birth weight and abnormal infant length (BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth, 2025).
- A meta-analysis of 17 studies with 57,693 participants found 1.27 times the odds of miscarriage with exposure to electromagnetic fields above 50 hertz or 16 milligauss (Open Medicine, 2021).
- Rats exposed in the womb to an active phone had fewer egg follicles and lower ovarian hormones, most of all after exposure in the first week of pregnancy (Reproductive Sciences, 2025).
- The Ramazzini Institute started exposure before birth and continued until natural death, and found heart schwannomas in male rats at 50 V/m (Environmental Research, 2018).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: the embryo keeps developing, but some of its instructions arrive mistimed, so cells specialize late, connect wrongly or build with less reserve. In development, an error in information becomes structure. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: timing decides the result. The egg-follicle study found the first week of pregnancy most sensitive, and the organoid study found that a gene-control step sits between the signal and the defect. The hypothesis also predicts that the source matters: in Mexico City, children with home power-line fields of 0.4 microtesla or more had 2.39 times the odds of brain and spinal-cord tumors, and prolonged tablet use had 2.53 times the odds with internet connection and 3.53 times without it, while cell phone call time showed no difference between cases and controls (Environmental Research, 2025).

This entry describes research. It cannot diagnose or treat anyone; for a personal health concern, see a medical professional and the entry on personal health questions and diagnosis.

entries.title: Body Systems: Digestive system and liver (digestive and hepatic system): What does the research show?
entries.question: Digestive system and liver (digestive and hepatic system): What does the research show?
entries.text:
Studies of the digestive system in RF Safe's directory found changes in the liver, the salivary glands and the gut, including liver tumors in mice at an exposure of 0.04 watts per kilogram, half the U.S. whole-body public limit.

What this system does. The liver clears toxins, builds proteins and controls blood sugar and fats, and it depends on mitochondria and steady antioxidant defenses. The salivary glands release saliva under nerve and calcium signals, and the parotid gland sits right under a phone held to the cheek. The gut lining and its microbes follow daily rhythms, and the gut renews its lining every few days. Phones carried below the waist sit against the abdomen.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 246 studies to the digestive system and liver (after removing 9 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 88 report harm, 74 report mixed results and 40 report a benefit. Together, 202 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 20 found no effect, and 24 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 7 as high and 12 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are oxidative stress and inflammation in the liver, liver tumors in mice, changes in parotid gland tissue and saliva, shifts in gut microbes and their chemical products, and early-onset colorectal cancer in a pilot study of phone carrying reported as a conference abstract.

Key findings:
- In mice given a cancer-causing chemical, exposure at 0.04, 0.4 and 2 W/kg significantly raised the number of liver and lung tumors, with no clear dose-response (Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications, 2015).
- Rats exposed to 6 GHz at 0.21 milliwatts per square centimeter and a specific absorption rate of 0.014 W/kg, 2 hours a day, had liver injury with oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, inflammation and a DNA-damage marker, and coenzyme Q10 reduced the damage (Scientific Reports, 2026).
- Fetal rat livers exposed in the womb to a 900 MHz GSM signal had more oxidative damage and lower antioxidant enzymes (2023).
- Rats exposed to phone radiation had activated fibroblasts in the parotid gland, reactive neck lymph nodes and, after 60 days, more fibrosis, scar-type tissue, in the skin and mouth lining, with more blood-vessel congestion in the parotid (European Review for Medical and Pharmacological Sciences, 2024).
- In 104 students, saliva from the parotid gland changed in flow, acidity and protein markers, and the changes followed years of phone use (International Journal of Risk and Safety in Medicine, 2025).
- Mice exposed to 4.9 GHz 5G at 50 watts per square meter, five times the U.S. public limit, for one hour a day for three weeks lost gut microbial diversity and showed 258 changed fecal metabolites (Scientific Reports, 2024).
- The 2025 WHO-commissioned review of animal cancer studies rated the evidence for hepatoblastoma, a liver tumor, as moderate certainty (Environment International, 2025).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: the liver and gut keep working, but their antioxidant defenses run lower, their daily rhythms drift and their cells copy DNA with more error. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the mouse tumor study found the effect at its lowest dose as well as its highest, so the response did not follow heat. The hypothesis predicts that tumor promotion in a tissue already carrying damage, as in those chemically treated mice, will show up before tumor starting in healthy tissue. It also predicts that tissue right next to the phone, such as the parotid gland or the colon under a pocket, will show effects that whole-body dose estimates miss. In INTERPHONE's Canadian data, parotid gland tumors showed little evidence of increased risk, which marks a limit of what call-time studies can detect. A 2024 pilot study of 50 cases and 50 controls, reported only as a conference abstract and not yet peer reviewed, found four times the odds of early-onset colorectal cancer in people who carried a phone below the waist.

This entry describes research. It cannot diagnose or treat anyone; for a personal health concern, see a medical professional and the entry on personal health questions and diagnosis.

entries.title: Body Systems: Ears (sensory system, auditory): What does the research show?
entries.question: Ears (sensory system, auditory): What does the research show?
entries.text:
Studies of the ears in RF Safe's directory found changes in hearing tests, inner-ear cells and the nerve-sheath cells that form acoustic neuromas, and the ear is the organ a phone call presses against.

What this system does. The inner ear turns sound into electrical signals. Its hair cells and the cochlear nerve fire with timing precise to fractions of a millisecond, and the cochlea runs on a carefully held voltage across its fluid spaces. The hearing nerve is wrapped in Schwann cells, the cells that grow into acoustic neuromas, also called vestibular schwannomas. During a handheld call, the ear and that nerve sit closer to the antenna than any other tissue.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 127 studies to the ears (after removing 3 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 26 report harm, 44 report mixed results and 1 reports a benefit. Together, 71 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 27 found no effect, and 29 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 4 as high and 9 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are worse hearing thresholds in the phone ear than in the other ear, changes in brainstem hearing signals, inner-ear cell death in animals, DNA damage in ear-canal cells, acoustic neuroma risk with long-term same-side use, and changed gene activity in human Schwann cells.

Key findings:
- Rats exposed to 2.45 GHz Wi-Fi from pregnancy through 45 days after birth had higher hearing thresholds at 5 volts per meter (V/m) and above, and more inner-ear cell death at 10 and 15 V/m, rising with field strength (Journal of International Advanced Otology, 2024).
- Medical students who had used mobile phones for five years had worse hearing thresholds in the phone ear than in their other ear (Journal of Postgraduate Medicine, 2017).
- In 100 long-term phone users, high-frequency hearing above 8 kilohertz was significantly worse in the ear they used for calls (Indian Journal of Otolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery, 2014).
- Cells from the ear canal of phone users showed more DNA damage than cells from controls, and the damage grew with daily call time (Electromagnetic Biology and Medicine, 2018).
- A meta-analysis found acoustic neuroma odds of 2.55 after 1,640 or more hours of mobile phone use on the same side as the tumor (Pathophysiology, 2013).
- Human Schwann cells exposed to electromagnetic fields changed how they grew and moved, made less cell-to-cell adhesion protein, and shifted genes that cluster with hearing loss (iScience, 2026).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: the ear's signals keep firing, but with more timing error and less complete repair. Hair cells and Schwann cells under that strain lose accuracy first, and lost hair cells are not replaced. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the ear shows that the body responds to the shape of a signal and not only its average power. In 1962, people heard modulated radio energy as sound, at average power densities as low as 400 microwatts per square centimeter. Whether they heard it depended on the carrier frequency and the modulation (Journal of Applied Physiology, 1962). The hypothesis predicts the same rule for damage: the pulse pattern, not average heating, decides the effect. It also predicts that short studies of tinnitus or self-reported hearing will miss slow cell loss.

Counter-study: a 2019 COSMOS paper (International Journal of Epidemiology) found no link between call time and self-reported tinnitus or hearing loss in Swedish and Finnish users. It used questionnaires, not hearing tests, and its heaviest callers did report more weekly headaches, an odds ratio of 1.13. The paper states that its Finnish data collection received contributions from Nokia, TeliaSonera, Elisa and the Mobile Manufacturers' Forum, and its Swedish data collection from TeliaSonera, Ericsson and Telenor, under contracts guaranteeing the researchers' independence. Its second author, Maria Feychting, was ICNIRP Vice Chair when it was published, and coauthor Anders Ahlbom served on ICNIRP from 1996 to 2008, according to ICNIRP's former-members page.

entries.title: Body Systems: Eyes (sensory system, ocular): What does the research show?
entries.question: Eyes (sensory system, ocular): What does the research show?
entries.text:
Most studies of the eyes in RF Safe's directory found the eye responding to wireless and microwave exposure, including damage to the lens and weaker signals in the optic nerve at absorption levels far below the phone limits.

What this system does. The eye turns light into electrical signals. The lens must stay perfectly clear, and its surface layer of cells has almost no blood supply and little capacity for repair. The retina and the optic nerve, the cable that carries vision to the brain, run on precise voltage changes and heavy energy use. The eye also sits in the path of a phone held to the face or a headset worn over it.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 138 studies to the eyes (after removing 2 retracted papers and retraction notices and 2 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 49 report harm, 39 report mixed results and 7 report a benefit. Together, 95 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 17 found no effect, and 26 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 1 as high and 12 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are damage to the lens surface cells, oxidative stress and stress-gene activity in eye tissue, weaker optic-nerve signals, and higher risk of some eye diseases in people with more exposure. Studies at millimeter-wave frequencies also report corneal heating injury, which is the known thermal issue.

Key findings:
- Cow lenses exposed to 1.1 gigahertz (GHz) microwaves at 2.22 milliwatts temporarily lost optical quality and had permanent damage to the lens surface cell layer. The damage was different from the damage caused by heat applied directly (The Open Ophthalmology Journal, 2008).
- Rabbit lens surface cells exposed to 2,450 MHz microwaves for 8 hours at 0.5, 1 and 2 milliwatts per square centimeter grew less, made less DNA and stalled in their cell cycle. 0.5 milliwatts per square centimeter is half the U.S. public limit (Molecular Vision, 2004).
- In monkeys, pulsed 2.45 GHz microwaves damaged the inner lining of the cornea and made iris blood vessels leak. After a common glaucoma eye drop, the power needed for that damage fell tenfold, from 10 to 1 milliwatt per square centimeter, an absorption of 0.26 W/kg. The authors wrote that a mechanism other than significant heating was involved (Bioelectromagnetics, 1992).
- Rats exposed to a 4.5G phone signal 2 hours a day for six weeks had weaker visual signals, thinner optic-nerve fibers with thinner myelin, and more oxidative stress. (Cutaneous and Ocular Toxicology, 2021).
- Rat eyes exposed to 1,800 MHz at 0.06 W/kg, 2 hours a day for eight weeks, switched on caspase-3, a cell-death gene, and p38MAPK, a stress-signaling gene (Bratislava Medical Journal, 2018).
- A genetic Mendelian randomization study linked mobile phone use to higher glaucoma risk, an odds ratio of about 1.36 (Medicine, 2024).
- In a nine-country study, women who worked near high-voltage electrical installations, a power-frequency magnetic-field exposure, had 5.81 times the odds (1.72 to 19.66) of uveal melanoma, an eye cancer, with the risk concentrated in people with dark eyes (Occupational and Environmental Medicine, 2010).
- Modeling showed that children's eyes and brains absorb substantially higher local radiation doses than adults' during phone calls and virtual-reality use (Environmental Research, 2018).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: the lens and retina keep working, but with more oxidative strain, less complete repair and noisier nerve signaling. In the lens, lost repair capacity adds up, because those cells are not replaced. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the monkey study shows that the threshold is not fixed. The same signal did more harm to an eye already under a drug's influence, which is what a reserve-based hypothesis predicts. The hypothesis also separates the two problems: millimeter-wave studies that heat the cornea describe thermal injury, which the limits do address, while eye changes at 0.06 to 0.26 W/kg describe a non-thermal effect that heating limits do not measure. A related rabbit lens-cell study at 5 and 10 milliwatts per square centimeter, 5 to 10 times the U.S. public limit, found irreversible damage that its authors suggested may be a non-thermal effect (Chinese Medical Journal, 2001); that dose is a high-dose test, not an everyday exposure.

entries.title: Body Systems: Heart and blood vessels (cardiovascular system): What does the research show?
entries.question: Heart and blood vessels (cardiovascular system): What does the research show?
entries.text:
The heart holds the strongest single finding in the animal research: malignant tumors of the heart's nerve-sheath cells in male rats, found in two independent lifetime studies and rated high certainty by a review commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO).

What this system does. Every heartbeat is an electrical wave. Heart muscle cells must open and close their calcium and sodium channels in a fixed order, beat after beat, for a lifetime. The heart also contains more mitochondria than almost any other tissue, and its Schwann cells sheathe the nerves that set its rhythm. RF Safe's density-gating hypothesis names heart Schwann cells among the tissues most likely to respond first.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 285 studies to the heart and blood vessels (after removing 11 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 96 report harm, 101 report mixed results and 24 report a benefit. Together, 221 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 26 found no effect, and 38 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 6 as high and 22 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are heart schwannomas in rats, changes in heart rhythm and electrocardiogram (ECG) intervals, heart-rate variability, blood pressure, and oxidative stress in heart muscle.

Key findings:
- The U.S. National Toxicology Program (NTP) found clear evidence of malignant heart schwannomas in male rats exposed to 900 MHz phone signals for about two years (NTP Technical Report 595, 2018).
- The Ramazzini Institute exposed rats from before birth until natural death to a 1.8 GHz signal like a cell tower's, 19 hours a day, and found more heart schwannomas in males at 50 V/m, below the ICNIRP public reference level of about 58 V/m at that frequency (Environmental Research, 2018).
- The 2025 WHO-commissioned review rated the evidence for these heart tumors in male rats as high certainty (Environment International, 2025).
- In 212,046 UK Biobank adults followed for about 12 years, phone users had more new high blood pressure, and the risk rose with weekly call time, to a hazard ratio of 1.25 above 6 hours a week (European Heart Journal: Digital Health, 2023).
- In people, ECG intervals and heart rate changed after phone exposure: heart rate and the PR and QRS intervals fell while the QT and ST intervals rose (International Journal of Cell Biology, 2024).
- Rats exposed to 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi 2 hours a day for 52 days had heavier hearts, thickened heart muscle and more oxidative stress (Health Scope, 2022).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: the heart keeps beating, but its electrical timing is less exact, its cells spend more energy to keep up, and its stress response has less room. In a heart, small timing errors repeat with every beat. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the Ramazzini study found the heart tumor at field levels like a cell tower's, far below the NTP doses, so more exposure did not simply mean more effect. The hypothesis also predicts a second-hit effect: in rats given doxorubicin, a cancer drug that strains the heart, 28 GHz exposure deepened the damage and lengthened the QT interval (Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, 2026). RF Safe's hypothesis is that spin chemistry also acts in red blood cells, which have no mitochondria and no voltage-sensing calcium channels; the report in RF Safe's directory is a single-volunteer case published as a hypothesis article.

Counter-study: the 2026 Korean arm of the Japan-Korea rat study (Toxicological Sciences) reported no significant heart, brain or adrenal effects. It tested one CDMA signal at one dose, 4 W/kg, in 70 male rats per group, and the only heart schwannomas were in exposed rats, 2 of 70 against 0 of 70 in each control group. The rfsafe.net safety-evidence audit documents that its last author, Young Hwan Ahn, joined ICNIRP's Main Commission in July 2024.

entries.title: Body Systems: Hormone glands (endocrine system): What does the research show?
entries.question: Hormone glands (endocrine system): What does the research show?
entries.text:
Studies of the hormone glands in RF Safe's directory found the thyroid, adrenal glands and insulin-making cells changing their output under wireless exposure, often with the gland still looking close to normal.

What this system does. Hormone glands release their hormones in timed pulses, controlled by calcium signals inside the gland cells. The thyroid sets the body's energy use, the adrenal glands release stress hormones, the pituitary directs the other glands, the pineal gland releases melatonin at night, and the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas fire in bursts that follow blood sugar. When the timing of those pulses changes, the hormone level changes even if the gland is intact.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 140 studies to the hormone glands (after removing 2 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 50 report harm, 60 report mixed results and 9 report a benefit. Together, 119 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 11 found no effect, and 10 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 5 as high and 9 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are lower thyroid activity and changed thyroid hormone levels, raised stress hormones, lower insulin release with higher blood sugar, changes in appetite and energy hormones, and adrenal tumors in rats.

Key findings:
- Young rats exposed for two weeks to a 3.5 GHz 5G signal at 1.5 V/m had enlarged thyroid follicles and a lower thyroid activation index, a sign of an underactive thyroid. The authors wrote that the pattern differed from the thyroid's response to cold (Annales d'Endocrinologie, 2025).
- Rats exposed to 1,800 MHz had lower thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroxine (T4), and the drop grew with daily exposure time (2023).
- Chronic, non-thermal 2,450 MHz exposure lowered the thyroid hormone triiodothyronine (T3), raised T4, and made rats hyperactive and aggressive (International Journal of Radiation Biology, 2008).
- In 83 medical students, more phone radiation exposure went with higher TSH, with or without a family history of thyroid disease (Indian Journal of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 2017).
- Rats exposed to 2.45 GHz Wi-Fi 4 hours a day for 45 days had high blood sugar, lower insulin release from pancreatic islets and more oxidative stress in the pancreas (2018).
- Healthy and diabetic rats exposed to 3.5 GHz at a whole-body 37 milliwatts per kilogram, below the 0.08 W/kg public limit, had lower insulin and higher blood sugar (Bioelectromagnetics, 2024).
- Rats exposed to 900 MHz had higher adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and cortisol, and the stress-hormone layer of the adrenal gland thickened (2018).
- The 2025 WHO-commissioned review of animal cancer studies rated the evidence for pheochromocytoma, an adrenal-gland tumor, as moderate certainty (Environment International, 2025).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: the glands keep working, but their timed pulses drift, so hormone levels move away from what the body asked for, and the cells spend more effort to make less. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the insulin study at 37 milliwatts per kilogram shows a change below the whole-body public limit, and the thyroid studies show function changing while structure stays close to normal. Both fit a timing problem, not a heating problem. The hypothesis predicts that gland effects depend on the time of day, the length of exposure and the gland's reserve, which is why a single short test of hormone levels can miss them.

Counter-study: the 2025 WHO-commissioned review led by Ken Karipidis (Environment International, Part II) found no link between mobile phone use and thyroid cancer, a pooled relative risk of 1.05. ICNIRP's commission page lists Karipidis as its Vice Chair since July 2024, yet the 2025 paper's competing-interest statement does not mention that role, although his team's 2024 companion paper did. The pooled estimate came from only 3 studies, published up to 2019, and the authors rated it low certainty. Thyroid cancer is a late outcome; the studies above measured hormone function.
