entries.title: Body Systems: Immune system, lymph and blood (immune and hematopoietic system): What does the research show?
entries.question: Immune system, lymph and blood (immune and hematopoietic system): What does the research show?
entries.text:
The immune system is the second-largest body group in RF Safe's directory, and most of its studies report a change in immune or blood cells, including weaker defenses and more cell death that appeared only after weeks of exposure.

What this system does. Immune cells sense danger and switch on through calcium signals. When a lymphocyte, a white blood cell, is activated, calcium pulses inside it decide which genes turn on and how strongly it responds. The bone marrow makes new blood cells every day, and that steady division depends on accurate DNA copying. Activated immune cells are among the tissues RF Safe's density-gating hypothesis expects to respond first.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 837 studies to the immune system, lymph and blood (after removing 1 retracted papers and retraction notices and 15 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 262 report harm, 305 report mixed results and 99 report a benefit. Together, 666 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 86 found no effect, and 85 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 1 as high and 24 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are changes in lymphocytes and cytokines, the immune system's chemical messengers, weaker innate immune defenses, more cell death and DNA damage in blood and bone-marrow cells, autoimmune markers, and lymphoma in animals.

Key findings:
- In 479,966 UK adults followed for a median of 13.63 years, mobile phone users had a 14 percent higher risk of rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune disease (PLoS One, 2026).
- Rats exposed for 30 days at a non-thermal 500 microwatts per square centimeter made more antibodies against their own brain tissue (Radiation Biology and Radioecology, 2011).
- In mice exposed to TD-SCDMA or LTE-Advanced phone signals, T-lymphocyte cell death rose after more than six weeks, the anti-inflammatory messenger interleukin-10 fell and interleukin-12 rose (Radiation Effects and Defects in Solids, 2025).
- In the same kind of experiment, neutrophils and macrophages, the first-line immune cells, moved and engulfed germs less well after more than six weeks, and blood lysozyme activity fell (Radiation Effects and Defects in Solids, 2024).
- Bone-marrow blood stem cells in mice showed more cell death and more micronuclei, a marker of broken chromosomes, after six to eight weeks of phone-signal exposure, but not after two or four weeks (2023).
- In human blood lymphocytes, a mobile phone signal caused chromosome damage by itself, and a single 15-minute exposure before gamma radiation increased the damage beyond the two added together (General Physiology and Biophysics, 2024).
- In a replication of a 2010 study, mice given a cancer-causing chemical and exposed at 0.04, 0.4 and 2 W/kg had significantly more lymphomas, with no clear dose-response; the authors noted that effects at 0.04 and 0.4 W/kg were "well below exposure limits" (Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications, 2015).
- The 2025 WHO-commissioned review of animal cancer studies rated the evidence for lymphoma as moderate certainty (Environment International, 2025).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: immune cells still respond, but their signals are noisier, so they can overreact, underreact or turn against the body's own tissue, and dividing blood cells copy DNA with more error. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the mouse studies show a time boundary. Two or four weeks of exposure changed little, while six to eight weeks changed stem cells, lymphocytes and first-line defenses. That is what a reserve-based hypothesis predicts, and it is why short studies report no effect. The hypothesis also predicts that the immune system can move either way, and the directory reflects that: some studies report immune activation and others report suppression, and both are a change from normal immune balance.

Counter-study: a 2025 WHO-commissioned review (Environment International, Part II) found no link between mobile phone use and leukemia or non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Its lead author, Ken Karipidis, has been ICNIRP Vice Chair since July 2024, according to ICNIRP's commission page, yet the 2025 paper's competing-interest statement does not mention his ICNIRP role, although the team's 2024 companion paper did. The 2025 statement does disclose that co-author Martin Röösli advised ICNIRP and sat from 2011 to 2018 on the board of the Swiss Research Foundation for Electricity and Mobile Communication, whose sponsors include Swisscom and Sunrise. The authors themselves rated their no-link finding as low certainty.

entries.title: Body Systems: Kidneys and bladder (renal and urinary system): What does the research show?
entries.question: Kidneys and bladder (renal and urinary system): What does the research show?
entries.text:
Nearly every study of the kidneys and bladder in RF Safe's directory found a change, most often oxidative stress, damaged kidney tubules and fewer filtering units after exposure before birth.

What this system does. The kidneys filter the blood through about a million tiny units called glomeruli and fine-tune salt and water in long tubules. Tubule cells move charged particles across their membranes all day, so they are packed with ion pumps and mitochondria. People are born with nearly all the glomeruli they will ever have, so a unit lost before birth is not replaced. The bladder lining holds a barrier that depends on healthy surface cells.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 97 studies to the kidneys and bladder (after removing 3 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 46 report harm, 36 report mixed results and 6 report a benefit. Together, 88 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 5 found no effect, and 4 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 1 as high and 4 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are oxidative stress, damaged tubule cells and cell death in kidney tissue, changed kidney size and fewer glomeruli after exposure in the womb, bladder lining damage, and urinary-tract birth defects linked to call time in pregnancy.

Key findings:
- Rats exposed to 900 MHz before birth had larger kidneys and renal cortex but fewer glomeruli at four weeks old, and melatonin or omega-3 prevented the changes (International Journal of Radiation Biology, 2015).
- Male rats exposed in the womb to 3.5 GHz, at a peak absorption of about 0.066 W/kg in the uterine region, had kidney tissue damage, higher autophagy markers and more DNA fragmentation, most after exposure through the whole pregnancy (Histochemistry and Cell Biology, 2026).
- Young male rats exposed to 2,100 MHz for 6 or 12 hours a day for 30 days lost the brush border of their kidney tubules and had more tubule cell death and oxidative stress (Archives of Medical Research, 2018).
- Rats exposed to an electromagnetic field had oxidative stress in both kidney and bladder, damaged glomeruli and tubules, and a degenerated bladder lining (2017).
- Rats exposed to 0.9 GHz one hour a day from postnatal day 21 to 45 had heavier kidneys, oxidative stress markers and tissue damage (Journal of Molecular Histology, 2024).
- Mothers of babies born with kidney and urinary-tract malformations reported more daily call time in pregnancy, and higher effective absorption, absorption rate times call time, went with higher risk (Turkish Journal of Medical Sciences, 2024).
- Kidney cells exposed to a mobile phone simulator had up to 40 percent lower survival than unexposed cells (2018).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: the kidney keeps filtering, but its tubule cells spend more energy, hold less antioxidant reserve and repair less completely, and a kidney that develops under that strain is built with fewer filtering units. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the kidney findings cluster in exposure before birth and in young animals, the windows the hypothesis predicts are most sensitive, because a missing glomerulus cannot be rebuilt. In the kidney-cell study, one and two hours a day caused similar losses, so the effect did not simply double with dose. Melatonin and omega-3 preventing the prenatal changes points to oxidative strain as the step between signal and damage, which is the mitochondrial step of the hypothesis.

entries.title: Body Systems: Lungs (respiratory system): What does the research show?
entries.question: Lungs (respiratory system): What does the research show?
entries.text:
The lungs are one of the smallest groups in RF Safe's directory, but almost every study in it found the lung responding to a field, including more lung tumors in mice at 0.04 watts per kilogram.

What this system does. The lungs move air through branching airways lined with cells that beat tiny hairs in coordinated waves and pass signals to each other through gap junctions. The thin air-sac wall must stay intact for oxygen to cross. Lung cells face a constant oxidative load from the air itself, so their antioxidant defenses are always working.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 47 studies to the lungs (after removing 6 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 11 report harm, 21 report mixed results and 9 report a benefit. Together, 41 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 1 found no effect, and 5 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 2 as high and 3 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are lung tumors in mice, inflammation in lung tissue, DNA damage in aged lung cells, slower repair in human airway cells, and lung responses to therapeutic radio fields.

Key findings:
- In mice given a cancer-causing chemical, exposure at 0.04, 0.4 and 2 W/kg significantly raised the number of lung tumors, with no clear dose-response. The lowest dose is half the U.S. whole-body public limit (Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications, 2015).
- Rabbits exposed to phone radiation for 16 weeks at below-heating levels, 1.0 W/kg to the head and 0.7 W/kg to the body, had more inflammatory cells in the lungs and liver (2020).
- A power-frequency 50 hertz magnetic field at 1.0 millitesla for 24 hours damaged DNA in senescent, aged human lung cells, but not in non-senescent ones, through reactive oxygen species from the mitochondria (Biophysical Chemistry, 2025).
- The 2025 WHO-commissioned review of animal cancer studies rated the evidence for lung tumors, bronchio-alveolar adenoma or carcinoma, as moderate certainty (Environment International, 2025).
- Human airway lining cells exposed to 1.8 GHz moved less and closed scratch wounds more slowly, without dying (The Laryngoscope, 2015).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: lung cells keep working, but their defenses against oxidative strain run lower and their DNA repair is less complete, which matters most in cells that are already old or damaged. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the aging lung-cell study is a clean reserve boundary. The same field damaged the DNA of aged cells and left younger cells alone, which is what a hypothesis built on remaining reserve predicts. The mouse tumor study found tumors at its lowest dose, so the effect did not follow heat. The directory also holds benefit studies, such as a radio field that reduced lung injury in rats after blood flow was cut and restored (Pulmonary Circulation, 2025). A benefit is still proof that lung tissue is not inert to the field: the exposure changed inflammation, cell death and oxidative signaling. In hamster lung cells, a 1,950 MHz signal raised chromosome-damage markers at 0.15 and 0.3 W/kg but not at 0.6 or 1.25 W/kg, and in a separate test, pre-exposure at 1.25 W/kg triggered an adaptive response, so the lower doses produced the damage.

entries.title: Body Systems: Muscles and bones (musculoskeletal system): What does the research show?
entries.question: Muscles and bones (musculoskeletal system): What does the research show?
entries.text:
Bones and muscles respond to electromagnetic fields so reliably that medicine uses pulsed fields to help some fractures heal, and studies in RF Safe's directory found phone signals slowing fracture healing and bone growth, the other side of the same fact.

What this system does. Bone is living tissue that is built and broken down all the time by cells that answer mechanical, electrical and calcium signals. Muscle contracts when calcium is released inside the fiber on command. Bone growth plates in children and the developing skeleton before birth follow strict timing. Because these cells read electrical signals, medicine uses pulsed electromagnetic fields to steer them.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 150 studies to the muscles and bones (after removing 15 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 24 report harm, 52 report mixed results and 53 report a benefit. Together, 129 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 5 found no effect, and 16 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 0 as high and 2 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are slower fracture healing, poorer bone growth around implants, changes in bone strength and bone-turnover signals, oxidative stress in muscle, and abnormal skeletal development after exposure before birth. The directory also holds many therapy studies where pulsed fields helped bone or tendon repair.

Key findings:
- Rats with a broken bone exposed to 900 MHz had lower healing scores on X-ray, under the microscope and in strength testing (Acta Orthopaedica et Traumatologica Turcica, 2013).
- In rabbits, bone grew less tightly onto implants after phone radiation exposure, with more inflammation (2019).
- Rats exposed to 1,800 MHz before birth had lower calcineurin activity, a calcium-controlled enzyme, more dying cartilage and muscle cells and poorer development of the femur, tibia and ulna, worst at 24 hours a day (Acta Cirúrgica Brasileira, 2016).
- Rat pups exposed to 900 MHz before birth had vertebral cartilage turning to bone and a wider central canal in the spine (Acta Histochemica, 2020).
- Rats exposed to 900, 1,800 and 2,100 MHz phone-like signals had changes in tibia strength and X-ray findings and oxidative stress in skeletal muscle (Electromagnetic Biology and Medicine, 2023).
- Healthy and diabetic rats exposed to 3.5 GHz at a whole-body 37 milliwatts per kilogram, below the 0.08 W/kg public limit, had weaker bone mechanics (Biotechnology and Biotechnological Equipment, 2023).
- Rats exposed to 2.45 GHz before and after birth had raised bone-turnover signals, sRANKL and osteoprotegerin, with matching tissue changes at 10 and 15 V/m (Physiological Research, 2024).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: bone and muscle cells keep working, but they receive mistimed instructions, so building and breaking down fall out of balance and repair is slower and less complete. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: this group has more benefit studies than harm studies, and that supports the hypothesis rather than weakening it. In one 2026 study, a 50 hertz field made stem cells migrate by opening store-operated calcium channels, and blocking those channels removed the effect (Journal of Bioenergetics and Biomembranes, 2026). A therapy works because the field changes calcium signaling. A designed, timed signal can steer that signaling toward repair. An unplanned phone or Wi-Fi signal reaches the same channels with no design, and the harm studies show repair going the wrong way. Either way, bone is not inert to the field.

entries.title: Body Systems: Nervous system (brain and nerves, neurological): What does the research show?
entries.question: Nervous system (brain and nerves, neurological): What does the research show?
entries.text:
The nervous system is the body group with the most research in RF Safe's directory, and most of those studies found a biological change, not silence. That includes the brain tumors in the U.S. government's rat study and memory changes in teenagers that tracked the radio dose to the brain.

What this system does. The brain, spinal cord and nerves carry information as voltage spikes and calcium pulses. A nerve cell only works if those signals open and close on time, millisecond by millisecond. Brain tissue also packs in voltage-sensing ion channels and mitochondria, the cell's power plants, and it uses more energy per gram than almost any other tissue. RF Safe's density-gating hypothesis predicts that tissue built this way responds first.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 1376 studies to the nervous system (after removing 6 retracted papers and retraction notices and 38 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 434 report harm, 508 report mixed results and 109 report a benefit. Together, 1051 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 133 found no effect, and 192 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 23 as high and 111 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are brain tumors in animals and in long-term phone users, memory and learning problems, oxidative stress, reactive glial cells and damaged nerve cells, and changes in brain waves and sleep.

Key findings:
- The U.S. National Toxicology Program (NTP) exposed rats to 900 megahertz (MHz) phone signals at 1.5, 3 and 6 watts per kilogram (W/kg) for about two years. It found clear evidence of malignant heart schwannomas and some evidence of malignant brain gliomas in male rats (NTP Technical Report 595, 2018).
- A 2025 review commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) assessed 51 animal cancer studies, after a 2026 correction, and rated the evidence for brain gliomas and heart schwannomas in male rats as high certainty (Environment International, 2025).
- A meta-analysis of case-control studies found glioma odds of 1.90 at the highest cumulative use of mobile and cordless phones, and 2.01 after 20 or more years, with the excess in the temporal lobe, the part of the brain nearest the phone (2017).
- Canadian data from the INTERPHONE study, corrected for selection and recall bias, gave a glioma odds ratio of 2.2 in the heaviest quarter of users (American Journal of Epidemiology, 2017).
- A 2024 meta-analysis found significantly higher risk for three brain tumor types on the same side of the head where the phone was held (Environmental Health, 2024).
- In 439 teenagers followed for one year, figural memory fell as the cumulative radio dose to the brain rose. The study's senior author, Martin Röösli, later served on ICNIRP from 2016 to 2024. Texting and gaming, which give off very little radio energy, showed no such link (Environment International, 2015).
- Rats exposed head-only to a 900 MHz GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) signal at a brain-averaged 1.5 W/kg, 45 minutes a day for eight weeks, had more glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), a marker of reactive astrocytes, in several brain areas (International Journal of Radiation Biology, 2010).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: the brain still runs, but its signals arrive with more timing noise, its repair is less complete, and each new stress starts from a lower reserve. In the brain that shows up as memory and learning errors, reactive glial cells and, over years, a higher chance that a cell copies the wrong instructions. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the hypothesis predicts effects that depend on the signal's timing and modulation, the dose that actually reaches the tissue, and the reserve left in that brain. The teenager study fits that pattern, because memory tracked the radio dose to the head and not phone use in general. The hypothesis also predicts weaker or missing effects in short tests, at doses or signals that do not reach the tissue, and in studies that cannot separate heavy users from light ones.

Counter-study: COSMOS, 2024 (Environment International), followed 264,574 people for a median of 7.12 years and reported no link between call time and glioma. ICNIRP's own former-members page lists its lead author, Maria Feychting, as a member of the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP), which writes heating-based exposure guidelines, from 2008 to 2020 and its Vice Chair from 2012 to 2020. The rfsafe.net safety-evidence audit flags that the heavy-use estimate was wide, a hazard ratio of 1.07 with a range of 0.62 to 1.86, which cannot rule out a moderate increase. The cohort's 2019 paper reports partial funding of its Finnish and Swedish data collection by Nokia, TeliaSonera, Elisa, Ericsson, Telenor and the Mobile Manufacturers' Forum, under contracts guaranteeing the researchers' independence.

This entry describes research. It cannot diagnose or treat anyone; for a personal health concern, see a medical professional and the entry on personal health questions and diagnosis.

entries.title: Body Systems: Reproductive system (fertility, testes, ovaries, breast and prostate): What does the research show?
entries.question: Reproductive system (fertility, testes, ovaries, breast and prostate): What does the research show?
entries.text:
The reproductive system has the most consistent findings in RF Safe's directory. Sperm quality falls with phone exposure in pooled studies, and a review commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) rated reduced pregnancy rates after male exposure as high certainty.

What this system does. Sperm and eggs carry the genetic instructions for the next generation, so any copying error is passed on. Sperm swim by calcium-controlled beating, and the cells that make sperm and testosterone are packed with mitochondria and voltage-sensing channels. Ovaries release hormones in timed cycles. Phones are carried in pockets and bras, right next to these organs.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 477 studies to the reproductive system (after removing 8 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 212 report harm, 159 report mixed results and 30 report a benefit. Together, 401 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 36 found no effect, and 40 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 11 as high and 25 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are lower sperm motility, viability and count, sperm DNA damage, reduced pregnancy rates in animals, changes in testosterone-making Leydig cells, fewer egg follicles after exposure in the womb, and higher breast cancer odds with heavy phone use.

Key findings:
- A meta-analysis of 10 studies and 1,492 samples found phone exposure lowered sperm motility by about 8.1 percent and viability by about 9.1 percent, consistent in lab and human studies (Environment International, 2014).
- An updated meta-analysis of 18 studies and 4,280 samples found phone exposure tied to lower sperm motility, viability and concentration (Environmental Research, 2021).
- The WHO-commissioned review of animal male-fertility studies, after a 2025 correction, rated the evidence that exposure in males reduces pregnancy rates as high certainty (Environment International, 2025).
- Melnick and Moskowitz, 2026, estimated that protecting male fertility needs a whole-body exposure of 3.3 to 10 milliwatts per kilogram, so the current public limit is "8- to 24-fold higher than levels that are protective of male reproductive health" (Environmental Health, 2026).
- Mouse Leydig cells, which make testosterone, made less DNA and stalled in their cell cycle after 15 to 120 minutes at 1,800 or 2,450 MHz under non-thermal conditions (Scientific Reports, 2026).
- Rats exposed in the womb to an active phone had lower estrogen and progesterone, fewer egg follicles and more follicle cell death, most of all after exposure in the first week of pregnancy (Reproductive Sciences, 2025).
- Women who talked on a mobile phone more than 60 minutes a day had 3.49 times the odds of breast cancer of women who talked under 10 minutes, in a multicenter case-control study based on self-report (Journal of Research in Medical Sciences, 2025).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: sperm and egg cells keep forming, but with more oxidative damage and less accurate copying, and those errors are carried forward instead of being cleared. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: in mice, a father's 4.9 GHz 5G exposure caused anxiety-like behavior and poorer sperm in his sons, linked to a gene switched off by methylation, but did not change their fertility or memory (Reproductive Toxicology, 2026). The hypothesis predicts exactly this kind of selective, inherited change in information rather than broad failure. It also predicts that the dose reaching the tissue decides the result, which is why a phone in a front pocket matters more than call time recorded by a network. A 2024 WHO-commissioned review of human male-fertility studies called its evidence "very uncertain", and the rfsafe.net audit notes that it measured phone time rather than the dose reaching the testes.

This entry describes research. It cannot diagnose or treat anyone; for a personal health concern, see a medical professional and the entry on personal health questions and diagnosis.

entries.title: Body Systems: Skin (integumentary system): What does the research show?
entries.question: Skin (integumentary system): What does the research show?
entries.text:
The skin takes the first contact with every phone, and studies in RF Safe's directory found skin and lining cells changing their structure, pigment, gene activity and DNA under wireless exposure, in some cases in the opposite direction from heat.

What this system does. The skin is a barrier that renews itself, with stem cells in its base layer dividing to replace the surface. Pigment cells make melanin under hormone and calcium signals. The lining of the mouth and cheek renews just as fast and sits under a phone held to the face. At higher frequencies, such as 5G millimeter waves, most of the energy is absorbed in the skin itself.

What the studies report. RF Safe's research directory, which covers fields from power lines to wireless signals, tags 165 studies to the skin (after removing 20 off-topic records, such as medical ablation or static magnets). Of these, 44 report harm, 60 report mixed results and 15 report a benefit. Together, 119 report a measurable biological change from the exposure. Another 20 found no effect, and 26 are unclear or not yet rated. For evidence strength, the directory rates 0 as high and 10 as moderate. A mixed or benefit result is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert to the field.

The main kinds of findings are structural changes in skin layers, oxidative stress and tissue-remodeling enzymes in skin cells, changes in melanin production, changed DNA structure and gene activity under millimeter waves, micronuclei in cheek cells of heavy phone users, and faster skin cancer in mice given a cancer-causing chemical.

Key findings:
- Rats exposed to a 900 MHz phone signal for 10 days had a thickened outer horny layer while the rest of the epidermis thinned, extra basal-cell growth and collagen changes, and melatonin prevented most of them (Toxicology and Industrial Health, 2004).
- Heavy phone users had more micronuclei, a marker of chromosome damage, in cheek cells than light users, and more on the side they held the phone (Journal of International Clinical Dental Research Organization, 2023).
- A systematic review of seven studies found phone radiation tied to micronuclei and other genetic-damage markers in cheek-lining cells (2020).
- Human skin cells exposed to 1,760 MHz had more reactive oxygen species and more matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes that break down skin structure (2021).
- Mouse pigment cells exposed to 1,760 MHz at 4 W/kg made more melanin, while warming the same cells to 38 degrees Celsius made less, so heat did not explain the effect (International Journal of Molecular Sciences, 2024).
- Human skin fibroblasts exposed repeatedly to 60 GHz millimeter waves changed their gene activity and the folded shapes of their DNA, without DNA breaks (2022).

How RF Safe reads it. RF Safe does not say radio-frequency (RF) radiation by itself causes a disease in any one person. RF Safe proposes that exposure lowers biological fidelity: skin cells keep renewing, but with more oxidative strain and noisier signaling, so the barrier repairs less exactly and dividing cells copy DNA with more error. RF Safe's hypothesis is that lower fidelity raises the risk of error and, over time, a collapse of cellular information. RF Safe calls this proposed process bioelectrical dissonance, and calls the state it leaves behind low-fidelity biology, which raises disease risk. This is RF Safe's hypothesis, a proposed and testable explanation, not an agency finding.

Boundary conditions for RF Safe's S4-Mito-Spin hypothesis: the skin is where the hypothesis expects the fewest effects, because resting skin cells carry fewer voltage-sensing channels and mitochondria than brain, heart or testis. At a high dose, a 1,762 MHz LTE signal at 8 W/kg, four to five times the local limits, slightly lowered skin cancer-cell survival and growth, and it reduced DNA damage from ionizing radiation (International Journal of Molecular Sciences, 2021). That protective response is still a change from normal biology. The keratinocyte and pigment-cell studies used 4 W/kg, above the public limits; the pigment study shows that even then, the direction of the effect was opposite to heating. In mice painted with a cancer-causing chemical, 2,450 MHz at 5 and 15 milliwatts per square centimeter, which the authors called athermal and subthermal but which is 5 to 15 times the U.S. public limit, sped up skin cancer and shortened survival (Archives of Dermatological Research, 1982).

This entry describes research. It cannot diagnose or treat anyone; for a personal health concern, see a medical professional and the entry on personal health questions and diagnosis.

entries.title: Government Agencies: How did the FCC end up in charge of phone radiation limits, and what has it done with that role?
entries.question: How did the FCC end up in charge of phone radiation limits, and what has it done with that role?
entries.text:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) sets the phone radiation limits because it licenses every transmitter and approves every phone, and federal environmental law requires it to consider the effects of what it approves. The FCC has said for decades that it is not a health agency. It adopted heating-based limits written by outside groups, relied on the health agencies to tell it they were safe, and has not changed them since 1996.

How it happened:
- The National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) requires federal agencies to consider how their actions affect the human environment. The FCC adopted rules to comply in September 1974.
- In February 1985 the FCC adopted the 1982 American National Standards Institute (ANSI) exposure standard "for lack of a federal standard or guideline." That standard excluded devices of 7 watts or less below 1,000 megahertz, so the FCC did not require routine evaluation of hand-held cell phones.
- In March 1993 the FCC proposed a newer standard in ET Docket No. 93-62. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and other agencies sent comments.
- On February 8, 1996, Section 704(b) of the Telecommunications Act ordered the FCC to finish that rulemaking within 180 days. Section 704(a) barred state and local governments from regulating "the placement, construction, and modification of personal wireless service facilities on the basis of the environmental effects of radio frequency emissions to the extent that such facilities comply with the Commission's regulations concerning such emissions."
- On August 1, 1996, the FCC adopted its limits in order FCC 96-326. It said they were "based substantially on the recommendations" of the EPA, the FDA and other federal health and safety agencies.

The limits, at 47 CFR 1.1310: a specific absorption rate (SAR), the rate at which the body absorbs radio energy, of 1.6 watts per kilogram averaged over 1 gram of tissue for phones, and 0.08 watts per kilogram averaged over the whole body for the public. The rule also lets exposure "be averaged over a time period not to exceed 30 minutes." In 2001 the Government Accountability Office (GAO) explained the basis. Animals showed harmful behavior changes when radio energy raised their body temperature by 1 degree Celsius. The public standard was set at one-fiftieth of that exposure, and the phone limit was adjusted from it. The GAO wrote that the limit "is not designed to address the possibility of any non-heating-related effects, such as cancer." The FCC itself told the GAO that "it has neither primary jurisdiction nor expertise in health and safety matters." The federal appeals court wrote in 2021: "The limits are designed to protect against 'thermal effects' of exposure to RF radiation, but not 'non-thermal' effects."

What the FCC decided about pulsed signals: in the 1996 order the FCC wrote, "We agree with those commenters who maintain that there is insufficient evidence to give special consideration to modulation effects at this time," and that it "would be premature at this time to adopt the NCRP modulation criteria." The NCRP is the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements, whose 1986 report was one of the two sources of the limits. Modulation is the pattern of pulses and changes a phone signal carries, which is the property RF Safe's work focuses on.

What happened next:
- In July 2012 the GAO told the FCC to formally reassess its limit and its testing of phones held against the body. The GAO found the FCC "has not formally asked FDA or EPA for their assessment of the limit since 1996." The GAO later closed both recommendations as "Not Implemented."
- In March 2013 the FCC opened an inquiry into whether its 1996 limits were still adequate (ET Docket No. 13-84). On November 27, 2019, in order FCC 19-126, it closed that inquiry and kept the 1996 limits. It quoted the FDA's April 2019 letter that "no changes to the current standards are warranted at this time."
- On August 13, 2021, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit found that decision "arbitrary and capricious in its failure to respond to record evidence that exposure to RF radiation at levels below the Commission's current limits may cause negative health effects unrelated to cancer," and sent it back to the FCC. The court held that this failure also undermined the FCC's conclusions on children, long-term exposure, "exposure to RF pulsation or modulation," and technology developed since 1996. The court accepted the FCC's explanation on cancer.
- The FCC's consumer page "Wireless Devices and Health Concerns," last updated November 4, 2020 and still posted on November 15, 2026, still quotes and links the FDA safety page that the FDA removed by January 2026. It also says: "at this time, there is no basis on which to establish a different safety threshold than our current requirements."
- In 2019 the FCC's own lab retested phones at 2 millimeters from the body. The FCC later released the results in response to a Freedom of Information Act request, writing: "at a 2 mm separation distance, the FCC RF exposure limits were exceeded." Five of the eight models went over the limit, with the highest reading, 5.2 watts per kilogram, from a Samsung Galaxy J3. Every phone met the limit at the distance it was certified at, which is the gap the GAO flagged in 2012.

RF Safe's position: the FCC adopted heating limits, set aside the evidence on modulation in 1996, and then pointed to the health agencies when asked whether the limits protect people. Those health agencies never wrote a limit, and the FDA has now removed its old conclusions. The FCC should manage the airwaves, and health agencies should set exposure limits that address non-thermal effects, meaning biological effects at levels too low to heat tissue.

entries.title: Government Agencies: How does HHS tie into wireless radiation through Public Law 90-602, and which parts of HHS work on it?
entries.question: How does HHS tie into wireless radiation through Public Law 90-602, and which parts of HHS work on it?
entries.text:
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) holds the legal duty for electronic product radiation, including radio-frequency radiation from phones, under Public Law 90-602, the Radiation Control for Health and Safety Act of 1968. The law gives that duty to the HHS Secretary, who has assigned the day-to-day work to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Other parts of HHS research radio-frequency exposure, but HHS has never issued a radio-frequency performance standard for phones.

The law:
- Public Law 90-602 was enacted on October 18, 1968. It first gave the duty to the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. A 1979 law changed that to the Secretary of HHS.
- It was first part of the Public Health Service Act. The Safe Medical Devices Act of 1990 moved it into the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, where it is now 21 U.S.C. 360hh to 360ss.
- It covers "any ionizing or non-ionizing electromagnetic or particulate radiation" given off by an electronic product. Non-ionizing radiation includes the radio-frequency energy from phones, Wi-Fi and cell towers.
- It directs the Secretary to "plan, conduct, coordinate, and support research, development, training, and operational activities to minimize the emissions of and the exposure of people to, unnecessary electronic product radiation," and to "study and evaluate emissions of, and conditions of exposure to, electronic product radiation and intense magnetic fields."
- It lets the Secretary publish research "relating to the nature and extent of the hazards and control of electronic product radiation" and "make such recommendations relating to such hazards and control as he considers appropriate."
- Under 21 U.S.C. 360kk the Secretary sets performance standards when they are "necessary for the protection of the public health and safety," and must consider "the latest available scientific and medical data." Before setting a standard, the Secretary must consult a 15-member Technical Electronic Product Radiation Safety Standards Committee: five from government, five from industry and five from the public.
- The law once required a yearly report to Congress on the program. Congress repealed that requirement in 1998.

The parts of HHS involved:
- FDA, through its Center for Devices and Radiological Health: runs the radiation control program. It has a standard for microwave ovens, and none for phones.
- National Toxicology Program (NTP), housed at the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences within the National Institutes of Health: ran the cell phone study the FDA nominated. In 2018 it reported "clear evidence" of malignant heart tumors in male rats, and "some evidence" of malignant brain tumors (gliomas) and adrenal gland tumors. In January 2024 the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS) posted that "no further work with this RFR exposure system will be conducted and NIEHS has no further plans to conduct additional RFR exposure studies at this time." It said its system "is not representative of newer technologies such as 4G/4G-LTE, or 5G."
- National Cancer Institute: began a study of brain cancer patients and cell phone use in 1993, according to the Government Accountability Office (GAO).
- National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), part of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: in June 1999 a NIOSH branch chief wrote to the group revising the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) exposure standard on behalf of the federal Radiofrequency Interagency Work Group, which included the FDA, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the Occupational Safety and Health Administration and the National Telecommunications and Information Administration. The letter said studies "continue to be published describing biological responses to nonthermal ELF-modulated and pulse-modulated RF radiation exposures that are not produced by CW (unmodulated) RF radiation," and that limits based on heating, using time-averaged measurements that "mask any differences" between pulsed and steady signals, "may not adequately protect the public." It added: "time-averaging erases the unique characteristics of an intensity-modulated RF radiation that may be responsible for producing an effect." ELF means extremely low frequency, and CW means continuous wave. The letter said these were the members' views, not official agency policy.

What HHS is doing now:
- In September 2025 the White House MAHA (Make America Healthy Again) strategy report stated: "HHS, in partnership with other departments and Federal agencies, will undertake a study on electromagnetic radiation and health research to identify gaps in knowledge, including on new technologies, to ensure safety and efficacy." On January 15, 2026, an HHS spokesman told Reuters that the FDA had removed webpages with "old conclusions" while HHS does that study.
- On September 21, 2026, HHS published a request for information on electromagnetic fields and wireless radiation, docket HHS-OASH-2026-0397, with comments due October 21, 2026. More than 7,000 comments were filed.

RF Safe's position: Public Law 90-602 is a sleeping mandate. For more than 50 years it has given HHS the duty to study radio-frequency exposure, publish what research shows about its hazards, and minimize unnecessary exposure. HHS let the FCC, a communications agency, set the only limits, and those limits cover heating only. HHS should issue a modern performance standard for phones, starting with testing at the body, restart exposure research on pulsed signals, and publish a reasoned determination on non-thermal effects. RF Safe does not claim that phones directly cause disease. It says HHS has a legal duty to follow the research.

entries.title: Government Agencies: What did the EPA do about wireless radiation, and why did it stop?
entries.question: What did the EPA do about wireless radiation, and why did it stop?
entries.text:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) studied radio-frequency radiation from the early 1970s, proposed federal exposure guidance in 1986, and then stopped. According to the EPA's own 1995 summary, its research on the biological effects of radio-frequency radiation stopped in 1987, and its work on guidance stopped in 1988. In 2002 an EPA radiation official wrote that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) limits "are thermally based, and do not apply to chronic, nonthermal exposure situations."

The EPA's authority: in 1970, Reorganization Plan No. 3 moved the old Federal Radiation Council's authority to the EPA. That gives the EPA the job of advising the President and providing "guidance for all federal agencies in the formulation of radiation standards." The guidance would not be a regulation. It would tell agencies such as the FCC what exposure levels to use.

What the EPA did:
- 1973: the EPA began measuring radio-frequency levels from broadcast towers, radar and satellite stations. By February 1978 it had measured 11 metropolitan areas, according to the Government Accountability Office (GAO).
- 1978: EPA scientists at Research Triangle Park, North Carolina, were studying rats, mice and monkeys chronically exposed to radio-frequency radiation, including at low levels, to investigate low-level effects reported in the Soviet Union. The GAO put the budget at 830,000 dollars and 30 staff-years. The GAO reported that the EPA listed confirming "the existence of nonheating effects" as one of its three major open questions.
- 1978: the GAO reported that EPA officials agreed the 10 milliwatts per square centimeter exposure guideline needed reevaluation because "a large number of studies have reported biological effects at low exposure levels," and because it was set for workers, not for the public around the clock.
- September 1984: the EPA published "Biological Effects of Radiofrequency Radiation" (EPA-600/8-83-026F).
- July 30, 1986: the EPA proposed four options in the Federal Register. Three set whole-body limits of 0.04, 0.08 or 0.4 watts per kilogram of specific absorption rate (SAR), the rate at which the body absorbs radio energy. The fourth was no guidance, only information programs. The strictest option, 0.04, is half of the 0.08 whole-body public limit the FCC adopted in 1996. The notice said radio-frequency radiation "should, for now, be treated as a noncarcinogen, and an uncertainty factor should be used in deriving exposure limits." The same notice reported a University of Washington study of rats exposed for life to pulsed microwaves at 0.4 watts per kilogram, five times today's FCC whole-body public limit, that found "a statistically higher incidence of primary malignancies in exposed animals." It said the data were "insufficient" for effects below 1 to 4 watts per kilogram, "and this leaves potentially significant issues unresolved," including "low-frequency modulated RF fields" and "the potential for cancer promotion." The notice noted that Portland, Oregon already used zoning guidance of 0.04 watts per kilogram, "10 times more stringent than the ANSI voluntary standard."
- 1987 and 1988: research stopped in 1987 and guidance work stopped in 1988. The GAO reported in 1994 that the EPA stopped because federal agencies did not agree on which option to take. In 1993 the head of the EPA's radiation office said the agency "decided to put our efforts into other issues." In 2001 the GAO wrote that the EPA's in-house program "was largely eliminated in the 1980s for budgetary reasons." The EPA wrote in 1995 that when the work stopped, "numerous health issues remained unresolved," including "the effects associated with low-frequency modulated RF fields; the role of RF radiation exposure in carcinogenesis; potential effects of low-level, long-term exposure; and biophysical mechanisms."
- 1990: the EPA released a review draft, "Evaluation of the Potential Carcinogenicity of Electromagnetic Fields," covering both power-line and radio-frequency fields. Its Science Advisory Board recommended that the EPA finish the radio-frequency guidance.
- April 1993: the EPA held a conference in Bethesda, Maryland. Its panel on molecular and cellular effects called for more research on "Low intensity athermal effects" and "Effects from pulse- or ELF-modulated RF radiation," meaning radio signals pulsed at extremely low frequencies. That panel also found that the 1992 ANSI/IEEE (American National Standards Institute and Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) standard "does not adequately include or address in vitro effects, but rather addresses only systemic effects." Some epidemiology panelists said the EPA "should not continue to state with certainty that RF radiation is not a carcinogen."
- November 9, 1993: the EPA sent the FCC comments recommending, "with certain reservations," limits from the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP). The FCC summarized the EPA's view that "some of the provisions of the new ANSI/IEEE guidelines are not acceptable." In its 1996 order the FCC wrote: "as recommended by the EPA, we are adopting exposure limits for field strength and power density based on those recommended by the NCRP."

The 2002 letter: on July 16, 2002, Norbert Hankin of the EPA's Radiation Protection Division wrote that the FCC limits protect against heating "but not from all possible mechanisms. Therefore, the generalization by many that the guidelines protect human beings from harm by any or all mechanisms is not justified." He wrote that the limits "did not consider information that addresses nonthermal, prolonged exposures," and that "Federal health and safety agencies have not yet developed policies concerning possible risk from long-term, nonthermal exposures." Hankin also wrote that "there are reports that suggest that potentially adverse health effects, such as cancer, may occur," that since 1993 "the number of studies reporting effects associated with both acute and chronic low-level exposure to RF radiation has increased," and that compliant exposures "generally have been represented as 'safe'" by system operators "even though there is uncertainty."

Since then: in 2012 the GAO reported that the FCC had not formally asked the EPA or the FDA for an assessment of the limit since 1996.

RF Safe's position: the EPA was the federal agency built to set radiation guidance for the whole government, and it asked the right questions about non-heating effects and pulsed signals by 1978 and 1993. It never answered them, because the work was stopped. RF Safe asks that the EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services lead on health, starting with the non-thermal research the EPA left unfinished.

entries.title: Government Agencies: What has the Government Accountability Office (GAO) told Congress about wireless radiation?
entries.question: What has the Government Accountability Office (GAO) told Congress about wireless radiation?
entries.text:
The Government Accountability Office (GAO), the investigative arm of Congress, has reported on federal handling of radio-frequency radiation at least five times since 1978. Its reports show health agencies that did not set limits, a communications agency that says it is not a health agency, and recommendations the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) did not carry out. Until 2004 the GAO was named the General Accounting Office.

The reports:
- March 29, 1978, "Efforts by the Environmental Protection Agency To Protect the Public from Environmental Nonionizing Radiation Exposures" (CED-78-79): found "no official U.S. environmental public health standard for exposure to nonionizing radiation sources." It noted that Eastern European standards protected against "nonheating effects of long-term exposure to low-level radiation," while U.S. standards "were designed to protect against heating effects from high-level exposures." It reported that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) listed confirming "the existence of nonheating effects" as a major open question and might need new laws to set an enforceable standard. It noted that the U.S. standard for extended occupational exposure to microwave radiation "is approximately 1,000 times greater than the Soviet Union's published standard."
- November 30, 1978, "More Protection From Microwave Radiation Hazards Needed" (HRD-79-7): reviewed the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) program under Public Law 90-602. It found that more than half of 112 research reports tied to the FDA's microwave oven standard reported biological effects in animals and humans at 10 milliwatts per square centimeter or less, and ten reported effects in animals at 0.1 or less. Officials from the FDA, the EPA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration and the National Telecommunications and Information Administration said the 10 milliwatt guideline needed reevaluation. The GAO recommended that the EPA and the Labor Department "establish mandatory standards to protect the public and workers from exposure to microwave radiation."
- November 4, 1994, "Telecommunications: Status of Research on the Safety of Cellular Telephones" (RCED-95-32): requested by Representative Edward J. Markey, with the review done from March 1993 to October 1994. It found that the FCC "does not consider itself a health agency," that the FDA "will not set" phone standards "without clear scientific evidence," and that the EPA had stopped its guidance work in 1988. It reported that in early 1993 phone makers agreed with the FDA to look at moving the antenna away from the head, and had "not reported back" by October 1994. It recommended that the FDA and the EPA, with the FCC, work with the industry's research group to make that research independent and objective.
- May 2001, "Telecommunications: Research and Regulatory Efforts on Mobile Phone Health Issues" (GAO-01-545): wrote that the phone limit "is not designed to address the possibility of any non-heating-related effects, such as cancer," and that the EPA's in-house radio-frequency research "was largely eliminated in the 1980s for budgetary reasons." It reported that the industry-funded group Wireless Technology Research spent about 28 million dollars over 5 years, that it "rarely solicited input from FDA and did not always follow the input that was given," and that "in the end, no federal agency had a role overseeing WTR's research activities."
- July 24, 2012, "Telecommunications: Exposure and Testing Requirements for Mobile Phones Should Be Reassessed" (GAO-12-771): found that the FCC "has not formally asked FDA or EPA for their assessment of the limit since 1996," and that using phones against the body, which the FCC did not test, could result in exposure higher than the FCC limit. It recommended that the FCC formally reassess its limit and its testing. The GAO closed both recommendations as "Not Implemented," writing: "Despite many years of consideration, FCC still has no specific plans to take any actions that would satisfy our recommendations."

What the GAO did not do: it did not conclude that phones are dangerous. In 1994 it reported that federal scientists said the research did not settle the question, and in 2012 it reported that research "has not demonstrated adverse human health effects," while finding that the FCC's limit "may not reflect the latest research." What it documented is that no agency took responsibility for answering the question.

RF Safe's position: for more than 45 years Congress's own auditor has found the same gap. The agencies with health authority did not set limits, and the agency that set them would not reassess them. RF Safe asks Congress to enforce Public Law 90-602 and require health agencies to answer the research on non-thermal effects, meaning biological effects at levels too low to heat tissue.

entries.title: Government Agencies: What is the FDA's role in cell phone radiation, and what has it said and removed over the years?
entries.question: What is the FDA's role in cell phone radiation, and what has it said and removed over the years?
entries.text:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is the agency that runs the federal program Congress created to control radiation from electronic products, including cell phones, but it has never set a radio-frequency safety standard for phones. For decades it told the public and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) that phones were safe. Between late 2025 and early 2026 it took down the detailed pages that said so.

The FDA's legal duty: Public Law 90-602, the Radiation Control for Health and Safety Act of 1968, covers "any ionizing or non-ionizing electromagnetic or particulate radiation" from an electronic product. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) described the FDA's job in 1994 as "developing and administering performance standards for electronic products" and research "to minimize the emissions of, and exposure of people to, unnecessary radiation from electronic products." The FDA does not approve phones before they are sold. In 2001 the GAO reported that the FDA can require a recall if a phone is shown to emit hazardous radiation.

What the FDA has done:
- It has a standard for microwave ovens. Federal rule 21 CFR 1030.10 limits oven leakage to 1 milliwatt per square centimeter at 5 centimeters from the oven before sale, and 5 milliwatts afterward. There is no comparable standard for phones.
- In 1978 the GAO reported that more than half of the 112 research reports tied to the FDA's oven standard found biological effects in animals and humans at 10 milliwatts per square centimeter or less, and ten found effects in animals at 0.1 or less. Officials from the FDA and three other agencies said the 10 milliwatt guideline needed to be reevaluated.
- In early 1993 the FDA met with phone makers, and they agreed to look at moving the antenna away from the head. The GAO reported in 1994 that the industry "had not reported back to FDA." For people who wanted to avoid even potential risks, the FDA's advice then was to hold lengthy conversations on regular phones and use hand-held cell phones for shorter calls. An FDA official told the GAO that recent research on low-level radio-frequency radiation from other sources "has the agency concerned about the possible adverse health effects of this type of radiation." The GAO reported that "FDA follows the principle that exposure to radiation should be kept to a level as low as can reasonably be achieved."
- In a December 12, 1994 letter to the FCC, the FDA cited studies showing that hand-held phones that met the old low-power exemption could exceed the 1.6 watts per kilogram limit. In one study, phones held against a model head reached about 8.8 watts per kilogram for each watt of output power, five and a half times the limit. That limit is a specific absorption rate (SAR), the rate at which the body absorbs a phone's radio energy. The FCC wrote in 1996: "Based on the concerns expressed by the FDA," it would not exempt low-power phones from the limit. Because of that decision, every phone must show it meets the SAR limit.
- The FDA nominated cell phone radiation for study by the National Toxicology Program (NTP). The NTP reported in 2018 "clear evidence" of malignant heart tumors (schwannomas) in male rats, and "some evidence" of malignant brain tumors (gliomas) and of adrenal gland tumors. The FDA's "Scientific Evidence for Cell Phone Safety" page, later removed, said its scientists' conclusions "differ from those of the NTP, and the FDA determination is that the study did not demonstrate that cell phones cause cancer."
- In an April 24, 2019 letter, the FDA told the FCC that "no changes to the current standards are warranted at this time." The FCC quoted that letter when it kept its 1996 limits.
- In 2021 a federal appeals court found the FDA's statements gave "no articulation of the factual . . . bases" for its conclusion. The court said they "represent a failure by the FDA to address the implication of Petitioners' studies: The factual premise—the non-existence of non-thermal biological effects—underlying the current RF guidelines may no longer be accurate."

What the FDA removed, as archived by the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine:
- "Do Cell Phones Pose a Health Hazard?" was last archived live on December 5, 2025, and was redirected by December 14, 2025. It said: "The available scientific data on exposure to radio frequency energy show no categorical proof of any adverse biological effects other than tissue heating."
- "Scientific Evidence for Cell Phone Safety" was last archived live on December 14, 2025, and was redirected by January 4, 2026. It said there was "no consistent or credible scientific evidence of health problems caused by the exposure to radio frequency energy emitted by cell phones."
- "Children and Teens and Cell Phones" was last archived live on December 14, 2025, and was redirected by December 20, 2025. It said: "Current scientific evidence does not show a danger to any users of cell phones from radio frequency (RF) energy, including children and teenagers." The same page told children and teens to "Avoid making calls when the signal is weak as this causes cell phones to boost RF transmission power" and to use "speaker mode, head phones, or ear buds to place more distance between the head and the cell phone."
- "Radio Frequency Radiation and Cell Phones" was last archived live on November 23, 2025, and was redirected by December 10, 2025. It said: "Scientific consensus shows that non-ionizing radiation is not a carcinogen."
- "Reducing Radio Frequency Exposure from Cell Phones" was last archived live on December 14, 2025, and was redirected by March 4, 2026. It said: "There is no established health benefit from reducing an individual's RF exposure from cell phones."
All five addresses now send visitors to the FDA's main Cell Phones page. On January 15, 2026, HHS spokesman Andrew Nixon told Reuters: "The FDA removed webpages with old conclusions about cell phone radiation while HHS undertakes a study on electromagnetic radiation and health research to identify gaps in knowledge, including on new technologies, to ensure safety and efficacy."

What is still up, as of November 15, 2026: the main Cell Phones page still says "The weight of scientific evidence has not linked cell phone radio frequency radiation with any health problems," and still says the evidence does not show a danger to children and teenagers. Those lines link to the pages that were removed. The FDA's February 2020 review, titled "Review of Published Literature between 2008 and 2018 of Relevance to Radiofrequency Radiation and Cancer," is still posted. The FCC's consumer page still sends readers to two of the removed FDA pages, "Scientific Evidence for Cell Phone Safety" and "Reducing Radio Frequency Exposure from Cell Phones." The FDA's own main page still links to all five removed addresses.

RF Safe's position: the FDA has retired its old conclusions. Public Law 90-602 says the HHS Secretary "shall establish and carry out an electronic product radiation control program designed to protect the public health and safety," including research "to minimize the emissions of and the exposure of people to, unnecessary electronic product radiation." RF Safe says that duty requires the FDA to replace the old conclusions with a position grounded in the research, including research on non-thermal effects. The same FDA approved the TheraBionic P1, a cancer treatment that works through a radio-frequency signal too weak to heat tissue.

entries.title: Government Agencies: Which U.S. government agencies are responsible for wireless radiation safety, and what has each one done?
entries.question: Which U.S. government agencies are responsible for wireless radiation safety, and what has each one done?
entries.text:
Five parts of the U.S. government have a role in wireless radiation safety, and none of the agencies with health authority has ever set a radio-frequency exposure limit for phones. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which manages the airwaves, wrote the limits in 1996, and it says it relies on the health agencies to tell it whether they are safe.

Who does what:
- Federal Communications Commission (FCC): sets the exposure limits and approves every phone before it is sold.
- Food and Drug Administration (FDA): runs the federal program to control radiation from electronic products, including phones, under Public Law 90-602, the Radiation Control for Health and Safety Act of 1968.
- Department of Health and Human Services (HHS): the department that holds the FDA, the National Toxicology Program (NTP), the National Cancer Institute and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. The law gives the duty to the HHS Secretary.
- Environmental Protection Agency (EPA): has federal authority to recommend radiation protection guidance to the President and all federal agencies. It ran a radio-frequency research program from the early 1970s until 1987.
- Government Accountability Office (GAO): the investigative arm of Congress. It has reported on these agencies' handling of radio-frequency radiation since 1978.

What the record shows:
- The FCC says it is not a health agency. The GAO reported in 1994: "FCC does not consider itself a health agency and turns to health and radiation experts outside the agency for guidance on these issues."
- The health agencies did not set a limit. The EPA proposed federal radio-frequency guidance in 1986 and dropped the effort in 1988. In 1994 the GAO reported that the FDA "will not set them without clear scientific evidence that an electronic product poses a hazard to human health," meaning performance standards for phones.
- The limits cover heating only. The GAO wrote in 2001: "the exposure limit is not designed to address the possibility of any non-heating-related effects, such as cancer." In 2002 an EPA radiation official wrote that the FCC's limits "are thermally based, and do not apply to chronic, nonthermal exposure situations." The federal appeals court wrote in 2021: "The limits are designed to protect against 'thermal effects' of exposure to RF radiation, but not 'non-thermal' effects."
- Congress's auditor asked for a review, and the FCC never completed one. In 2012 the GAO told the FCC to formally reassess its limit and its testing of phones held against the body. The FCC opened an inquiry in March 2013, then closed it in 2019 without changing the limit or the test. The GAO closed both recommendations as "Not Implemented," writing: "Despite many years of consideration, FCC still has no specific plans to take any actions that would satisfy our recommendations."
- A court found the FDA's word was not enough. In 2021 a federal appeals court found that the FCC relied on the FDA's "conclusory statements." The court wrote that the FCC "may turn to the FDA to provide such an explanation, but if the FDA fails to do so, as it did in this case, the Commission must turn elsewhere or provide its own explanation."
- The FDA retired its old conclusions. Between late 2025 and early 2026 the FDA took down its detailed cell phone safety pages, and in January 2026 an HHS spokesman called them "old conclusions."

RF Safe's position: the agencies with health expertise stepped back, and the agency that sells the airwaves set heating-only limits. Public Law 90-602 already gives HHS the duty to study electronic product radiation and to reduce unnecessary exposure. RF Safe asks HHS and the EPA to lead on health, with limits that account for non-thermal effects, meaning biological effects at levels too low to heat tissue, and asks that the FCC remain the spectrum manager. RF Safe does not claim that phones directly cause disease. It says the agencies have a duty to follow the research on non-thermal effects.

Our support covers orders placed on the QuantaCase website (quantacase.com).

entries.title: Orders and Shipping: Where is my order?
entries.question: Where is my order?
entries.text:
Thanks for reaching out about your order. We want to get it to you as soon as possible.

If you already sent your order number or the email used on the order, thank you. Our team will look up your order and reply with its status and tracking information.

If not, please reply with your order number. You can find it in your original order confirmation email or on the packing slip that came with your product. If you can't find it, reply with the name, email address, and phone number used when the order was placed, and our team will look up your order details and get back to you with the status.

Orders ship by USPS from Seminole, Florida. Most arrive in about 1 to 3 business days on the East Coast and 4 to 6 business days on the West Coast. USPS says its standard service takes 2 to 5 business days.

For now, orders ship only within the United States.

entries.title: Does a phone give off radiation when not on a call (standby, in pocket, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on)?
entries.question: Does a phone give off radiation when not on a call (standby, in pocket, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on)?
entries.text: Does my phone give off radiation when I'm not on a call? Yes. Even when you're not on a call, your phone still sends short signals now and then to stay connected to the cell tower, and Wi-Fi and Bluetooth also send signals while they're on. These signals are usually shorter and less frequent than during a call, but they don't stop. To cut down on them, turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth when you're not using them, because having them on at the same time as the cell signal raises your phone's SAR, which is how fast your body absorbs the phone's radio energy. Keep the phone off your body when you can. The QuantaCase puts thin shielding only in the front flap, between you and the screen, so the phone's antenna isn't blocked and the phone doesn't raise its power. Carry it with the flap facing your body. It isn't complete protection; it works best with distance and good habits.

body_systems.name: Brain and nerves
body_systems.summary: Nervous system: 1062 of the 1391 studies tagged here report a biological change from electromagnetic exposure: 437 harm, 516 mixed and 109 benefit. Another 134 found no effect. Phone safety limits are set to prevent heating. Heating is a known issue, but many of these studies found changes at levels below heating, and that is the part the "phones are safe" story leaves out. Findings here include brain tumors in rats exposed at cell-phone frequencies, memory changes in teenagers that followed the radio dose to the head, and reactive glial cells and oxidative stress at absorption levels at or below phone limits. A benefit finding is not neutral. It is still an alteration of normal biology caused by the exposure, which shows the tissue is not inert. RF Safe's hypothesis, called low-fidelity biology, is that cells keep working, but with more timing error and less complete repair, which raises the risk of error over time. That is a hypothesis, not proof that a phone caused anyone's illness. Use the filters below to sort by effect and evidence.
